paragraphs: The paper asks how many words an associative memory can store while reliably retrieving them from imperfect addresses. Reliability is defined through a sphere of attraction: addresses within a specified Hamming distance of a stored address should recover its contents. Capacity is therefore tied to the fraction of address errors the memory must correct.

Using sphere-packing arguments, the authors establish an exponential upper growth rate as address length increases. The rate is one minus the binary entropy of the permitted error fraction. They show that Kanerva's memory can achieve this growth when its parameters are set optimally, and provide formulas for those settings.

The capacity definition concerns most address-and-data sequences in a probabilistic sense, because arbitrary sequences can create unavoidable conflicts, such as different contents assigned to the same address. Within that definition, the exponential result contrasts with the stated sublinear capacity growth of Hopfield memory. The significance is a capacity claim with both a specified retrieval tolerance and an explicit condition on parameter choice.
summary.tldr: With optimal parameters, Kanerva memory achieves exponential capacity growth under a probabilistic, error-tolerant retrieval definition.

title: The Capacity of the Kanerva Associative Memory is Exponential

abstract: In the present paper we survey and utilize results from the qualitative theory of large scale interconnected dynamical systems in order to develop a qualitative theory for the Hopfield model of neural networks. In our approach we view such networks as an inter(cid:173) connection of many single neurons. Our results are phrased in terms of the qualitative properties of the individual neurons and in terms of the properties of the interconnecting structure of the neural networks. Aspects of neural networks which we address include asymptotic stability, exponential stability, and instability of an equilibrium; estimates of trajectory bounds; estimates of the domain of attraction of an asymptotically stable equilibrium; and stability of neural networks under structural perturbations.

paragraphs: The paper develops a qualitative theory of Hopfield networks using results about large interconnected dynamical systems. It views a network as many individual neurons linked together. The resulting analysis expresses network behavior through properties of the neurons and the structure of their interconnections.

Several questions concern what happens near an equilibrium, a state that remains unchanged under the network dynamics. The paper addresses asymptotic stability, exponential stability, and instability. These distinguish whether nearby states approach an equilibrium, whether that approach has an exponential rate, or whether the equilibrium fails to retain nearby trajectories.

The analysis also estimates bounds on trajectories and the domain of attraction of a stable equilibrium: the set of starting states that move toward it. Finally, it considers stability when network structure is perturbed. Together, these results connect local component properties with the behavior of the complete system. This provides a mathematical framework for asking where a network can move, which states it can settle into, and how those conclusions depend on its connections.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes Hopfield-network stability through individual neuron properties and the structure of their interconnections.

title: Stability Results for Neural Networks

abstract: Seven different pattern classifiers were implemented on a serial computer and compared using artificial and speech recognition tasks. Two neural network (radial basis function and high order polynomial GMDH network) and five conventional classifiers (Gaussian mixture, linear tree, K nearest neighbor, KD-tree, and condensed K nearest neighbor) were evaluated. Classifiers were chosen to be representative of different approaches to pat(cid:173) tern classification and to complement and extend those evaluated in a previous study (Lee and Lippmann, 1989). This and the previous study both demonstrate that classification error rates can be equivalent across different classifiers when they are powerful enough to form minimum er(cid:173) ror decision regions, when they are properly tuned, and when sufficient training data is available. Practical characteristics such as training time, classification time, and memory requirements, however, can differ by or(cid:173) ders of magnitude. These results suggest that the selection of a classifier for a particular task should be guided not so much by small differences in error rate, but by practical considerations concerning memory usage, com(cid:173) putational resources, ease of implementation, and restrictions on training and classification times.

paragraphs: The paper compares seven pattern classifiers on artificial tasks and speech recognition, with all implementations running on a serial computer. The comparison includes two neural approaches, radial basis functions and a high-order polynomial GMDH network, alongside Gaussian mixtures, linear trees, nearest-neighbor methods, and a KD-tree. This range makes the study a comparison of different ways to organize classification.

Its central finding is that different classifiers can reach equivalent error rates under three conditions: they can represent the required decision regions, they are properly tuned, and they receive enough training data. The result is conditional: it does not say that every classifier works equally well on every task.

Even when prediction errors are similar, training time, classification time, and memory use can differ by orders of magnitude. The practical implication is that classifier selection should account for deployment constraints. A small accuracy difference may matter less than whether a system fits available memory, trains within the allotted time, or responds quickly enough.
summary.tldr: Classifiers can achieve similar accuracy while differing dramatically in speed and memory requirements.

title: A Comparative Study of the Practical Characteristics of Neural Network and Conventional Pattern Classifiers

abstract: Maps of orientation preference and ocular dominance were recorded optically from the cortices of 5 infant macaque monkeys, ranging in age from 3.5 to 14 weeks. In agreement with previous observations, we found that basic features of orientation and ocular dominance maps, as well as correlations between them, are present and robust by 3.5 weeks of age. We did observe changes in the strength of ocular dominance signals, as well as in the spacing of ocular dom(cid:173) inance bands, both of which increased steadily between 3.5 and 14 weeks of age. The latter finding suggests that the adult spacing of ocular dominance bands depends on cortical growth in neonatal animals. Since we found no corresponding increase in the spacing of orientation preferences, however, there is a possibility that the orientation preferences of some cells change as the cortical surface expands. Since correlations between the patterns of orientation selectivity and ocular dominance are present at an age, when the visual system is still immature, it seems more likely that their de(cid:173) velopment may be an innate process and may not require extensive visual experience.

paragraphs: The researchers used optical recordings to map orientation preference and ocular dominance in five infant macaques aged 3.5 to 14 weeks. These maps describe cortical preferences for visual orientation and input from either eye. Basic features of both maps, together with relationships between them, were already robust at the youngest age examined.

Development nevertheless changed some aspects of the maps. Ocular dominance signals strengthened, and the spacing between ocular dominance bands increased steadily across the age range. The authors interpret the spacing change as evidence that neonatal cortical growth contributes to the eventual adult spacing of these bands.

Orientation preference spacing did not show a corresponding increase. This difference raises the possibility that some cells change orientation preference as the cortical surface expands. The early presence of relationships between the two map types also favors the possibility of an innate developmental process without extensive visual experience. These are interpretations supported by the observed patterns, rather than direct demonstrations of cell preference changes or experience-independent development.
summary.tldr: Infant macaques already show organized visual cortical maps, while subsequent growth affects ocular dominance spacing differently from orientation spacing.

title: Development of Orientation and Ocular Dominance Columns in Infant Macaques

abstract: In the present paper, we propose a method to unify information maximization and minimization in hidden units. The information maximization and minimization are performed on two different lev(cid:173) els: collective and individual level. Thus, two kinds of information: collective and individual information are defined. By maximizing collective information and by minimizing individual information, simple networks can be generated in terms of the number of con(cid:173) nections and the number of hidden units. Obtained networks are expected to give better generalization and improved interpretation of internal representations. This method was applied to the infer(cid:173) ence of the maximum onset principle of an artificial language. In this problem, it was shown that the individual information min(cid:173) imization is not contradictory to the collective information max(cid:173) imization. In addition, experimental results confirmed improved generalization performance, because over-training can significantly be suppressed.

paragraphs: Maximizing and minimizing information can sound like opposing goals. This paper combines them by applying them at different levels of a neural network's hidden representation. It defines collective information for the hidden units together and individual information for units considered separately, allowing the two objectives to play distinct roles.

The method maximizes collective information while minimizing individual information. The authors argue that this can produce simpler networks with fewer connections and hidden units. They expect that simplification to support better generalization and more interpretable internal representations. The key idea is that preserving useful information across the group can coexist with reducing the information attributed to individual components.

The method is applied to learning the maximum onset principle in an artificial language. In that task, the results show that individual information minimization is compatible with collective information maximization. Experiments also confirm improved generalization through substantial suppression of over-training. The findings support the proposed compatibility and connect the information objectives to a demonstrated improvement in learning behavior.
summary.tldr: Maximizing collective hidden-unit information while minimizing individual information produces simpler networks and improves generalization on an artificial-language task.

title: Unification of Information Maximization and Minimization

abstract: We are frequently called upon to perform multiple tasks that com(cid:173) pete for our attention and resource. Often we know the optimal solution to each task in isolation; in this paper, we describe how this knowledge can be exploited to efficiently find good solutions for doing the tasks in parallel. We formulate this problem as that of dynamically merging multiple Markov decision processes (MDPs) into a composite MDP, and present a new theoretically-sound dy(cid:173) namic programming algorithm for finding an optimal policy for the composite MDP. We analyze various aspects of our algorithm and illustrate its use on a simple merging problem. Every day, we are faced with the problem of doing mUltiple tasks in parallel, each of which competes for our attention and resource. If we are running a job shop, we must decide which machines to allocate to which jobs, and in what order, so that no jobs miss their deadlines. If we are a mail delivery robot, we must find the intended recipients of the mail while simultaneously avoiding fixed obstacles (such as walls) and mobile obstacles (such as people), and still manage to keep ourselves sufficiently charged up. Frequently we know how to perform each task in isolation; this paper considers how we can take the information we have about the individual tasks and combine it to efficiently find an optimal solution for doing the entire set of tasks in parallel. More importantly, we describe a theoretically-sound algorithm for doing this merging dynamically; new tasks (such as a new job arrival at a job shop) can be assimilated online into the solution being found for the ongoing set of simultaneous tasks.

paragraphs: Knowing how to perform several tasks separately does not immediately tell an agent how to perform them together. Tasks may compete for attention or resources, making their individual solutions incompatible. This paper asks how existing knowledge of separate tasks can help solve the combined decision problem efficiently.

The authors represent each task as a Markov decision process and merge these into a composite process. They introduce a theoretically grounded dynamic programming algorithm for finding an optimal policy for that composite problem. The approach uses information about the individual tasks to support decisions about the entire collection.

A central feature is that merging can happen dynamically: new tasks can be incorporated online while a solution for ongoing tasks is being developed. The paper analyzes the algorithm and illustrates it with a simple merging example. Its significance lies in treating changing workloads as structured combinations of decision problems, so that knowledge of individual tasks remains useful when the set of simultaneous responsibilities changes.
summary.tldr: A dynamic programming algorithm combines individual task models into an optimal joint policy and can incorporate new tasks online.

title: How to Dynamically Merge Markov Decision Processes

abstract: This paper presents a novel and fast k-NN classifier that is based on a binary CMM (Correlation Matrix Memory) neural network. A robust encoding method is developed to meet CMM input requirements . A hardware implementation of the CMM is described, which gives over 200 times the speed of a current mid-range workstation, and is scaleable to very large problems. When tested on several benchmarks and compared with a simple k-NN method, the CMM classifier gave less than I % lower accuracy and over 4 and 12 times speed-up in software and hardware respectively.

A robust encoding method is developed to meet CMM input requirements . A hardware implementation of the CMM is described, which gives over 200 times the speed of a current mid-range workstation, and is scaleable to very large problems. When tested on several benchmarks and compared with a simple k-NN method, the CMM classifier gave less than I % lower accuracy and over 4 and 12 times speed-up in software and hardware respectively.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a fast nearest-neighbor classifier built around a binary Correlation Matrix Memory, or CMM, neural network. The central engineering challenge is making classification data fit the memory's binary input requirements. The authors develop a robust encoding method to support this step, connecting the classifier's input representation to the machinery that performs the computation.

The work includes both software and hardware implementations. The dedicated CMM hardware is reported to run more than 200 times faster than a contemporary mid-range workstation and to scale to very large problems. That hardware comparison is distinct from the reported speed improvements for the complete classification method on benchmark tasks.

Against a simple k-nearest-neighbor method on several benchmarks, the CMM classifier has less than 1% lower accuracy while providing speedups exceeding four times in software and twelve times in hardware. These results describe an empirical accuracy–speed tradeoff: the new representation and implementation substantially accelerate classification while retaining accuracy close to the comparison method on the tested tasks.
summary.tldr: A binary memory-based nearest-neighbor classifier achieves substantial benchmark speedups with less than 1% lower accuracy than a simple k-NN method.

title: A High Performance k-NN Classifier Using a Binary Correlation Matrix Memory

abstract: Competitive learning is a technique for training classification and clustering networks. We have designed and fabricated an 11- transistor primitive, that we term an automaximizing bump circuit, that implements competitive learning dynamics. The circuit per(cid:173) forms a similarity computation, affords nonvolatile storage, and implements simultaneous local adaptation and computation. We show that our primitive is suitable for implementing competitive learning in VLSI, and demonstrate its effectiveness in a standard clustering task.
originalAbstract: Competitive learning is a technique for training classification and clustering networks. We have designed and fabricated an 11- transistor primitive, that we term an automaximizing bump circuit, that implements competitive learning dynamics. The circuit per(cid:173) forms a similarity computation, affords nonvolatile storage, and implements simultaneous local adaptation and computation. We show that our primitive is suitable for implementing competitive learning in VLSI, and demonstrate its effectiveness in a standard clustering task.

paragraphs: Competitive learning trains networks for classification and clustering through competition among their units. This paper puts the learning dynamics into a small physical circuit. The authors designed and fabricated an eleven-transistor building block, called an automaximizing bump circuit, that carries out the operations needed for this kind of learning.

The circuit combines three capabilities: computing similarity, retaining information in nonvolatile storage, and adapting locally while computation continues. Similarity provides the comparison needed to organize inputs, while storage preserves the circuit's learned state. Combining adaptation and computation in the same primitive makes learning part of the hardware's ongoing operation, rather than a separate activity performed elsewhere.

The authors show that this primitive is suitable for implementing competitive learning in very-large-scale integrated circuits and demonstrate its effectiveness on a standard clustering task. The result connects a fabricated transistor-level design to a recognizable learning problem. Its significance is the demonstration that one compact circuit can support both the computations and the local changes involved in competitive learning.
summary.tldr: An eleven-transistor circuit combines similarity computation, persistent storage, and local adaptation to implement competitive learning in hardware.

title: A Silicon Primitive for Competitive Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of reconstructing patterns from a feature map. Learning algorithms using kernels to operate in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) express their solutions in terms of input points mapped into the RKHS. We introduce a technique based on kernel princi- pal component analysis and regression to reconstruct corresponding pat- terns in the input space (aka pre-images) and review its performance in several applications requiring the construction of pre-images. The intro- duced technique avoids difﬁcult and/or unstable numerical optimization, is easy to implement and, unlike previous methods, permits the compu- tation of pre-images in discrete input spaces.

We introduce a technique based on kernel princi- pal component analysis and regression to reconstruct corresponding pat- terns in the input space (aka pre-images) and review its performance in several applications requiring the construction of pre-images. The intro- duced technique avoids difﬁcult and/or unstable numerical optimization, is easy to implement and, unlike previous methods, permits the compu- tation of pre-images in discrete input spaces.

paragraphs: Kernel learning methods express their solutions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, where input patterns have been mapped into a feature representation. Some applications also need a corresponding pattern back in the original input space. This reconstruction problem is called finding a pre-image, and it is the focus of the paper.

The authors introduce a technique that combines kernel principal component analysis with regression to reconstruct input-space patterns. The approach makes reconstruction a learning problem. It avoids difficult or unstable numerical optimization and is described as easy to implement, addressing practical obstacles that can arise when trying to recover an input from a feature-space result.

A distinctive capability is computing pre-images in discrete input spaces, which the authors contrast with previous methods. This extends where the reconstruction technique can be used. The paper reviews its performance across several applications requiring pre-images. Its contribution is thus a practical connection between kernel-space solutions and usable input-space patterns, including settings where inputs take discrete values.
summary.tldr: Kernel PCA and regression provide a practical way to reconstruct input patterns from kernel features, including in discrete input spaces.

title: Learning to Find Pre-Images

abstract: We propose an information-theoretic clustering approach that incorporates a pre-known partition of the data, aiming to identify common clusters that cut across the given partition. In the standard clustering setting the formation of clusters is guided by a single source of feature information. The newly utilized pre-partition factor introduces an additional bias that counterbalances the impact of the features whenever they become correlated with this known partition. The resulting algorithmic framework was applied successfully to synthetic data, as well as to identifying text-based cross-religion correspondences.
originalAbstract: We propose an information-theoretic clustering approach that incorporates a pre-known partition of the data, aiming to identify common clusters that cut across the given partition. In the standard clustering setting the formation of clusters is guided by a single source of feature information. The newly utilized pre-partition factor introduces an additional bias that counterbalances the impact of the features whenever they become correlated with this known partition. The resulting algorithmic framework was applied successfully to synthetic data, as well as to identifying text-based cross-religion correspondences.

paragraphs: The paper considers clustering data that already comes divided into known groups. The goal is to discover common structure that crosses those existing divisions. A clustering method guided only by the observed features can instead follow the known partition when those features are correlated with group membership.

The proposed information-theoretic approach explicitly incorporates the existing partition. It adds a source of bias that counterbalances feature information when that information aligns with the known groups. The known division therefore helps guide the search toward shared clusters across groups, rather than serving simply as another set of labels to reproduce.

The authors report successful applications to synthetic data and to finding text-based correspondences across religions. The latter application illustrates the intended use: identifying relationships that connect material from different predefined categories. The broader contribution is a clustering framework in which prior knowledge of a partition changes what counts as useful structure, making cross-group commonalities an explicit objective of the analysis.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic clustering method uses known group divisions to uncover common structure that cuts across them.

title: Identifying Structure across Pre-partitioned Data

abstract: Although non-parametric tests have already been proposed for that purpose, statistical significance tests for non-standard measures (different from the classification error) are less often used in the literature. This paper is an attempt at empirically verifying how these tests compare with more classical tests, on various conditions. More precisely, using a very large dataset to estimate the whole "population", we analyzed the behavior of several statistical test, varying the class unbalance, the compared models, the performance measure, and the sample size. The main result is that providing big enough evaluation sets non-parametric tests are relatively reliable in all conditions.

This paper is an attempt at empirically verifying how these tests compare with more classical tests, on various conditions. More precisely, using a very large dataset to estimate the whole "population", we analyzed the behavior of several statistical test, varying the class unbalance, the compared models, the performance measure, and the sample size. paragraphs: This paper examines how reliably statistical tests compare predictive models when performance is measured using something other than classification error. Nonparametric tests had already been proposed for such comparisons, but the authors note that significance testing for these alternative measures was less common. Their goal is an empirical comparison with more classical tests across varied conditions.

The study uses a very large dataset to approximate the full population against which test behavior can be assessed. It varies class imbalance, the models being compared, the performance measure, and evaluation sample size. This design examines whether the usefulness of a statistical test persists as several important features of the comparison change.

The main finding is conditional: with sufficiently large evaluation sets, nonparametric tests are relatively reliable across all examined conditions. Evaluation size is therefore central to interpreting the result. The study provides empirical support for using these tests with a broader range of performance measures, while keeping that support tied to adequate evaluation data and the conditions investigated.
summary.tldr: Nonparametric significance tests were relatively reliable across the studied conditions when evaluation sets were sufficiently large.

title: Benchmarking Non-Parametric Statistical Tests

abstract: There is experimental evidence that cortical neurons show avalanche activity with the intensity of firing events being distributed as a power-law. We present a biologically plausible extension of a neural network which exhibits a power-law avalanche distribution for a wide range of connectivity parameters.
originalAbstract: There is experimental evidence that cortical neurons show avalanche activity with the intensity of firing events being distributed as a power-law. We present a biologically plausible extension of a neural network which exhibits a power-law avalanche distribution for a wide range of connectivity parameters.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a statistical pattern observed in cortical activity: neuronal firing can occur in avalanches whose event intensities follow a power-law distribution. The modeling question is how a neural network can produce this kind of collective activity. The authors present a biologically plausible extension of a neural network, with dynamical synapses identified as the central mechanism in the title.

The stated finding is that the extended network exhibits a power-law avalanche distribution across a wide range of connectivity parameters. The breadth of that range matters because connectivity determines how activity can pass through the network. The result indicates that the reported distribution is compatible with multiple connectivity settings within the proposed model.

The contribution is a model-based explanation for a feature of neuronal avalanche activity that has experimental support. Its strength lies in connecting biologically motivated network dynamics to the observed distributional pattern. The model establishes that such behavior can arise in the proposed setting; the abstract does not claim that dynamical synapses are the unique explanation for cortical avalanches.
summary.tldr: A biologically plausible neural network with dynamical synapses produces power-law avalanche activity across a wide range of connectivity parameters.

title: Dynamical Synapses Give Rise to a Power-Law Distribution of Neuronal Avalanches

abstract: A new bottom-up visual saliency model, Graph-Based Visual Saliency (GBVS), is proposed. It consists of two steps: rst forming activation maps on certain feature channels, and then normalizing them in a way which highlights conspicuity and admits combination with other maps. The model is simple, and biologically plausible insofar as it is naturally parallelized. This model powerfully predicts human xations on 749 variations of 108 natural images, achieving 98% of the ROC area of a human-based control, whereas the classical algorithms of Itti & Koch ([2], [3], [4]) achieve only 84%.

The paper organizes this process into two stages: creating activation maps for selected feature channels, then normalizing those maps. The normalization emphasizes conspicuous locations and makes the different maps suitable for combination.

This design places map processing at the center of the saliency calculation. Each channel contributes an activation map, and normalization prepares those separate contributions for a combined prediction. The authors describe the model as simple and biologically plausible in the specific sense that its computation can naturally run in parallel.

Evaluation uses human fixation data for 749 variations of 108 natural images. The model reaches 98% of the ROC area obtained by a human-based control, compared with 84% for the classical Itti and Koch algorithms. These percentages compare ROC areas, rather than reporting the percentage of fixations predicted correctly. The result supports the model's ability to predict human viewing patterns on the evaluated image set.
summary.tldr: GBVS combines normalized feature activation maps to predict human fixations, reaching 98% of a human-based control's ROC area in the reported evaluation.

title: Graph-Based Visual Saliency

abstract: One of the intuitions underlying many graph-based methods for clustering and semi-supervised learning, is that class or cluster boundaries pass through areas of low probability density. In this paper we provide some formal analysis of that notion for a probability distribution. We introduce a notion of weighted boundary volume, which measures the length of the class/cluster boundary weighted by the density of the underlying probability distribution. We show that sizes of the cuts of certain commonly used data adjacency graphs converge to this continuous weighted volume of the boundary. keywords: Clustering, Semi-Supervised Learning

paragraphs: Many graph-based clustering and semi-supervised learning methods draw on the intuition that boundaries should pass through regions where the underlying data distribution has low density. This paper gives a formal analysis of that idea. It asks how a cut in a graph built from data relates to a boundary in the probability distribution itself.

The authors introduce weighted boundary volume, which measures boundary length while accounting for the density along it. This quantity combines the geometry of the boundary with the amount of probability density it crosses. It provides a continuous object against which the discrete graph-cut quantity can be compared.

The central result shows that cut sizes for certain commonly used data adjacency graphs converge to this density-weighted boundary volume. This establishes a mathematical connection between graph cuts and the low-density-separation intuition. The restriction to particular graph constructions matters: the result identifies a relationship for those graphs, rather than asserting that every graph-based clustering procedure necessarily finds an appropriate low-density boundary.
summary.tldr: For certain data graphs, cut sizes converge to density-weighted boundary volume, formalizing a link to low-density separation.

title: On the Relation Between Low Density Separation, Spectral Clustering and Graph Cuts

abstract: The expectation maximization (EM) algorithm is a widely used maximum likelihood estimation procedure for statistical models when the values of some of the variables in the model are not observed. Very often, however, our aim is primarily to find a model that assigns values to the latent variables that have intended meaning for our data and maximizing expected likelihood only sometimes accomplishes this. Unfortunately, it is typically difficult to add even simple a-priori information about latent variables in graphical models without making the models overly complex or intractable. In this paper, we present an efficient, principled way to inject rich constraints on the posteriors of latent variables into the EM algorithm. Our method can be used to learn tractable graphical models that satisfy additional, otherwise intractable constraints. Focusing on clustering and the alignment problem for statistical machine translation, we show that simple, intuitive posterior constraints can greatly improve the performance over standard baselines and be competitive with more complex, intractable models.

paragraphs: Expectation maximization learns statistical models when some variables are unobserved. However, fitting the observed data well does not always make those hidden variables take on the meanings a practitioner intends. Prior knowledge about their behavior could help, but encoding even simple requirements directly in a graphical model can make computation difficult.

This paper introduces an efficient way to incorporate constraints on the posterior distributions of latent variables into EM. These distributions express what the model infers about hidden variables after seeing data. Constraining them lets the learning procedure use additional knowledge while retaining a tractable graphical model, including requirements that would otherwise be intractable to impose.

The authors demonstrate the approach in clustering and word alignment for statistical machine translation. Simple, intuitive posterior constraints substantially improve performance over standard baselines and achieve results competitive with more complex, intractable models. The findings show that guiding the interpretation of hidden variables can materially improve learning without requiring the underlying model to absorb all that knowledge through added complexity.
summary.tldr: Adding posterior constraints to EM guides latent variables toward intended meanings while preserving tractable models and improving the evaluated tasks.

title: Expectation Maximization and Posterior Constraints

abstract: This paper proposes constraint propagation relaxation (CPR), a probabilistic approach to classical constraint propagation that provides another view on the whole parametric family of survey propagation algorithms SP(ρ), ranging from belief propagation (ρ = 0) to (pure) survey propagation(ρ = 1). More importantly, the approach elucidates the implicit, but fundamental assumptions underlying SP(ρ), thus shedding some light on its effectiveness and leading to applications beyond k-SAT.
originalAbstract: This paper proposes constraint propagation relaxation (CPR), a probabilistic approach to classical constraint propagation that provides another view on the whole parametric family of survey propagation algorithms SP(ρ), ranging from belief propagation (ρ = 0) to (pure) survey propagation(ρ = 1). More importantly, the approach elucidates the implicit, but fundamental assumptions underlying SP(ρ), thus shedding some light on its effectiveness and leading to applications beyond k-SAT.

paragraphs: Constraint satisfaction problems ask for assignments that obey a collection of constraints. Constraint propagation uses those constraints to restrict possible assignments. This paper proposes constraint propagation relaxation, or CPR, which gives a probabilistic treatment of that process and uses it to reinterpret a family of survey propagation algorithms.

The family is indexed by a parameter, rho. At rho equal to zero, it corresponds to belief propagation; at rho equal to one, it corresponds to pure survey propagation. CPR supplies another way to understand the entire family between these endpoints. Its contribution is therefore a common conceptual account of algorithms connected by this parameter.

The authors emphasize that the interpretation makes fundamental, previously implicit assumptions behind the family more explicit. Clarifying those assumptions helps explain its effectiveness and leads to applications beyond k-SAT. The stated significance is explanatory and methodological: understanding the basis of survey propagation can guide its use in a wider range of constraint problems, rather than treating it only as a procedure associated with one problem class.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic view of constraint propagation clarifies the assumptions behind the survey propagation family and enables applications beyond k-SAT.

title: CPR for CSPs: A Probabilistic Relaxation of Constraint Propagation

abstract: We introduce a kernel-based method for change-point analysis within a sequence of temporal observations. Change-point analysis of an (unlabelled) sample of observations consists in, first, testing whether a change in the distribution occurs within the sample, and second, if a change occurs, estimating the change-point instant after which the distribution of the observations switches from one distribution to another different distribution. We propose a test statistics based upon the maximum kernel Fisher discriminant ratio as a measure of homogeneity between segments. We derive its limiting distribution under the null hypothesis (no change occurs), and establish the consistency under the alternative hypothesis (a change occurs). This allows to build a statistical hypothesis testing procedure for testing the presence of change-point, with a prescribed false-alarm probability and detection probability tending to one in the large-sample setting. If a change actually occurs, the test statistics also yields an estimator of the change-point location. Promising experimental results in temporal segmentation of mental tasks from BCI data and pop song indexation are presented.

paragraphs: Change-point analysis asks whether a sequence's observations switch from one distribution to another and, if so, when that switch occurs. This paper proposes a kernel-based method that addresses both questions using unlabeled temporal data. Its test statistic uses the maximum kernel Fisher discriminant ratio to assess differences between candidate segments.

The authors derive the statistic's limiting distribution when no change is present. They also establish consistency when a change does occur. These results support a hypothesis test with a prescribed false-alarm probability and a probability of detecting a change that approaches one as the sample size grows. The latter guarantee is explicitly a large-sample result.

When there is a distributional change, the same statistic supplies an estimate of its location. The authors present promising experiments on segmenting mental tasks from brain-computer-interface data and indexing pop songs. The contribution joins detection and localization in one statistical framework, with theory describing its asymptotic behavior and experiments illustrating its use on temporal segmentation problems.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based statistic detects and locates distribution changes, with false-alarm calibration and large-sample consistency.

title: Kernel Change-point Analysis

abstract: Aiming towards the development of a general clustering theory, we discuss abstract axiomatization for clustering. In this respect, we follow up on the work of Kelinberg, (Kleinberg) that showed an impossibility result for such axiomatization. We argue that an impossibility result is not an inherent feature of clustering, but rather, to a large extent, it is an artifact of the specific formalism used in Kleinberg. As opposed to previous work focusing on clustering functions, we propose to address clustering quality measures as the primitive object to be axiomatized. We show that principles like those formulated in Kleinberg's axioms can be readily expressed in the latter framework without leading to inconsistency. A clustering-quality measure is a function that, given a data set and its partition into clusters, returns a non-negative real number representing how strong' or conclusive' the clustering is. We analyze what clustering-quality measures should look like and introduce a set of requirements (`axioms') that express these requirement and extend the translation of Kleinberg's axioms to our framework. We propose several natural clustering quality measures, all satisfying the proposed axioms. In addition, we show that the proposed clustering quality can be computed in polynomial time.

paragraphs: A general theory of clustering needs clear statements about what makes a grouping good. Earlier axiomatic work produced an impossibility result for clustering functions, which map data to a partition. This paper argues that the difficulty depends substantially on that formal choice and proposes starting with measures of clustering quality instead.

A quality measure takes both a dataset and a proposed partition, then returns a nonnegative number describing how strong or conclusive that grouping is. This changes the object being evaluated: the theory specifies properties of a score for a given clustering. The authors translate principles resembling the earlier axioms into this framework and add further requirements for meaningful quality measures.

They show that the resulting requirements are consistent by presenting several natural measures that satisfy them. They also establish polynomial-time computation for the proposed clustering quality. The contribution therefore combines a conceptual reformulation with concrete mathematical constructions. It shows that these clustering principles can coexist within a quality-measure framework, giving a workable foundation for discussing the strength of proposed partitions.
summary.tldr: Axiomatizing clustering quality scores yields consistent principles and efficiently computable measures despite an earlier impossibility result for clustering functions.

title: Measures of Clustering Quality: A Working Set of Axioms for Clustering

abstract: In a recent paper Joachims (2006) presented SVM-Perf, a cutting plane method (CPM) for training linear Support Vector Machines (SVMs) which converges to an $\epsilon$ accurate solution in $O(1/\epsilon^{2})$ iterations. By tightening the analysis, Teo et al. (2010) showed that $O(1/\epsilon)$ iterations suffice. Given the impressive convergence speed of CPM on a number of practical problems, it was conjectured that these rates could be further improved. In this paper we disprove this conjecture. We present counter examples which are not only applicable for training linear SVMs with hinge loss, but also hold for support vector methods which optimize a \emph{multivariate} performance score. However, surprisingly, these problems are not inherently hard. By exploiting the structure of the objective function we can devise an algorithm that converges in $O(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ iterations.

paragraphs: Cutting-plane methods can train linear support vector machines quickly in practice, raising the question of whether their theoretical convergence rates are overly pessimistic. An earlier analysis required O(1/ε²) iterations to obtain an ε-accurate solution, and a tighter analysis reduced this to O(1/ε). This paper investigates whether that latter rate can be improved further.

The authors construct counterexamples that disprove the conjectured improvement for the cutting-plane methods under consideration. Their examples apply both to linear SVM training with hinge loss and to support vector methods optimizing multivariate performance scores. The result places a worst-case limit on these methods despite their strong behavior on many practical problems.

The same optimization problems nevertheless admit a faster approach. By exploiting the structure of the objective, the authors devise an algorithm converging in O(1/√ε) iterations. The distinction is consequential: the lower bound concerns the cutting-plane method, while additional use of problem structure permits better iteration complexity for solving the underlying task.
summary.tldr: Counterexamples limit cutting-plane convergence improvements, while an algorithm exploiting objective structure achieves a faster O(1/√ε) iteration rate.

title: Lower Bounds on Rate of Convergence of Cutting Plane Methods

abstract: The efficient coding hypothesis holds that neural receptive fields are adapted to the statistics of the environment, but is agnostic to the timescale of this adaptation, which occurs on both evolutionary and developmental timescales. In this work we focus on that component of adaptation which occurs during an organism's lifetime, and show that a number of unsupervised feature learning algorithms can account for features of normal receptive field properties across multiple primary sensory cortices. Furthermore, we show that the same algorithms account for altered receptive field properties in response to experimentally altered environmental statistics. Based on these modeling results we propose these models as phenomenological models of receptive field plasticity during an organism's lifetime. Finally, due to the success of the same models in multiple sensory areas, we suggest that these algorithms may provide a constructive realization of the theory, first proposed by Mountcastle (1978), that a qualitatively similar learning algorithm acts throughout primary sensory cortices.

paragraphs: The efficient-coding hypothesis connects neural receptive fields with the statistical structure of an organism's environment. It does not specify whether adaptation happens through evolution or during an individual's life. This paper focuses on the latter, asking whether unsupervised feature-learning algorithms can model receptive-field properties and their changes with experience.

The authors show that several such algorithms account for features of normal receptive fields across multiple primary sensory cortices. They also show that the same algorithms account for altered receptive-field properties when environmental statistics are experimentally changed. Using the same learning approaches for both cases connects ordinary receptive-field organization with its response to altered experience.

On that basis, the authors propose the algorithms as phenomenological models of receptive-field plasticity during an organism's lifetime. Their success across sensory areas also suggests a possible constructive realization of the idea that qualitatively similar learning operates throughout primary sensory cortex. This is a modeling-based proposal: the results support a shared computational account without establishing that the brain implements these algorithms directly.
summary.tldr: Unsupervised learning models explain features of normal and experience-altered receptive fields across multiple primary sensory areas.

title: Unsupervised learning models of primary cortical receptive fields and receptive field plasticity

abstract: Simple Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) learned from pixels of natural image patches have been recently shown to be surprisingly strong performers in modeling the statistics of natural images. Here we provide an in depth analysis of this simple yet rich model. We show that such a GMM model is able to compete with even the most successful models of natural images in log likelihood scores, denoising performance and sample quality. We provide an analysis of what such a model learns from natural images as a function of number of mixture components --- including covariance structure, contrast variation and intricate structures such as textures, boundaries and more. Finally, we show that the salient properties of the GMM learned from natural images can be derived from a simplified Dead Leaves model which explicitly models occlusion, explaining its surprising success relative to other models.

paragraphs: Gaussian mixture models learned directly from natural image patch pixels had shown unexpectedly strong performance. This paper investigates both how well this relatively simple model works and what it learns. The authors report that it competes with highly successful image models on likelihood scores, denoising, and the quality of generated samples.

The analysis examines how learned properties change with the number of mixture components. It considers covariance structure and contrast variation, as well as more intricate visual patterns such as textures and boundaries. This makes the investigation about the model’s representation of image structure, alongside its performance on evaluation tasks.

The paper then connects those learned properties to a simplified Dead Leaves model, which explicitly represents occlusion. Salient characteristics of the image-trained Gaussian mixture can be derived from this model. That connection offers an explanation for why a mixture learned from pixels can capture important natural-image regularities: its learned statistics are related to a model of objects obscuring one another. The result provides an account of its success beyond simply observing strong scores.
summary.tldr: An analysis of strong Gaussian mixture image models links their learned properties to an occlusion-based Dead Leaves model.

title: Natural Images, Gaussian Mixtures and Dead Leaves

abstract: Recently, it was shown that by dropping out hidden activities with a probability of 0.5, deep neural networks can perform very well. We describe a model in which a binary belief network is overlaid on a neural network and is used to decrease the information content of its hidden units by selectively setting activities to zero. This ''dropout network can be trained jointly with the neural network by approximately computing local expectations of binary dropout variables, computing derivatives using back-propagation, and using stochastic gradient descent. Interestingly, experiments show that the learnt dropout network parameters recapitulate the neural network parameters, suggesting that a good dropout network regularizes activities according to magnitude. When evaluated on the MNIST and NORB datasets, we found our method can be used to achieve lower classification error rates than other feather learning methods, including standard dropout, denoising auto-encoders, and restricted Boltzmann machines. For example, our model achieves 5.8% error on the NORB test set, which is better than state-of-the-art results obtained using convolutional architectures. "

paragraphs: Standard dropout can train neural networks effectively by randomly setting hidden activities to zero with a fixed probability. This paper makes the dropout mechanism itself trainable. It places a binary belief network over the neural network, allowing a learned probabilistic model to determine which hidden activities are suppressed.

The two networks are trained jointly. The method approximately computes local expectations of the binary dropout variables, obtains derivatives through backpropagation, and updates parameters using stochastic gradient descent. Experiments find that the learned dropout parameters resemble the underlying neural network parameters. The authors interpret this as suggesting that useful dropout regularizes activities according to their magnitude.

On MNIST and NORB, the method achieves lower classification errors than the compared feature learning approaches, including standard dropout, denoising autoencoders, and restricted Boltzmann machines. The reported NORB test error is 5.8%, better than the convolutional results cited in the abstract. These findings support learning how to suppress activities, while the magnitude-based interpretation remains a suggestion drawn from the experiments.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained dropout network learns which activities to suppress and improves classification results on MNIST and NORB.

title: Adaptive dropout for training deep neural networks

abstract: EDML is a recently proposed algorithm for learning parameters in Bayesian networks. It was originally derived in terms of approximate inference on a meta-network, which underlies the Bayesian approach to parameter estimation. While this initial derivation helped discover EDML in the first place and provided a concrete context for identifying some of its properties (e.g., in contrast to EM), the formal setting was somewhat tedious in the number of concepts it drew on. In this paper, we propose a greatly simplified perspective on EDML, which casts it as a general approach to continuous optimization. The new perspective has several advantages. First, it makes immediate some results that were non-trivial to prove initially. Second, it facilitates the design of EDML algorithms for new graphical models, leading to a new algorithm for learning parameters in Markov networks. We derive this algorithm in this paper, and show, empirically, that it can sometimes learn better estimates from complete data, several times faster than commonly used optimization methods, such as conjugate gradient and L-BFGS.

paragraphs: EDML was introduced as a method for learning Bayesian-network parameters, but its original explanation required approximate inference on a separate meta-network. That derivation helped uncover the algorithm and its properties, while also bringing considerable conceptual complexity. This paper offers a simpler way to understand the same approach.

The authors recast EDML as a general method for continuous optimization. From this perspective, some results that previously required substantial proofs become immediate. The reformulation also makes it easier to design related learning algorithms for other graphical models, turning an explanation of one method into a framework for extending it.

Using that framework, the paper derives an EDML algorithm for parameter learning in Markov networks. Empirical results show that, on complete data, it can sometimes produce better estimates several times faster than conjugate gradient and L-BFGS. The qualification matters: the reported advantage is an observed possibility in the evaluated setting. The contribution combines conceptual simplification with a concrete extension from directed to undirected graphical models.
summary.tldr: Viewing EDML as continuous optimization simplifies its theory and enables a Markov-network learning algorithm with promising empirical results.

title: EDML for Learning Parameters in Directed and Undirected Graphical Models

abstract: The greedy algorithm is extensively studied in the field of combinatorial optimization for decades. In this paper, we address the online learning problem when the input to the greedy algorithm is stochastic with unknown parameters that have to be learned over time. We first propose the greedy regret and $\epsilon$-quasi greedy regret as learning metrics comparing with the performance of offline greedy algorithm. We then propose two online greedy learning algorithms with semi-bandit feedbacks, which use multi-armed bandit and pure exploration bandit policies at each level of greedy learning, one for each of the regret metrics respectively. Both algorithms achieve $O(\log T)$ problem-dependent regret bound ($T$ being the time horizon) for a general class of combinatorial structures and reward functions that allow greedy solutions. We further show that the bound is tight in $T$ and other problem instance parameters.

We then propose two online greedy learning algorithms with semi-bandit feedbacks, which use multi-armed bandit and pure exploration bandit policies at each level of greedy learning, one for each of the regret metrics respectively. Both algorithms achieve $O(\log T)$ problem-dependent regret bound ($T$ being the time horizon) for a general class of combinatorial structures and reward functions that allow greedy solutions. paragraphs: Greedy algorithms build a solution through a sequence of locally selected steps. This paper studies what happens when the inputs guiding those choices are stochastic and their parameters are initially unknown. The learner must acquire that information over time while continuing to construct solutions, creating a learning problem inside the greedy procedure.

The authors introduce greedy regret and ε-quasi greedy regret to compare online performance with an offline greedy algorithm. That benchmark is important: the comparison measures the cost of learning relative to greedy performance. They propose one algorithm for each metric, using multi-armed bandit or pure-exploration policies at successive levels of the greedy process and learning from semi-bandit feedback.

Both algorithms achieve problem-dependent regret of O(log T), where T is the time horizon, for a general class of combinatorial structures and reward functions admitting greedy solutions. The authors also show that the bounds are tight in time and other problem parameters. This establishes that, within the analyzed setting, the learning cost grows only logarithmically and the stated dependence cannot generally be improved.
summary.tldr: Two online greedy algorithms learn unknown stochastic inputs with tight logarithmic regret relative to offline greedy performance.

title: Stochastic Online Greedy Learning with Semi-bandit Feedbacks

abstract: This paper proposes a framework for learning features that are robust to data variation, which is particularly important when only a limited number of trainingsamples are available. The framework makes it possible to tradeoff the discriminative value of learned features against the generalization error of the learning algorithm. Robustness is achieved by encouraging the transform that maps data to features to be a local isometry. This geometric property is shown to improve (K, \epsilon)-robustness, thereby providing theoretical justification for reductions in generalization error observed in experiments. The proposed optimization frameworkis used to train standard learning algorithms such as deep neural networks. Experimental results obtained on benchmark datasets, such as labeled faces in the wild,demonstrate the value of being able to balance discrimination and robustness.

Robustness is achieved by encouraging the transform that maps data to features to be a local isometry. This geometric property is shown to improve (K, \epsilon)-robustness, thereby providing theoretical justification for reductions in generalization error observed in experiments. The proposed optimization frameworkis used to train standard learning algorithms such as deep neural networks. Experimental results obtained on benchmark datasets, such as labeled faces in the wild,demonstrate the value of being able to balance discrimination and robustness.

paragraphs: A useful feature representation must distinguish relevant classes while remaining robust to variation in the data. This balance matters especially when training examples are scarce. The paper presents a framework that explicitly trades the discriminative value of learned features against the learning algorithm's generalization error.

The method encourages the transformation from data to features to be a local isometry: it should preserve geometry in local neighborhoods. The authors show that this property improves a formal notion called (K, ε)-robustness. That result supplies a theoretical connection between the geometric behavior of the feature transformation and its ability to generalize.

The optimization framework can train standard learning models, including deep neural networks. Experiments on benchmark datasets, including Labeled Faces in the Wild, demonstrate the value of controlling the discrimination-robustness balance and show reductions in generalization error. The contribution is therefore both a training principle and a mathematical justification for encouraging a particular kind of geometry in learned features.
summary.tldr: Encouraging feature transformations to preserve local geometry provides a principled way to balance discrimination and robustness.

title: Discriminative Robust Transformation Learning

abstract: A long-term goal of machine learning research is to build an intelligent dialog agent. Most research in natural language understanding has focused on learning from fixed training sets of labeled data, with supervision either at the word level (tagging, parsing tasks) or sentence level (question answering, machine translation). This kind of supervision is not realistic of how humans learn, where language is both learned by, and used for, communication. In this work, we study dialog-based language learning, where supervision is given naturally and implicitly in the response of the dialog partner during the conversation. We study this setup in two domains: the bAbI dataset of (Weston et al., 2015) and large-scale question answering from (Dodge et al., 2015). We evaluate a set of baseline learning strategies on these tasks, and show that a novel model incorporating predictive lookahead is a promising approach for learning from a teacher's response. In particular, a surprising result is that it can learn to answer questions correctly without any reward-based supervision at all.

The experiments therefore support conversational response prediction as a way to extract learning signals from an interaction itself.
summary.tldr: A predictive-lookahead model learns from a teacher's conversational responses and can answer questions correctly without reward-based supervision in the studied tasks.

title: Dialog-based Language Learning

abstract: Given $iid$ observations from an unknown continuous distribution defined on some domain $\Omega$, we propose a nonparametric method to learn a piecewise constant function to approximate the underlying probability density function. Our density estimate is a piecewise constant function defined on a binary partition of $\Omega$. The key ingredient of the algorithm is to use discrepancy, a concept originates from Quasi Monte Carlo analysis, to control the partition process. The resulting algorithm is simple, efficient, and has provable convergence rate. We demonstrate empirically its efficiency as a density estimation method. We also show how it can be utilized to find good initializations for k-means.

paragraphs: The paper estimates an unknown continuous probability density from independent, identically distributed observations. It uses a nonparametric representation: the domain is divided into regions, and the estimated density is constant inside each region. This produces a piecewise constant approximation without committing to a particular parametric family for the underlying distribution.

The regions form a binary partition, built through a sequential splitting process. The distinctive ingredient is discrepancy, a concept drawn from quasi-Monte Carlo analysis, which controls how the partition develops. Consequently, the construction of the regions is a central part of learning the density, rather than merely a preliminary choice of representation.

The authors describe the resulting algorithm as simple and efficient and establish a convergence rate. They also provide empirical evidence of its efficiency for density estimation. Beyond estimating probabilities, they show that the method can provide good initializations for k-means. This connects the learned partitioned density to a second practical task: choosing useful starting points for clustering.
summary.tldr: A discrepancy-guided binary partition produces an efficient density estimator with a convergence guarantee and applications to k-means initialization.

title: Density Estimation via Discrepancy Based Adaptive Sequential Partition

abstract: Many tasks in AI require the collaboration of multiple agents. Typically, the communication protocol between agents is manually specified and not altered during training. In this paper we explore a simple neural model, called CommNet, that uses continuous communication for fully cooperative tasks. The model consists of multiple agents and the communication between them is learned alongside their policy. We apply this model to a diverse set of tasks, demonstrating the ability of the agents to learn to communicate amongst themselves, yielding improved performance over non-communicative agents and baselines. In some cases, it is possible to interpret the language devised by the agents, revealing simple but effective strategies for solving the task at hand.

paragraphs: Cooperative tasks can require several agents to coordinate their actions through communication. Often, the rules for exchanging information are manually specified and remain fixed during training. This paper investigates whether agents can instead learn how to communicate as part of learning how to act, using a simple neural model called CommNet.

CommNet uses continuous communication among multiple agents in fully cooperative tasks. The communication mechanism is learned alongside the agents’ policy. This ties the development of messages to the behavior needed for the shared task, making communication part of the learning problem rather than a separately prescribed protocol.

Across a diverse set of tasks, the authors find that agents learn to communicate and improve performance over agents without communication and other baselines. In some cases, the learned language can be interpreted, revealing simple strategies that help solve the task. This interpretability claim is qualified: it applies to some cases. The broader empirical finding is that jointly learning communication and behavior can improve cooperation.
summary.tldr: CommNet learns continuous communication alongside cooperative policies, improving performance across tasks and sometimes revealing interpretable strategies.

title: Learning Multiagent Communication with Backpropagation

abstract: We present an algorithm based on posterior sampling (aka Thompson sampling) that achieves near-optimal worst-case regret bounds when the underlying Markov Decision Process (MDP) is communicating with a finite, though unknown, diameter. Our main result is a high probability regret upper bound of $\tilde{O}(D\sqrt{SAT})$ for any communicating MDP with $S$ states, $A$ actions and diameter $D$, when $T\ge S^5A$. Here, regret compares the total reward achieved by the algorithm to the total expected reward of an optimal infinite-horizon undiscounted average reward policy, in time horizon $T$. This result improves over the best previously known upper bound of $\tilde{O}(DS\sqrt{AT})$ achieved by any algorithm in this setting, and matches the dependence on $S$ in the established lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{DSAT})$ for this problem. Our techniques involve proving some novel results about the anti-concentration of Dirichlet distribution, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper develops a posterior-sampling reinforcement learning algorithm for communicating Markov decision processes with a finite but unknown diameter. Its objective is to control regret: the reward shortfall relative to an optimal infinite-horizon policy for undiscounted average reward, measured over a finite interaction horizon.

For S states, A actions, diameter D, and horizon T, the main result is a high-probability upper bound of order D√(SAT), suppressing logarithmic factors, when T is at least S⁵A. This improves the previously known upper bound of order DS√(AT). The improvement reduces the dependence on the number of states, an important distinction when comparing the guarantees as the state space grows.

The bound matches the state-count dependence of the established lower bound √(DSAT), while retaining a different dependence on diameter. The near-optimality claim therefore should not be read as exact agreement in every parameter. The proof also introduces anti-concentration results for Dirichlet distributions, providing mathematical tools that the authors suggest may be useful beyond this reinforcement learning analysis.
summary.tldr: Optimistic posterior sampling improves worst-case regret's dependence on state count for communicating MDPs under a stated horizon condition.

title: Optimistic posterior sampling for reinforcement learning: worst-case regret bounds

abstract: In this paper, we propose an accelerated first-order method for geodesically convex optimization, which is the generalization of the standard Nesterov's accelerated method from Euclidean space to nonlinear Riemannian space. We first derive two equations and obtain two nonlinear operators for geodesically convex optimization instead of the linear extrapolation step in Euclidean space. In particular, we analyze the global convergence properties of our accelerated method for geodesically strongly-convex problems, which show that our method improves the convergence rate from O((1-\mu/L)^{k}) to O((1-\sqrt{\mu/L})^{k}). Moreover, our method also improves the global convergence rate on geodesically general convex problems from O(1/k) to O(1/k^{2}). Finally, we give a specific iterative scheme for matrix Karcher mean problems, and validate our theoretical results with experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops an accelerated optimization method for problems whose variables lie on a curved Riemannian space. The relevant notion of convexity follows geodesics, the space's counterpart to straight lines. The aim is to bring the faster convergence associated with Nesterov's method into this nonlinear setting.

The central obstacle is the extrapolation step used in Euclidean acceleration. Ordinary linear extrapolation does not directly provide the required construction on a curved space. The authors derive two equations and corresponding nonlinear operators to perform this role, making the geometry part of the accelerated update itself.

For geodesically strongly convex problems, the analysis improves the convergence rate from O((1−μ/L)^k) to O((1−√(μ/L))^k). For general geodesically convex problems, it improves O(1/k) to O(1/k²). These results describe faster progress as the iteration count grows within the analyzed problem classes. The paper also supplies a concrete iterative method for matrix Karcher mean problems and reports experiments supporting its theoretical results.
summary.tldr: Nonlinear extrapolation operators extend accelerated optimization to geodesically convex problems, with improved convergence rates.

title: Accelerated First-order Methods for Geodesically Convex Optimization on Riemannian Manifolds

abstract: We consider Bayesian methods for multi-information source optimization (MISO), in which we seek to optimize an expensive-to-evaluate black-box objective function while also accessing cheaper but biased and noisy approximations ("information sources"). We present a novel algorithm that outperforms the state of the art for this problem by using a Gaussian process covariance kernel better suited to MISO than those used by previous approaches, and an acquisition function based on a one-step optimality analysis supported by efficient parallelization. We also provide a novel technique to guarantee the asymptotic quality of the solution provided by this algorithm. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that this algorithm consistently finds designs of higher value at less cost than previous approaches.

paragraphs: Optimizing an expensive black-box function becomes more complicated when cheaper approximations are available. Those sources can save evaluation cost, but their outputs may be biased and noisy. This paper studies how Bayesian optimization can use multiple such sources to find valuable designs while managing the cost of obtaining information.

The proposed algorithm uses a Gaussian-process covariance kernel designed for this setting, together with an acquisition function derived from a one-step optimality analysis. The kernel models relationships relevant to the multiple sources, while the acquisition function guides information gathering. Efficient parallelization supports the computation involved in choosing evaluations.

The authors also introduce a technique that guarantees the asymptotic quality of the algorithm's solution. This is a long-run guarantee, separate from the empirical cost comparison. In experiments, the method consistently finds higher-value designs at lower cost than previous approaches. The contribution combines better modeling of imperfect information sources, a principled evaluation rule, and a quality guarantee for the eventual solution.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian optimizer combines costly evaluations with cheaper biased sources to find better designs at lower cost in experiments.

title: Multi-Information Source Optimization

abstract: While a typical supervised learning framework assumes that the inputs and the outputs are measured at the same levels of granularity, many applications, including global mapping of disease, only have access to outputs at a much coarser level than that of the inputs. Aggregation of outputs makes generalization to new inputs much more difficult. We consider an approach to this problem based on variational learning with a model of output aggregation and Gaussian processes, where aggregation leads to intractability of the standard evidence lower bounds. We propose new bounds and tractable approximations, leading to improved prediction accuracy and scalability to large datasets, while explicitly taking uncertainty into account. We develop a framework which extends to several types of likelihoods, including the Poisson model for aggregated count data. We apply our framework to a challenging and important problem, the fine-scale spatial modelling of malaria incidence, with over 1 million observations.

paragraphs: Many prediction problems provide detailed inputs but only coarse outputs. Disease mapping, for example, may require fine-scale predictions even though observed outcomes are aggregated. This mismatch makes learning harder because the model must connect individual inputs to measurements that summarize groups of them, rather than observing a matching output for each input.

The paper combines Gaussian processes with an explicit model of output aggregation and variational learning. Aggregation makes standard evidence lower bounds intractable, so the authors derive new bounds and workable approximations. These changes support learning while explicitly accounting for uncertainty, and the framework accommodates several likelihood types, including a Poisson model for aggregated counts.

The authors report improved predictive accuracy and scalability to large datasets. They apply the framework to fine-scale spatial modeling of malaria incidence using more than one million observations. This application demonstrates the intended use: extracting finer-grained predictive information from coarser outcome measurements. The contribution addresses both the statistical mismatch between inputs and outputs and the computational difficulty introduced by modeling their aggregation.
summary.tldr: New variational bounds enable scalable Gaussian process learning from aggregated outputs, including fine-scale malaria modeling with over one million observations.

title: Variational Learning on Aggregate Outputs with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Despite achieving impressive performance, state-of-the-art classifiers remain highly vulnerable to small, imperceptible, adversarial perturbations. This vulnerability has proven empirically to be very intricate to address. In this paper, we study the phenomenon of adversarial perturbations under the assumption that the data is generated with a smooth generative model. We derive fundamental upper bounds on the robustness to perturbations of any classification function, and prove the existence of adversarial perturbations that transfer well across different classifiers with small risk. Our analysis of the robustness also provides insights onto key properties of generative models, such as their smoothness and dimensionality of latent space. We conclude with numerical experimental results showing that our bounds provide informative baselines to the maximal achievable robustness on several datasets.

We derive fundamental upper bounds on the robustness to perturbations of any classification function, and prove the existence of adversarial perturbations that transfer well across different classifiers with small risk.
