paragraphs: The paper investigates whether adversarial vulnerability reflects limits that extend beyond particular classifier designs. Its analysis assumes that a smooth generative model produces the data. Within this setting, the question is how robust a classification function can be against input perturbations, rather than how to improve one specific trained network.

The authors derive upper bounds on robustness that apply to any classification function under their assumptions. They also prove the existence of adversarial perturbations that transfer well between classifiers with small risk. This connects vulnerability across different classifiers to the shared data-generating setting, rather than treating every successful transfer as an isolated property of a particular model pair.

The analysis further relates robustness to properties of the generative model, including smoothness and the dimensionality of its latent space. Numerical experiments on several datasets indicate that the bounds provide informative reference points for the greatest achievable robustness. The scope of the conclusion rests on the smooth generative-model assumption: the contribution is a conditional account of fundamental limits, supported by numerical evidence.
summary.tldr: Under a smooth generative-model assumption, the paper bounds classifier robustness and proves transferable adversarial perturbations exist.

title: Adversarial vulnerability for any classifier

abstract: We introduce Bayesian distributed stochastic gradient descent (BDSGD), a high-throughput algorithm for training deep neural networks on parallel clusters. This algorithm uses amortized inference in a deep generative model to perform joint posterior predictive inference of mini-batch gradient computation times in a compute cluster specific manner. Specifically, our algorithm mitigates the straggler effect in synchronous, gradient-based optimization by choosing an optimal cutoff beyond which mini-batch gradient messages from slow workers are ignored. In our experiments, we show that eagerly discarding the mini-batch gradient computations of stragglers not only increases throughput but actually increases the overall rate of convergence as a function of wall-clock time by virtue of eliminating idleness. The principal novel contribution and finding of this work goes beyond this by demonstrating that using the predicted run-times from a generative model of cluster worker performance improves substantially over the static-cutoff prior art, leading to reduced deep neural net training times on large computer clusters.

In our experiments, we show that eagerly discarding the mini-batch gradient computations of stragglers not only increases throughput but actually increases the overall rate of convergence as a function of wall-clock time by virtue of eliminating idleness. paragraphs: When neural-network training is distributed across a cluster, synchronous updates can leave faster workers waiting for slower ones. These delayed workers, or stragglers, make the time spent waiting part of the training cost. Bayesian distributed stochastic gradient descent addresses this problem by deciding when to stop accepting gradient messages for an update.

The algorithm uses amortized inference in a deep generative model to jointly predict mini-batch gradient computation times for the particular cluster. Those predictions determine an optimal cutoff, beyond which messages from slow workers are ignored. The central idea is to use a learned account of worker performance to guide the cutoff rather than rely on a fixed threshold.

In the reported experiments, eagerly discarding straggler computations improves throughput and convergence measured against elapsed time by reducing idleness. Using predicted runtimes improves substantially over static-cutoff approaches and reduces neural-network training time on large clusters. The findings show that accepting fewer gradient messages can still accelerate training in practice when the avoided waiting time outweighs the cost of discarding them.
summary.tldr: Predicting worker runtimes lets distributed training discard late gradients strategically and reduce elapsed training time.

title: Bayesian Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Future mobile devices are anticipated to perceive, understand and react to the world on their own by running multiple correlated deep neural networks on-device. Yet the complexity of these neural networks needs to be trimmed down both within-model and cross-model to fit in mobile storage and memory. Previous studies focus on squeezing the redundancy within a single neural network. In this work, we aim to reduce the redundancy across multiple models. We propose Multi-Task Zipping (MTZ), a framework to automatically merge correlated, pre-trained deep neural networks for cross-model compression. Central in MTZ is a layer-wise neuron sharing and incoming weight updating scheme that induces a minimal change in the error function. MTZ inherits information from each model and demands light retraining to re-boost the accuracy of individual tasks. Evaluations show that MTZ is able to fully merge the hidden layers of two VGG-16 networks with a 3.18% increase in the test error averaged on ImageNet and CelebA, or share 39.61% parameters between the two networks with <0.5% increase in the test errors for both tasks. The number of iterations to retrain the combined network is at least 17.8 times lower than that of training a single VGG-16 network. Moreover, experiments show that MTZ is also able to effectively merge multiple residual networks.

paragraphs: Running several neural networks on a mobile device creates storage and memory pressure. Compressing each network independently leaves another opportunity: related models may contain redundant computation or parameters across networks. Multi-Task Zipping, or MTZ, targets this redundancy by merging correlated networks that have already been trained.

MTZ shares neurons layer by layer and updates their incoming weights to induce minimal change in the error function. It preserves information from the original models and uses light retraining to recover task accuracy. This makes cross-model sharing the central compression mechanism while allowing each task to retain its learned information.

Experiments also merged multiple residual networks, showing applicability beyond the two-network example and illustrating the tradeoff between sharing and accuracy.
summary.tldr: MTZ compresses related pretrained networks by sharing neurons across models, with light retraining and measured accuracy tradeoffs.

title: Multi-Task Zipping via Layer-wise Neuron Sharing

abstract: We introduce a novel scalable approach to identifying common latent structure in neural population spike-trains, which allows for variability both in the trajectory and in the rate of progression of the underlying computation. Our approach is based on shared latent Gaussian processes (GPs) which are combined linearly, as in the Gaussian Process Factor Analysis (GPFA) algorithm. We extend GPFA to handle unbinned spike-train data by incorporating a continuous time point-process likelihood model, achieving scalability with a sparse variational approximation. Shared variability is separated into terms that express condition dependence, as well as trial-to-trial variation in trajectories. Finally, we introduce a nested GP formulation to capture variability in the rate of evolution along the trajectory. We show that the new method learns to recover latent trajectories in synthetic data, and can accurately identify the trial-to-trial timing of movement-related parameters from motor cortical data without any supervision.

paragraphs: This paper seeks common hidden structure in the spike trains of neural populations while allowing repeated trials to unfold differently. Variation can affect both the trajectory of the underlying computation and how quickly it progresses. Separating those effects is central to identifying shared activity without confusing timing changes with changes in the trajectory itself.

The approach extends Gaussian Process Factor Analysis using linearly combined shared latent Gaussian processes. A continuous-time point-process likelihood handles unbinned spike trains, and a sparse variational approximation provides scalability. The model separates condition-dependent effects from trial-specific trajectory variation. A nested Gaussian process formulation then represents differences in the rate of progression along a trajectory.

On synthetic data, the method recovers latent trajectories. Applied to motor cortical recordings, it accurately identifies trial-to-trial timing of movement-related parameters without supervision. These findings show that modeling trajectory variation and temporal progression together can reveal shared neural structure and movement-related timing directly from the observed population activity.
summary.tldr: A scalable Gaussian process model separates neural trajectory variation from timing variation in unbinned population spike trains.

title: Temporal alignment and latent Gaussian process factor inference in population spike trains

abstract: Covariance matrices have attracted attention for machine learning applications due to their capacity to capture interesting structure in the data. The main challenge is that one needs to take into account the particular geometry of the Riemannian manifold of symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices they belong to. In the con- text of deep networks, several architectures for these matrices have recently been proposed. In our article, we introduce a Riemannian batch normalization (batch- norm) algorithm, which generalizes the one used in Euclidean nets. This novel layer makes use of geometric operations on the manifold, notably the Riemannian barycenter, parallel transport and non-linear structured matrix transformations. We derive a new manifold-constrained gradient descent algorithm working in the space of SPD matrices, allowing to learn the batchnorm layer. We validate our proposed approach with experiments in three different contexts on diverse data types: a drone recognition dataset from radar observations, and on emotion and action recognition datasets from video and motion capture data. Experiments show that the Riemannian batchnorm systematically gives better classification performance compared with leading methods and a remarkable robustness to lack of data.

paragraphs: Covariance matrices can capture useful data structure, but networks that operate on symmetric positive definite matrices must account for their geometry. The paper introduces a batch-normalization layer for this setting, extending the familiar normalization idea to the Riemannian manifold on which these matrices lie.

The layer uses geometric operations including a Riemannian barycenter, parallel transport, and nonlinear structured matrix transformations. These provide the ingredients for performing normalization within the relevant matrix geometry. Evaluation covers drone recognition from radar observations and emotion and action recognition using video and motion-capture data. Across these experiments, the proposed normalization consistently improves classification performance relative to leading methods and shows strong robustness when data are scarce. The contribution combines a geometry-aware network operation with a compatible learning procedure, and the experiments demonstrate its value across several types of recognition data.
summary.tldr: Riemannian batch normalization respects SPD matrix geometry and improves classification across the evaluated radar, video, and motion-capture tasks.

title: Riemannian batch normalization for SPD neural networks

abstract: The information-theoretic analysis by Russo and Van Roy [2014] in combination with minimax duality has proved a powerful tool for the analysis of online learning algorithms in full and partial information settings. In most applications there is a tantalising similarity to the classical analysis based on mirror descent. We make a formal connection, showing that the information-theoretic bounds in most applications are derived from existing techniques from online convex optimisation. Besides this, we improve best known regret guarantees for $k$-armed adversarial bandits, online linear optimisation on $\ell_p$-balls and bandits with graph feedback.

Some settings reveal full information, while others reveal only part of what would be useful for choosing the next action. Researchers analyze these problems using several mathematical approaches, including information-theoretic arguments and optimization methods such as mirror descent.

This paper formalizes a connection between those approaches. Information-theoretic analysis combined with minimax duality has produced powerful guarantees, but its arguments often resemble classical mirror-descent analysis. The authors show that, in most applications, the information-theoretic bounds can be derived from existing techniques in online convex optimization. This explains a recurring similarity between analyses that otherwise appear to use different conceptual machinery.

The connection also accompanies improved regret guarantees for adversarial bandits with k choices, online linear optimization over lp balls, and bandits with graph feedback. Regret measures accumulated performance loss relative to a comparison strategy. The stated improvements therefore strengthen theoretical control of sequential decision quality across several feedback structures, while giving the analyses a more unified mathematical foundation.
summary.tldr: The paper connects information-theoretic online-learning analyses to mirror-descent techniques and improves regret guarantees in several decision settings.

title: Connections Between Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling and the Information Ratio

abstract: We consider objective evaluation measures of saliency explanations for complex black-box machine learning models. We propose simple robust variants of two notions that have been considered in recent literature: (in)fidelity, and sensitivity. We analyze optimal explanations with respect to both these measures, and while the optimal explanation for sensitivity is a vacuous constant explanation, the optimal explanation for infidelity is a novel combination of two popular explanation methods. By varying the perturbation distribution that defines infidelity, we obtain novel explanations by optimizing infidelity, which we show to out-perform existing explanations in both quantitative and qualitative measurements. Another salient question given these measures is how to modify any given explanation to have better values with respect to these measures. We propose a simple modification based on lowering sensitivity, and moreover show that when done appropriately, we could simultaneously improve both sensitivity as well as fidelity.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to evaluate saliency explanations for complex machine-learning models. It develops robust versions of two measures: infidelity, concerning how well an explanation reflects model behavior, and sensitivity, concerning how much an explanation changes under perturbations. It then examines which explanations are optimal according to each measure.

Optimizing sensitivity alone produces a constant explanation, which is stable but uninformative. Optimizing infidelity instead yields a new combination of two popular explanation methods. The distribution of perturbations used to define infidelity also matters: changing it produces additional explanations through optimization, and the authors report quantitative and qualitative improvements over existing explanations.

The work further asks how an existing explanation can be improved without replacing its underlying method. A simple modification aimed at lowering sensitivity can, when applied appropriately, improve fidelity as well. The findings show why explanation evaluation needs more than stability alone, while also demonstrating that stability and fidelity need not always conflict. The simultaneous improvement is conditional on how the modification is performed.
summary.tldr: Robust fidelity and sensitivity measures yield new saliency explanations and show that appropriate modifications can improve both qualities simultaneously.

title: On the (In)fidelity and Sensitivity of Explanations

abstract: Graph neural network (GNN) has powerful representation ability, but optimal configurations of GNN are non-trivial to obtain due to diversity of graph structure and cascaded nonlinearities. This paper aims to understand some properties of GNN from a computer vision (CV) perspective. In mathematical analysis, we propose an adaptive GNN model by recursive definition, and derive its relation with two basic operations in CV: filtering and propagation operations. The proposed GNN model is formulated as a label propagation system with guided map, graph Laplacian and node weight. It reveals that 1) the guided map and node weight determine whether a GNN leads to filtering or propagation diffusion, and 2) the kernel of graph Laplacian controls diffusion pattern. In practical verification, we design a new regularization structure with guided feature to produce GNN-based filtering and propagation diffusion to tackle the ill-posed inverse problems of quotient image analysis (QIA), which recovers the reflectance ratio as a signature for image analysis or adjustment. A flexible QIA-GNN framework is constructed to achieve various image-based editing tasks, like face illumination synthesis and low-light image enhancement. Experiments show the effectiveness of the QIA-GNN, and provide new insights of GNN for image analysis and editing.

title: Adaptive GNN for Image Analysis and Editing

abstract: Natural images are virtually surrounded by low-density misclassified regions that can be efficiently discovered by gradient-guided search --- enabling the generation of adversarial images. While many techniques for detecting these attacks have been proposed, they are easily bypassed when the adversary has full knowledge of the detection mechanism and adapts the attack strategy accordingly. In this paper, we adopt a novel perspective and regard the omnipresence of adversarial perturbations as a strength rather than a weakness. We postulate that if an image has been tampered with, these adversarial directions either become harder to find with gradient methods or have substantially higher density than for natural images. We develop a practical test for this signature characteristic to successfully detect adversarial attacks, achieving unprecedented accuracy under the white-box setting where the adversary is given full knowledge of our detection mechanism.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to detect images deliberately changed to mislead a classifier. Its starting point is that natural images have nearby regions where the classifier makes mistakes, and gradient-guided searches can locate these regions. Detectors are difficult to build because an attacker who knows their rules can adapt an attack to evade them.

The authors propose using the surrounding adversarial directions as a detection signal. They hypothesize that an already manipulated image has a different local pattern: further adversarial directions either become harder for gradient methods to discover or occur at substantially higher density. They turn this proposed distinction into a practical test for identifying manipulated inputs.

The abstract reports unusually strong detection accuracy in a white-box setting, where attackers know the detection mechanism. The contribution is therefore a way to inspect how a classifier behaves around an image, using the availability of adversarial perturbations as evidence. The proposed signature remains a hypothesis motivating the method, while the reported detection success is an empirical finding rather than a universal guarantee against adaptive attacks.
summary.tldr: The paper detects adversarial images by testing whether nearby adversarial directions have become unusually dense or difficult to find.

title: A New Defense Against Adversarial Images: Turning a Weakness into a Strength

abstract: In this paper we propose Stochastic Deep Gaussian Processes over Graphs (DGPG), which are deep structure models that learn the mappings between input and output signals in graph domains. The approximate posterior distributions of the latent variables are derived with variational inference, and the evidence lower bound is evaluated and optimized by the proposed recursive sampling scheme. The Bayesian non-parametric natural of our model allows it to resist overfitting, while the expressive deep structure grants it the potential to learn complex relations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior performances in both small size (< 50) and large size (> 35,000) datasets. We show that DGPG outperforms another Gaussian-based approach, and is competitive to a state-of-the-art method in the challenging task of traffic flow prediction. Our model is also capable of capturing uncertainties in a mathematical principled way and automatically discovering which vertices and features are relevant to the prediction.

Training requires reasoning about latent variables whose posterior distributions are approximated through variational inference. A proposed recursive sampling scheme evaluates and optimizes the evidence lower bound, the objective used for this approximate Bayesian learning. This supplies a computational procedure for fitting the deep probabilistic model to graph-structured observations.

Experiments report strong performance on datasets ranging from fewer than 50 to more than 35,000 examples. For traffic-flow prediction, DGPG outperforms another Gaussian-based approach and is competitive with a state-of-the-art method. Beyond prediction quality, it represents uncertainty in a mathematically principled way and automatically identifies relevant vertices and features. The contribution therefore joins predictive modeling with information about confidence and relevance, useful properties when graph signals have complex dependencies and varying amounts of available data.
summary.tldr: DGPG combines deep Gaussian processes with graph modeling to predict graph signals, quantify uncertainty, and identify relevant vertices and features.

title: Stochastic Deep Gaussian Processes over Graphs

abstract: Robustness of machine learning models to various adversarial and non-adversarial corruptions continues to be of interest. In this paper, we introduce the notion of the boundary thickness of a classifier, and we describe its connection with and usefulness for model robustness. Thick decision boundaries lead to improved performance, while thin decision boundaries lead to overfitting (e.g., measured by the robust generalization gap between training and testing) and lower robustness. We show that a thicker boundary helps improve robustness against adversarial examples (e.g., improving the robust test accuracy of adversarial training) as well as so-called out-of-distribution (OOD) transforms, and we show that many commonly-used regularization and data augmentation procedures can increase boundary thickness. On the theoretical side, we establish that maximizing boundary thickness during training is akin to the so-called mixup training. Using these observations, we show that noise-augmentation on mixup training further increases boundary thickness, thereby combating vulnerability to various forms of adversarial attacks and OOD transforms. We can also show that the performance improvement in several lines of recent work happens in conjunction with a thicker boundary.

The central question is how the structure of the region separating predictions relates to performance under changed or corrupted inputs. The authors connect thicker boundaries with better robustness and thinner boundaries with overfitting, including a larger gap between robust performance on training and test data.

They examine both adversarial examples and transformations that move inputs outside the training distribution. Their results show that increasing boundary thickness can improve robustness in these settings, including the robust test accuracy of adversarial training. They also find that several familiar regularization and data augmentation procedures can increase thickness, providing a shared perspective on methods usually discussed separately.

The theoretical analysis connects maximizing boundary thickness during training with mixup training. Building on that connection, the authors add noise augmentation to mixup and show further increases in thickness alongside improved resistance to attacks and distribution changes. They also identify thicker boundaries accompanying improvements in several existing approaches.
summary.tldr: Boundary thickness connects classifier geometry with robustness and motivates adding noise augmentation to mixup training.

title: Boundary thickness and robustness in learning models

abstract: Structural equation models (SEMs) are widely used in sciences, ranging from economics to psychology, to uncover causal relationships underlying a complex system under consideration and estimate structural parameters of interest. We study estimation in a class of generalized SEMs where the object of interest is defined as the solution to a linear operator equation. We formulate the linear operator equation as a min-max game, where both players are parameterized by neural networks (NNs), and learn the parameters of these neural networks using the stochastic gradient descent. We consider both 2-layer and multi-layer NNs with ReLU activation functions and prove global convergence in an overparametrized regime, where the number of neurons is diverging. The results are established using techniques from online learning and local linearization of NNs, and improve in several aspects the current state-of-the-art. For the first time we provide a tractable estimation procedure for SEMs based on NNs with provable convergence and without the need for sample splitting.

This paper studies a generalized class in which the quantity to estimate is defined by a linear operator equation. The problem is to turn that mathematical definition into a tractable neural-network estimation procedure with a convergence guarantee.

The authors express the equation as a min-max game and represent both players with neural networks. They learn the network parameters using stochastic gradient descent. Their analysis covers both two-layer and multilayer networks with ReLU activations, connecting an adversarial training formulation to the original estimation task.

The convergence proof uses online-learning techniques and local linear approximations of the networks. It establishes global convergence in an overparameterized regime where the number of neurons diverges. Within that regime, the paper provides a computationally tractable neural estimator with provable convergence and no requirement to split the sample. The significance is a theoretical bridge between neural adversarial optimization and structural estimation, with the convergence claim explicitly tied to the network-width regime.
summary.tldr: A neural min-max formulation yields structural-equation estimators with global convergence guarantees in a diverging-width regime, without sample splitting.

title: Provably Efficient Neural Estimation of Structural Equation Models: An Adversarial Approach

abstract: We consider a repeated sequential game between a learner, who plays first, and an opponent who responds to the chosen action. We seek to design strategies for the learner to successfully interact with the opponent. While most previous approaches consider known opponent models, we focus on the setting in which the opponent's model is unknown. To this end, we use kernel-based regularity assumptions to capture and exploit the structure in the opponent's response. We propose a novel algorithm for the learner when playing against an adversarial sequence of opponents. The algorithm combines ideas from bilevel optimization and online learning to effectively balance between exploration (learning about the opponent's model) and exploitation (selecting highly rewarding actions for the learner). Our results include algorithm's regret guarantees that depend on the regularity of the opponent's response and scale sublinearly with the number of game rounds. Moreover, we specialize our approach to repeated Stackelberg games, and empirically demonstrate its effectiveness in a traffic routing and wildlife conservation task.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated games in which a learner acts first and an opponent responds to that action. The learner does not know the opponent's response model in advance. This makes choosing a rewarding action inseparable from learning how the opponent reacts, especially when the learner faces an adversarial sequence of opponents.

The authors impose kernel-based regularity assumptions to describe exploitable structure in those responses. Their algorithm combines bilevel optimization, which accounts for the responding player's decision, with online learning. It balances exploration of the unknown response model against exploitation of actions that currently appear rewarding.

The authors also specialize the method to repeated Stackelberg games and demonstrate it in traffic routing and wildlife conservation tasks. These examples support the usefulness of jointly learning an opponent's behavior and deciding how to act before that opponent responds.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based online algorithm learns unknown opponents' responses while achieving sublinear regret under response-regularity assumptions.

title: Learning to Play Sequential Games versus Unknown Opponents

abstract: Modeling dependencies in multivariate discrete data is a challenging problem, especially in high dimensions. The Potts model is a versatile such model, suitable when each coordinate is a categorical variable. However, the full Potts model has too many parameters to be accurately fit when the number of categories is large. We introduce a variation on the Potts model that allows for general categorical marginals and Ising-type multivariate dependence. This reduces the number of parameters from $\Omega(d^2 K^2)$ in the full Potts model to $O(d^2 + Kd)$, where $K$ is the number of categories and $d$ is the dimension of the data. We show that the complexity of fitting this new Potts-Ising model is the same as that of an Ising model. In particular, adopting the neighborhood regression framework, the model can be fit by solving $d$ separate logistic regressions. We demonstrate the ability of the model to capture multivariate dependencies by comparing with existing approaches.

paragraphs: Modeling many categorical variables requires describing both the categories each variable takes and the relationships among variables. The full Potts model offers flexibility, but its parameter count becomes difficult to support when there are many categories. This paper introduces a smaller model intended to retain useful multivariate dependence structure.

The Potts-Ising model combines general categorical marginal distributions with Ising-type dependence. For d variables with K categories, it reduces the parameter count from at least order d squared times K squared to order d squared plus K times d. The reduction separates the category-related parameter burden from the much larger category-by-category interaction burden of the full Potts model.

The authors show that fitting the new model has the same complexity as fitting an Ising model. Using neighborhood regression, estimation reduces to d separate logistic regressions. Comparisons with existing approaches demonstrate that the model can capture multivariate dependencies. The contribution is a specific balance between categorical flexibility and structured dependence, making estimation substantially more compact while preserving the ability to model relationships among variables.
summary.tldr: The Potts-Ising model captures categorical dependencies with far fewer parameters than a full Potts model and can be fitted through separate logistic regressions.

title: The Potts-Ising model for discrete multivariate data

abstract: In recent years, graph neural networks (GNNs) have become the de facto tool for performing machine learning tasks on graphs. Most GNNs belong to the family of message passing neural networks (MPNNs). These models employ an iterative neighborhood aggregation scheme to update vertex representations. Then, to compute vector representations of graphs, they aggregate the representations of the vertices using some permutation invariant function. One would expect the hidden layers of a GNN to be composed of parameters that take the form of graphs. However, this is not the case for MPNNs since their update procedure is parameterized by fully-connected layers. In this paper, we propose a more intuitive and transparent architecture for graph-structured data, so-called Random Walk Graph Neural Network (RWNN). The first layer of the model consists of a number of trainable ``hidden graphs'' which are compared against the input graphs using a random walk kernel to produce graph representations. These representations are then passed on to a fully-connected neural network which produces the output. The employed random walk kernel is differentiable, and therefore, the proposed model is end-to-end trainable. We demonstrate the model's transparency on synthetic datasets. Furthermore, we empirically evaluate the model on graph classification datasets and show that it achieves competitive performance.

paragraphs: Most graph neural networks repeatedly combine information from neighboring vertices, then pool vertex representations into a representation of the whole graph. Although their inputs are graphs, the update rules are typically parameterized by fully connected layers. This paper proposes an architecture whose learned components include graphs themselves, aiming for greater transparency.

The Random Walk Graph Neural Network begins with a collection of trainable hidden graphs. A random walk kernel compares each input graph with those learned graphs to produce a representation. A fully connected network then turns that representation into an output. Because the kernel is differentiable, the hidden graphs and the remaining network can be trained together.

The learned graph comparisons provide a more direct structural view of the model's representation. The authors demonstrate transparency on synthetic datasets and evaluate prediction on graph-classification datasets, where performance is competitive. The findings support graph-shaped learned components as a viable alternative architecture that combines interpretable structure with useful predictive performance.
summary.tldr: RWNN learns hidden graphs and compares them with inputs through a differentiable random walk kernel.

title: Random Walk Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Existing deep hierarchical topic models are able to extract semantically meaningful topics from a text corpus in an unsupervised manner and automatically organize them into a topic hierarchy. However, it is unclear how to incorporate prior belief such as knowledge graph to guide the learning of the topic hierarchy. To address this issue, we introduce TopicNet as a deep hierarchical topic model that can inject prior structural knowledge as inductive bias to influence the learning. TopicNet represents each topic as a Gaussian-distributed embedding vector, projects the topics of all layers into a shared embedding space, and explores both the symmetric and asymmetric similarities between Gaussian embedding vectors to incorporate prior semantic hierarchies. With a variational auto-encoding inference network, the model parameters are optimized by minimizing the evidence lower bound and supervised loss via stochastic gradient descent. Experiments on widely used benchmark show that TopicNet outperforms related deep topic models on discovering deeper interpretable topics and mining better document representations.

paragraphs: Hierarchical topic models discover themes in a text collection and organize them into levels. This paper addresses how prior structural knowledge, such as a knowledge graph, can guide that organization. TopicNet incorporates such knowledge as an inductive bias, allowing an existing semantic hierarchy to influence the hierarchy learned from documents.

Each topic is represented by a Gaussian-distributed embedding, and topics from every level share a common embedding space. The model uses both symmetric and asymmetric similarities between these distributions to incorporate semantic hierarchy information. This supplies a way to express relationships across levels while still learning the topics themselves from the corpus.

TopicNet uses a variational auto-encoding inference network and trains with an evidence-lower-bound objective together with supervised loss through stochastic gradient descent. Benchmark experiments report better discovery of deeper, interpretable topics and improved document representations compared with related deep topic models. The contribution is a concrete mechanism for combining prior semantic structure with hierarchical topic discovery, with the reported benefits covering both topic interpretation and the representations extracted for documents.
summary.tldr: TopicNet uses Gaussian topic embeddings and prior semantic hierarchies to guide interpretable topic discovery and improve document representations.

title: TopicNet: Semantic Graph-Guided Topic Discovery

abstract: Recently, there has been great success in applying deep neural networks on graph structured data. Most work, however, focuses on either node- or graph-level supervised learning, such as node, link or graph classification or node-level unsupervised learning (e.g. node clustering). Despite its wide range of possible applications, graph-level unsupervised learning has not received much attention yet. This might be mainly attributed to the high representation complexity of graphs, which can be represented by $n!$ equivalent adjacency matrices, where $n$ is the number of nodes.In this work we address this issue by proposing a permutation-invariant variational autoencoder for graph structured data. Our proposed model indirectly learns to match the node ordering of input and output graph, without imposing a particular node ordering or performing expensive graph matching. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model for graph reconstruction, generation and interpolation and evaluate the expressive power of extracted representations for downstream graph-level classification and regression.

Our proposed model indirectly learns to match the node ordering of input and output graph, without imposing a particular node ordering or performing expensive graph matching. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model for graph reconstruction, generation and interpolation and evaluate the expressive power of extracted representations for downstream graph-level classification and regression.

paragraphs: Learning a representation of an entire graph without labels is complicated by arbitrary node ordering. A graph with n nodes admits n-factorial node orderings, yielding equivalent adjacency-matrix representations. An encoder and decoder must therefore handle differences in ordering without confusing them with differences in the underlying graph.

The paper proposes a permutation-invariant variational autoencoder for graph-level learning. Its model indirectly learns to align the node ordering of the input graph with that of the output graph. It does so without prescribing a fixed ordering or performing expensive graph matching, addressing a central representational obstacle to unsupervised graph learning.

The authors demonstrate the model on graph reconstruction, generation, and interpolation, covering both reproducing observed graphs and working with their learned representation space. They also evaluate whether the extracted representations support graph-level classification and regression. These evaluations connect the ordering solution to two purposes: modeling graphs themselves and providing useful features for later predictive tasks. The abstract reports effectiveness without assigning a numerical improvement to those tasks.
summary.tldr: A permutation-invariant graph variational autoencoder learns input-output node alignment without fixed node ordering or expensive graph matching.

title: Permutation-Invariant Variational Autoencoder for Graph-Level Representation Learning

abstract: We study data clustering problems with $\ell_p$-norm objectives (e.g. \textsc{$k$-Median} and \textsc{$k$-Means}) in the context of individual fairness. The dataset consists of $n$ points, and we want to find $k$ centers such that (a) the objective is minimized, while (b) respecting the individual fairness constraint that every point $v$ has a center within a distance at most $r(v)$, where $r(v)$ is $v$'s distance to its $(n/k)$th nearest point. Jung, Kannan, and Lutz [FORC 2020] introduced this concept and designed a clustering algorithm with provable (approximate) fairness and objective guarantees for the $\ell_\infty$ or \textsc{$k$-Center} objective. Mahabadi and Vakilian [ICML 2020] revisited this problem to give a local-search algorithm for all $\ell_p$-norms. Empirically, their algorithms outperform Jung et. al.'s by a large margin in terms of cost (for \textsc{$k$-Median} and \textsc{$k$-Means}), but they incur a reasonable loss in fairness. In this paper, our main contribution is to use Linear Programming (LP) techniques to obtain better algorithms for this problem, both in theory and in practice. We prove that by modifying known LP rounding techniques, one gets a worst-case guarantee on the objective which is much better than in MV20, and empirically, this objective is extremely close to the optimal. Furthermore, our theoretical fairness guarantees are comparable with MV20 in theory, and empirically, we obtain noticeably fairer solutions.Although solving the LP {\em exactly} might be prohibitive, we demonstrate that in practice, a simple sparsification technique drastically improves the run-time of our algorithm.

summary.tldr: Linear-programming-based clustering improves cost guarantees and empirically produces fairer solutions under neighborhood-based individual fairness constraints.

title: Better Algorithms for Individually Fair $k$-Clustering

abstract: Despite the recent popularity of neural network-based solvers for optimal transport (OT), there is no standard quantitative way to evaluate their performance. In this paper, we address this issue for quadratic-cost transport---specifically, computation of the Wasserstein-2 distance, a commonly-used formulation of optimal transport in machine learning. To overcome the challenge of computing ground truth transport maps between continuous measures needed to assess these solvers, we use input-convex neural networks (ICNN) to construct pairs of measures whose ground truth OT maps can be obtained analytically. This strategy yields pairs of continuous benchmark measures in high-dimensional spaces such as spaces of images. We thoroughly evaluate existing optimal transport solvers using these benchmark measures. Even though these solvers perform well in downstream tasks, many do not faithfully recover optimal transport maps. To investigate the cause of this discrepancy, we further test the solvers in a setting of image generation. Our study reveals crucial limitations of existing solvers and shows that increased OT accuracy does not necessarily correlate to better results downstream.

paragraphs: Neural optimal transport solvers can perform well inside applications, but that does not directly show whether they solve the transport problem accurately. This paper develops a quantitative benchmark for transport with quadratic cost, the setting associated with the Wasserstein-2 distance. The central obstacle is obtaining known correct transport maps between continuous distributions.

The authors use input-convex neural networks to construct pairs of distributions whose optimal transport maps can be calculated analytically. This makes it possible to compare a solver’s output against an actual reference solution. The construction also supports high-dimensional continuous distributions, including distributions in image spaces.

Evaluating existing solvers reveals that many fail to recover the correct transport maps faithfully despite useful downstream performance. Further experiments in image generation examine this mismatch and show that greater transport accuracy does not necessarily correspond to better application results. The benchmark therefore separates two questions that can otherwise be conflated: whether a method solves optimal transport accurately and whether it produces useful results in a downstream task.
summary.tldr: Analytically solvable transport benchmarks reveal that downstream success can coexist with inaccurate neural optimal transport maps.

title: Do Neural Optimal Transport Solvers Work? A Continuous Wasserstein-2 Benchmark

abstract: The performance of ML models degrades when the training population is different from that seen under operation. Towards assessing distributional robustness, we study the worst-case performance of a model over all subpopulations of a given size, defined with respect to core attributes $Z$. This notion of robustness can consider arbitrary (continuous) attributes $Z$, and automatically accounts for complex intersectionality in disadvantaged groups. We develop a scalable yet principled two-stage estimation procedure that can evaluate the robustness of state-of-the-art models. We prove that our procedure enjoys several finite-sample convergence guarantees, including dimension-free convergence. Instead of overly conservative notions based on Rademacher complexities, our evaluation error depends on the dimension of $Z$ only through the out-of-sample error in estimating the performance conditional on $Z$. On real datasets, we demonstrate that our method certifies the robustness of a model and prevents deployment of unreliable models.

paragraphs: A model's overall performance can conceal poor results for particular parts of a population. This paper evaluates the worst performance among all subpopulations of a specified size, with membership defined through selected core attributes. Those attributes can be continuous, and the formulation accommodates complex intersections of characteristics in disadvantaged groups.

The authors develop a scalable two-stage estimation procedure for this robustness measure. Estimating model performance conditional on the attributes is central to its accuracy. The procedure comes with finite-sample convergence guarantees, including dimension-free convergence results. The influence of attribute dimension enters through the out-of-sample error of the conditional-performance estimate, rather than a direct complexity penalty based on that dimension.

This distinction matters because it ties evaluation accuracy to how well the relevant performance pattern can actually be learned. On real datasets, the authors demonstrate robustness certification and identification of unreliable models before deployment. These findings concern the defined family of attribute-based subpopulations and provide a more targeted assessment than an aggregate score over the whole population.
summary.tldr: A two-stage estimator assesses worst-case performance across attribute-defined subpopulations, with finite-sample guarantees and practical robustness evaluations.

title: Evaluating model performance under worst-case subpopulations

abstract: We consider interpolation learning in high-dimensional linear regression with Gaussian data, and prove a generic uniform convergence guarantee on the generalization error of interpolators in an arbitrary hypothesis class in terms of the class’s Gaussian width. Applying the generic bound to Euclidean norm balls recovers the consistency result of Bartlett et al. (2020) for minimum-norm interpolators, and confirms a prediction of Zhou et al. (2020) for near-minimal-norm interpolators in the special case of Gaussian data. We demonstrate the generality of the bound by applying it to the simplex, obtaining a novel consistency result for minimum $\ell_1$-norm interpolators (basis pursuit). Our results show how norm-based generalization bounds can explain and be used to analyze benign overfitting, at least in some settings.

paragraphs: An interpolating model fits its training observations exactly, yet it can sometimes still predict well on new data. This paper studies that phenomenon in high-dimensional linear regression with Gaussian data. It asks how generalization guarantees based on the size or geometry of a hypothesis class can explain such benign overfitting.

The authors prove a uniform bound for interpolators in an arbitrary hypothesis class, expressed through the class's Gaussian width. Applying it to Euclidean norm balls recovers an existing consistency result for minimum-norm interpolators. It also confirms a prediction about interpolators whose norms are close to minimal, specifically in the Gaussian-data setting considered here.

A further application to the simplex yields a new consistency result for minimum l1-norm interpolation, also called basis pursuit. These applications demonstrate that one general bound can address different restrictions on fitted models. The conclusion is qualified: norm-based generalization bounds can explain benign overfitting in some settings, with the paper's guarantees developed under its Gaussian linear-regression assumptions.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-width generalization bound explains benign overfitting for several norm-constrained interpolators in Gaussian linear regression.

title: Uniform Convergence of Interpolators: Gaussian Width, Norm Bounds and Benign Overfitting

abstract: When facing uncertainty, decision-makers want predictions they can trust. A machine learning provider can convey confidence to decision-makers by guaranteeing their predictions are distribution calibrated--- amongst the inputs that receive a predicted vector of class probabilities q, the actual distribution over classes is given by q. For multi-class prediction problems, however, directly optimizing predictions under distribution calibration tends to be infeasible, requiring sample complexity that grows exponentially in the number of classes C. In this work, we introduce a new notion---decision calibration---that requires the predicted distribution and true distribution over classes to be ``indistinguishable'' to downstream decision-makers. This perspective gives a new characterization of distribution calibration: a predictor is distribution calibrated if and only if it is decision calibrated with respect to all decision-makers. Our main result shows that under a mild restriction, unlike distribution calibration, decision calibration is actually feasible. We design a recalibration algorithm that provably achieves decision calibration efficiently, provided that the decision-makers have a bounded number of actions (e.g., polynomial in C). We validate our recalibration algorithm empirically: compared to existing methods, decision calibration improves decision-making on skin lesion and ImageNet classification with modern neural network predictors.

paragraphs: A calibrated multiclass predictor should report class probabilities that agree with observed class frequencies. Full distribution calibration requires this agreement for every predicted probability vector. Although attractive as a trust guarantee, directly achieving it can require a number of samples that grows exponentially with the number of classes.

The paper introduces decision calibration, which asks whether predicted and true class distributions are distinguishable to downstream decision-makers. This connects probability accuracy to the decisions those probabilities support. The authors show that full distribution calibration is equivalent to decision calibration for all decision-makers. Restricting the relevant decision-makers therefore offers a way to target a more manageable guarantee.

The main algorithm efficiently achieves decision calibration when decision-makers have a bounded number of available actions, such as a number polynomial in the class count. That restriction is central to the feasibility result. Experiments with skin lesion and ImageNet classifiers show improved decision-making compared with existing recalibration methods. The contribution is both a theoretical connection and a practical way to calibrate predictions around their intended use.
summary.tldr: Decision calibration makes multiclass recalibration tractable by targeting downstream decision-makers with a bounded number of actions.

title: Calibrating Predictions to Decisions: A Novel Approach to Multi-Class Calibration

abstract: The visual world around us can be described as a structured set of objects and their associated relations. An image of a room may be conjured given only the description of the underlying objects and their associated relations. While there has been significant work on designing deep neural networks which may compose individual objects together, less work has been done on composing the individual relations between objects. A principal difficulty is that while the placement of objects is mutually independent, their relations are entangled and dependent on each other. To circumvent this issue, existing works primarily compose relations by utilizing a holistic encoder, in the form of text or graphs. In this work, we instead propose to represent each relation as an unnormalized density (an energy-based model), enabling us to compose separate relations in a factorized manner. We show that such a factorized decomposition allows the model to both generate and edit scenes that have multiple sets of relations more faithfully. We further show that decomposition enables our model to effectively understand the underlying relational scene structure.

paragraphs: A scene is defined partly by its objects and partly by the relationships among them. Generating a scene from those relationships is difficult because they depend on one another: satisfying one relationship can affect how the others fit together. This paper focuses on composing those relationships as individually represented components.

The proposed method represents each relation with an energy-based model, described mathematically as an unnormalized density. This gives separate relations their own representations that can be combined in a factorized way. The approach differs from encoding the entire collection of relations through one holistic text or graph representation.

The authors show that this decomposition supports more faithful generation and editing of scenes involving multiple sets of relations. They also report that the model can effectively understand the underlying relational structure. These findings suggest that separately modeling relations can be useful even when the relations themselves are interdependent. The contribution is a compositional representation that serves both changing a scene and interpreting how its objects relate.
summary.tldr: Representing visual relations as separate energy-based models enables more faithful scene generation, editing, and relational understanding.

title: Learning to Compose Visual Relations

abstract: In traditional software programs, it is easy to trace program logic from variables back to input, apply assertion statements to block erroneous behavior, and compose programs together. Although deep learning programs have demonstrated strong performance on novel applications, they sacrifice many of the functionalities of traditional software programs. With this as motivation, we take a modest first step towards improving deep learning programs by jointly training a generative model to constrain neural network activations to "decode" back to inputs. We call this design a Decodable Neural Network, or DecNN. Doing so enables a form of compositionality in neural networks, where one can recursively compose DecNN with itself to create an ensemble-like model with uncertainty. In our experiments, we demonstrate applications of this uncertainty to out-of-distribution detection, adversarial example detection, and calibration --- while matching standard neural networks in accuracy. We further explore this compositionality by combining DecNN with pretrained models, where we show promising results that neural networks can be regularized from using protected features.

paragraphs: Traditional software allows intermediate variables to be traced back to inputs and components to be composed into larger programs. This paper takes a step toward related capabilities in neural networks. Its Decodable Neural Network, or DecNN, jointly trains a generative model that constrains internal activations to decode back into inputs.

These findings present decoding as a useful route toward limited compositional capabilities, with demonstrated applications to uncertainty and an exploratory application to feature use.
summary.tldr: DecNN makes internal representations decodable to inputs, enabling recursive composition and useful uncertainty estimates while retaining classification accuracy.

title: Improving Compositionality of Neural Networks by Decoding Representations to Inputs

abstract: Matching is one of the most fundamental and broadly applicable problems across many domains. In these diverse real-world applications, there is often a degree of uncertainty in the input which has led to the study of stochastic matching models. Here, each edge in the graph has a known, independent probability of existing derived from some prediction. Algorithms must probe edges to determine existence and match them irrevocably if they exist. Further, each vertex may have a patience constraint denoting how many of its neighboring edges can be probed. We present new ordered contention resolution schemes yielding improved approximation guarantees for some of the foundational problems studied in this area. For stochastic matching with patience constraints in general graphs, we provide a $0.382$-approximate algorithm, significantly improving over the previous best $0.31$-approximation of Baveja et al. (2018). When the vertices do not have patience constraints, we describe a $0.432$-approximate random order probing algorithm with several corollaries such as an improved guarantee for the Prophet Secretary problem under Edge Arrivals. Finally, for the special case of bipartite graphs with unit patience constraints on one of the partitions, we show a $0.632$-approximate algorithm that improves on the recent $1/3$-guarantee of Hikima et al. (2021).

An algorithm must probe an edge to discover whether it exists and commit to matching it if it does. Vertices may also have patience constraints that limit how many adjacent edges can be probed.

These are theoretical performance guarantees for distinct matching settings. Together, they show how better resolution of competing matching opportunities can improve achievable guarantees when uncertainty, irreversible choices, and probing limits interact.
summary.tldr: New ordered contention resolution schemes improve approximation guarantees for several stochastic matching problems with uncertain edges and probing constraints.

title: Improved Guarantees for Offline Stochastic Matching via new Ordered Contention Resolution Schemes

abstract: Contextual bandit algorithms are increasingly replacing non-adaptive A/B tests in e-commerce, healthcare, and policymaking because they can both improve outcomes for study participants and increase the chance of identifying good or even best policies. To support credible inference on novel interventions at the end of the study, nonetheless, we still want to construct valid confidence intervals on average treatment effects, subgroup effects, or value of new policies. The adaptive nature of the data collected by contextual bandit algorithms, however, makes this difficult: standard estimators are no longer asymptotically normally distributed and classic confidence intervals fail to provide correct coverage. While this has been addressed in non-contextual settings by using stabilized estimators, variance stabilized estimators in the contextual setting pose unique challenges that we tackle for the first time in this paper. We propose the Contextual Adaptive Doubly Robust (CADR) estimator, a novel estimator for policy value that is asymptotically normal under contextual adaptive data collection. The main technical challenge in constructing CADR is designing adaptive and consistent conditional standard deviation estimators for stabilization. Extensive numerical experiments using 57 OpenML datasets demonstrate that confidence intervals based on CADR uniquely provide correct coverage.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits adapt decisions as a study proceeds, potentially improving participants' outcomes while learning useful policies. That adaptation complicates later statistical analysis. Standard estimators may lose asymptotic normality, so familiar confidence intervals can fail to cover the true quantity at their intended rate.

The paper introduces the Contextual Adaptive Doubly Robust estimator, or CADR, for policy value. Its central construction stabilizes estimation under contextual, adaptive data collection. The technical challenge is to estimate conditional standard deviations in a way that is both adaptive and consistent. This addresses difficulties that arise when observations depend on context as well as previous learning.

The authors establish asymptotic normality for CADR, providing a basis for confidence intervals after adaptive collection. Numerical experiments using 57 OpenML datasets report that CADR-based intervals uniquely achieve correct coverage among the evaluated approaches. The contribution connects adaptive decision-making with credible post-study policy evaluation: collecting data to improve decisions need not preclude useful uncertainty estimates when the estimator accounts for the collection process.
summary.tldr: CADR stabilizes policy-value estimation from contextual bandit data to support asymptotically normal inference and valid confidence intervals.

title: Post-Contextual-Bandit Inference

abstract: With the tremendous advances in the architecture and scale of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) over the past few decades, they can easily reach or even exceed the performance of humans in certain tasks. However, a recently discovered shortcoming of CNNs is that they are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Although the adversarial robustness of CNNs can be improved by adversarial training, there is a trade-off between standard accuracy and adversarial robustness. From the neural architecture perspective, this paper aims to improve the adversarial robustness of the backbone CNNs that have a satisfactory accuracy. Under a minimal computational overhead, the introduction of a dilation architecture is expected to be friendly with the standard performance of the backbone CNN while pursuing adversarial robustness. Theoretical analyses on the standard and adversarial error bounds naturally motivate the proposed neural architecture dilation algorithm. Experimental results on real-world datasets and benchmark neural networks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm to balance the accuracy and adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: Convolutional neural networks can achieve strong task performance while remaining vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Adversarial training can improve robustness, but it introduces a trade-off with standard accuracy. This paper approaches that trade-off through architecture, starting with a backbone network whose ordinary predictive accuracy is already satisfactory.

The proposed neural architecture dilation algorithm introduces an architectural addition intended to improve robustness with minimal computational overhead. Preserving the backbone's standard performance is a design goal, alongside making it more resistant to adversarial inputs. The authors motivate the algorithm through theoretical analyses of both standard and adversarial error bounds, linking the architectural proposal to the two performance criteria it must balance.

Experiments on real-world datasets and benchmark networks support the algorithm's effectiveness in balancing accuracy and robustness. The findings indicate that architectural changes can contribute to this balance in the studied settings. The abstract frames compatibility with standard accuracy as an aim of the method; it does not claim that every backbone receives robustness improvements with no accuracy cost.
summary.tldr: Neural architecture dilation seeks to improve adversarial robustness with little computational overhead while maintaining a useful balance with standard accuracy.

title: Neural Architecture Dilation for Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Isaac Gym offers a high-performance learning platform to train policies for a wide variety of robotics tasks entirely on GPU. Both physics simulation and neural network policy training reside on GPU and communicate by directly passing data from physics buffers to PyTorch tensors without ever going through CPU bottlenecks. This leads to blazing fast training times for complex robotics tasks on a single GPU with 2-3 orders of magnitude improvements compared to conventional RL training that uses a CPU-based simulator and GPUs for neural networks. We host the results and videos at https://sites.google.com/view/isaacgym-nvidia and Isaac Gym can be downloaded at https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac-gym. The benchmark and environments are available at https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse/IsaacGymEnvs.
originalAbstract: Isaac Gym offers a high-performance learning platform to train policies for a wide variety of robotics tasks entirely on GPU. Both physics simulation and neural network policy training reside on GPU and communicate by directly passing data from physics buffers to PyTorch tensors without ever going through CPU bottlenecks. This leads to blazing fast training times for complex robotics tasks on a single GPU with 2-3 orders of magnitude improvements compared to conventional RL training that uses a CPU-based simulator and GPUs for neural networks. We host the results and videos at https://sites.google.com/view/isaacgym-nvidia and Isaac Gym can be downloaded at https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac-gym. The benchmark and environments are available at https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse/IsaacGymEnvs.

paragraphs: Training a robot control policy through reinforcement learning involves repeated interaction between a physics simulator and a learning system. Isaac Gym places both physics simulation and neural-network policy training on the GPU. The platform is intended to support a wide variety of robotics tasks through this integrated arrangement.

Its central implementation choice is direct communication between physics buffers and PyTorch tensors. Simulation data can therefore reach the learning system without passing through the CPU bottlenecks described in the paper. Keeping both parts of the training process on the same kind of processor makes this data path central to the platform’s performance.

For complex robotics tasks, the authors report training-time improvements of two to three orders of magnitude on a single GPU compared with conventional training that combines a CPU-based simulator with GPU neural networks. This is a claim about faster training in the reported comparison. The released simulator, benchmark, and environments provide resources for using and examining this GPU-based approach to robot learning.
summary.tldr: Isaac Gym keeps physics simulation and policy training on the GPU, reporting training speedups of two to three orders of magnitude.

title: Isaac Gym: High Performance GPU Based Physics Simulation For Robot Learning

abstract: Artificial electromagnetic materials (AEMs), including metamaterials, derive their electromagnetic properties from geometry rather than chemistry. With the appropriate geometric design, AEMs have achieved exotic properties not realizable with conventional materials (e.g., cloaking or negative refractive index). However, understanding the relationship between the AEM structure and its properties is often poorly understood. While computational electromagnetic simulation (CEMS) may help design new AEMs, its use is limited due to its long computational time. Recently, it has been shown that deep learning can be an alternative solution to infer the relationship between an AEM geometry and its properties using a (relatively) small pool of CEMS data. However, the limited publicly released datasets and models and no widely-used benchmark for comparison have made using deep learning approaches even more difficult. Furthermore, configuring CEMS for a specific problem requires substantial expertise and time, making reproducibility challenging. Here, we develop a collection of three classes of AEM problems: metamaterials, nanophotonics, and color filter designs. We also publicly release software, allowing other researchers to conduct additional simulations for each system easily. Finally, we conduct experiments on our benchmark datasets with three recent neural network architectures: the multilayer perceptron (MLP), MLP-mixer, and transformer. We identify the methods and models that generalize best over the three problems to establish the best practice and baseline results upon which future research can build.

Computational simulations help investigate it, although their long running times can limit design work. Learned surrogate models offer a way to infer these relationships from simulation data.

The paper addresses obstacles to comparing and reproducing such models: few public datasets and models, no widely adopted benchmark, and substantial expertise needed to configure simulations. It assembles problems in three areas—metamaterials, nanophotonics, and color filters—and releases software that allows researchers to run additional simulations for each system.

The authors compare multilayer perceptrons, MLP-mixers, and transformers on the benchmark datasets. They identify methods and models that generalize best across the three problems, establishing reference results and practical guidance for future work. The combination of datasets, simulation software, and model comparisons makes both evaluation and extension of these design problems more accessible.
summary.tldr: This benchmark pairs three electromagnetic material design problems with simulation software and neural network comparisons to support reproducible surrogate modeling.

title: Benchmarking Data-driven Surrogate Simulators for Artificial Electromagnetic Materials

abstract: Many promising approaches to symbolic regression have been presented in recent years, yet progress in the field continues to suffer from a lack of uniform, robust, and transparent benchmarking standards. In this paper, we address this shortcoming by introducing an open-source, reproducible benchmarking platform for symbolic regression. We assess 14 symbolic regression methods and 7 machine learning methods on a set of 252 diverse regression problems. Our assessment includes both real-world datasets with no known model form as well as ground-truth benchmark problems, including physics equations and systems of ordinary differential equations. For the real-world datasets, we benchmark the ability of each method to learn models with low error and low complexity relative to state-of-the-art machine learning methods. For the synthetic problems, we assess each method's ability to find exact solutions in the presence of varying levels of noise. Under these controlled experiments, we conclude that the best performing methods for real-world regression combine genetic algorithms with parameter estimation and/or semantic search drivers. When tasked with recovering exact equations in the presence of noise, we find that deep learning and genetic algorithm-based approaches perform similarly. We provide a detailed guide to reproducing this experiment and contributing new methods, and encourage other researchers to collaborate with us on a common and living symbolic regression benchmark.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for mathematical expressions that describe data. This paper introduces a reproducible, open-source platform for comparing methods, addressing a lack of consistent evaluation standards. The study evaluates 14 symbolic regression methods and seven machine learning methods across 252 regression problems, giving the comparison substantial variety.

The benchmark separates two goals. On real-world datasets, where the underlying equation is unknown, it evaluates whether methods produce models with low prediction error and low complexity. On synthetic problems with known equations, including physics equations and differential-equation systems, it tests whether methods can recover the exact expression under different amounts of noise.

Within these experiments, the strongest real-world methods combine genetic algorithms with parameter estimation, semantic search guidance, or both. For exact equation recovery in noisy data, deep learning and genetic algorithm approaches perform similarly. These findings depend on the evaluated tasks and goals, highlighting why prediction quality and equation recovery deserve separate assessment. Reproduction instructions and support for adding methods make the platform a basis for continued comparison.
summary.tldr: A broad symbolic regression benchmark finds task-dependent strengths, with hybrid genetic methods leading real-world regression in the reported experiments.

title: Contemporary Symbolic Regression Methods and their Relative Performance

abstract: In online learning problems, exploiting low variance plays an important role in obtaining tight performance guarantees yet is challenging because variances are often not known a priori. Recently, considerable progress has been made by Zhang et al. (2021) where they obtain a variance-adaptive regret bound for linear bandits without knowledge of the variances and a horizon-free regret bound for linear mixture Markov decision processes (MDPs). In this paper, we present novel analyses that improve their regret bounds significantly. For linear bandits, we achieve $\tilde O(\min\{d\sqrt{K}, d^{1.5}\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^K \sigma_k^2}\} + d^2)$ where $d$ is the dimension of the features, $K$ is the time horizon, and $\sigma_k^2$ is the noise variance at time step $k$, and $\tilde O$ ignores polylogarithmic dependence, which is a factor of $d^3$ improvement. For linear mixture MDPs with the assumption of maximum cumulative reward in an episode being in $[0,1]$, we achieve a horizon-free regret bound of $\tilde O(d \sqrt{K} + d^2)$ where $d$ is the number of base models and $K$ is the number of episodes. This is a factor of $d^{3.5}$ improvement in the leading term and $d^7$ in the lower order term. Our analysis critically relies on a novel peeling-based regret analysis that leverages the elliptical potential `count' lemma.

paragraphs: Online learners can benefit when observations contain little noise, but the noise variances may be unknown beforehand. This paper develops sharper regret analyses for variance-adaptive linear bandits and linear mixture Markov decision processes. Regret measures the accumulated performance loss associated with learning rather than already having the best decisions available.

For linear bandits, the bound is the smaller of d√K and d^1.5√(Σσ²), plus d², with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here d is feature dimension, K is the number of steps, and Σσ² is cumulative noise variance. The variance-dependent term captures potential benefits from lower noise without requiring advance knowledge of those variances. The authors report a factor-d³ improvement over the preceding analysis.

For linear mixture processes, the regret bound becomes d√K + d², again suppressing logarithmic factors. This horizon-free result assumes that maximum cumulative reward per episode lies in [0,1]; d counts base models and K counts episodes. A new peeling-based analysis using an elliptical potential count lemma drives the improvements, sharpening guarantees in both settings.
summary.tldr: New analyses substantially tighten variance-adaptive linear-bandit regret bounds and horizon-free bounds for normalized-reward linear mixture processes.

title: Improved Regret Analysis for Variance-Adaptive Linear Bandits and Horizon-Free Linear Mixture MDPs

abstract: Cross-domain few-shot learning (CD-FSL) has drawn increasing attention for handling large differences between the source and target domains--an important concern in real-world scenarios. To overcome these large differences, recent works have considered exploiting small-scale unlabeled data from the target domain during the pre-training stage. This data enables self-supervised pre-training on the target domain, in addition to supervised pre-training on the source domain. In this paper, we empirically investigate which pre-training is preferred based on domain similarity and few-shot difficulty of the target domain. We discover that the performance gain of self-supervised pre-training over supervised pre-training becomes large when the target domain is dissimilar to the source domain, or the target domain itself has low few-shot difficulty. We further design two pre-training schemes, mixed-supervised and two-stage learning, that improve performance. In this light, we present six findings for CD-FSL, which are supported by extensive experiments and analyses on three source and eight target benchmark datasets with varying levels of domain similarity and few-shot difficulty. Our code is available at https://github.com/sungnyun/understanding-cdfsl.
