paragraphs: Cross-domain few-shot learning aims to adapt to a target domain using few labeled examples when that domain differs from the source training data. Small amounts of unlabeled target data offer another resource: self-supervised pre-training within the target domain. This paper investigates when that option is preferable to supervised pre-training on the source domain.

The analysis focuses on two factors: similarity between source and target domains, and the difficulty of the target's few-shot task. Experiments find that the advantage of target-domain self-supervised pre-training grows when the domains are dissimilar or when the target has low few-shot difficulty. These are empirical relationships that help explain why a pre-training choice may work differently across tasks.

The authors also introduce mixed-supervised and two-stage pre-training schemes that improve performance. Their study presents six findings supported by experiments and analyses using three source and eight target benchmark datasets. The contribution is a more structured understanding of pre-training choices, alongside improved schemes that make use of the available supervised and self-supervised learning opportunities.
summary.tldr: Experiments connect pre-training effectiveness in cross-domain few-shot learning to domain similarity and target-task difficulty.

title: Understanding Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning Based on Domain Similarity and Few-Shot Difficulty

abstract: Current Graph Neural Networks (GNN) architectures generally rely on two important components: node features embedding through message passing, and aggregation with a specialized form of pooling. The structural (or topological) information is implicitly taken into account in these two steps. We propose in this work a novel point of view, which places distances to some learnable graph templates at the core of the graph representation. This distance embedding is constructed thanks to an optimal transport distance: the Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) distance, which encodes simultaneously feature and structure dissimilarities by solving a soft graph-matching problem. We postulate that the vector of FGW distances to a set of template graphs has a strong discriminative power, which is then fed to a non-linear classifier for final predictions. Distance embedding can be seen as a new layer, and can leverage on existing message passing techniques to promote sensible feature representations. Interestingly enough, in our work the optimal set of template graphs is also learnt in an end-to-end fashion by differentiating through this layer. After describing the corresponding learning procedure, we empirically validate our claim on several synthetic and real life graph classification datasets, where our method is competitive or surpasses kernel and GNN state-of-the-art approaches. We complete our experiments by an ablation study and a sensitivity analysis to parameters.

paragraphs: Many graph neural networks represent a graph through message passing followed by pooling, with structural information incorporated implicitly. This paper proposes representing a graph by its distances to a set of learnable template graphs. Each distance contributes one coordinate to a representation that a nonlinear classifier uses for prediction.

The distance is Fused Gromov-Wasserstein, an optimal transport measure that combines differences in node features with differences in graph structure. It obtains this comparison through soft graph matching. The resulting distance-embedding layer can also work with existing message-passing techniques, allowing learned node features to contribute to comparisons with the templates.

The template graphs themselves are learned end to end by differentiating through the distance layer. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graph-classification datasets show performance competitive with or better than the compared state-of-the-art kernel and GNN methods. Ablation and parameter-sensitivity studies further examine the approach. These results support the authors’ hypothesis that distances to learned graph templates can provide a discriminative representation.
summary.tldr: A graph classifier learns template graphs and represents each input through optimal transport distances that compare both features and structure.

title: Template based Graph Neural Network with Optimal Transport Distances

abstract: Generating precise class-aware pseudo ground-truths, a.k.a, class activation maps (CAMs), is essential for Weakly-Supervised Semantic Segmentation. The original CAM method usually produces incomplete and inaccurate localization maps. To tackle with this issue, this paper proposes an Expansion and Shrinkage scheme based on the offset learning in the deformable convolution, to sequentially improve the recall and precision of the located object in the two respective stages. In the Expansion stage, an offset learning branch in a deformable convolution layer, referred to as ``expansion sampler'', seeks to sample increasingly less discriminative object regions, driven by an inverse supervision signal that maximizes image-level classification loss. The located more complete object region in the Expansion stage is then gradually narrowed down to the final object region during the Shrinkage stage. In the Shrinkage stage, the offset learning branch of another deformable convolution layer referred to as the ``shrinkage sampler'', is introduced to exclude the false positive background regions attended in the Expansion stage to improve the precision of the localization maps. We conduct various experiments on PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO 2014 to well demonstrate the superiority of our method over other state-of-the-art methods for Weakly-Supervised Semantic Segmentation. The code is available at https://github.com/TyroneLi/ESOL_WSSS.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised semantic segmentation needs useful estimates of where each object class appears without relying on full pixel-level supervision. Class activation maps provide such estimates, but often cover only part of an object or include incorrect regions. This paper separates improving coverage from removing mistakes through an expansion stage followed by a shrinkage stage.

Expansion uses learned sampling offsets in a deformable convolution layer. Its sampler is driven by an inverse supervision signal that maximizes the image-level classification loss, encouraging it to seek less discriminative object regions. The purpose is to extend localization beyond the most recognizable parts and recover a more complete object area.

The expanded region can also include background. A second deformable-convolution sampler therefore narrows it by excluding false positives, improving localization precision after expansion has improved recall. Experiments on PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO 2014 report superiority over the compared state-of-the-art segmentation methods. The contribution is a sequential way to improve the pseudo ground truths on which weakly supervised segmentation depends.
summary.tldr: Learned expansion and shrinkage samplers improve object coverage and remove background from weakly supervised localization maps.

title: Expansion and Shrinkage of Localization for Weakly-Supervised Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Real-world classification problems must contend with domain shift, the (potential) mismatch between the domain where a model is deployed and the domain(s) where the training data was gathered. Methods to handle such problems must specify what structure is held in common between the domains and what is allowed to vary. A natural assumption is that causal (structural) relationships are invariant in all domains. Then, it is tempting to learn a predictor for label $Y$ that depends only on its causal parents. However, many real-world problems are ``anti-causal'' in the sense that $Y$ is a cause of the covariates $X$---in this case, $Y$ has no causal parents and the naive causal invariance is useless. In this paper, we study representation learning under a particular notion of domain shift that both respects causal invariance and that naturally handles the ``anti-causal'' structure. We show how to leverage the shared causal structure of the domains to learn a representation that both admits an invariant predictor and that also allows fast adaptation in new domains. The key is to translate causal assumptions into learning principles that disentangle ``invariant'' and ``non-stable'' features. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed learning algorithm.

paragraphs: A classifier may encounter different data conditions after deployment, making it important to specify what stays stable across domains. Causal relationships offer one possible source of stability. However, a strategy that predicts a label only from its causal parents is unhelpful in the anti-causal setting studied here, where the label causes the observed covariates.

The paper develops representation learning for a particular form of domain shift that preserves shared causal structure while accommodating this anti-causal relationship. It translates the causal assumptions into learning principles that separate invariant features from features that can change across domains. This separation is the central mechanism of the proposed approach.

The learned representation supports both an invariant predictor and fast adaptation to new domains. These are complementary uses of the shared structure: maintaining stable predictive information while retaining information useful for adjustment. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. The result is tied to the specified causal account of domain shift, rather than an unrestricted claim about every deployment mismatch.
summary.tldr: Separating stable and changing features under shared causal assumptions supports invariant prediction and fast domain adaptation.

title: Invariant and Transportable Representations for Anti-Causal Domain Shifts

abstract: We study sequential general online regression, known also as sequential probability assignments, under logarithmic loss when compared against a broad class of experts. We obtain tight, often matching, lower and upper bounds for sequential minimax regret, which is defined as the excess loss incurred by the predictor over the best expert in the class. After proving a general upper bound we consider some specific classes of experts from Lipschitz class to bounded Hessian class and derive matching lower and upper bounds with provably optimal constants. Our bounds work for a wide range of values of the data dimension and the number of rounds. To derive lower bounds, we use tools from information theory (e.g., Shtarkov sum) and for upper bounds, we resort to new "smooth truncated covering" of the class of experts. This allows us to find constructive proofs by applying a simple and novel truncated Bayesian algorithm. Our proofs are substantially simpler than the existing ones and yet provide tighter (and often optimal) bounds.

paragraphs: In sequential prediction, a learner assigns probabilities as observations arrive and incurs logarithmic loss. The paper studies how much extra loss the learner must suffer relative to the best expert in a specified class. This difference is regret, and minimax regret describes the best achievable worst-case performance.

The authors derive a general upper bound and then study particular expert classes, including those constrained by Lipschitz regularity or bounded Hessians. For these classes, they obtain matching lower and upper bounds with provably optimal constants. The bounds apply across a wide range of data dimensions and numbers of prediction rounds.

The lower bounds use information-theoretic tools, while the upper bounds rely on a new smooth truncated covering of the expert class. This construction supports a simple truncated Bayesian algorithm, making the upper-bound argument constructive. The authors report simpler proofs and tighter, often optimal bounds. Matching bounds matter because they identify both what an algorithm can achieve and what no algorithm can improve upon in the specified setting.
summary.tldr: A truncated Bayesian algorithm yields constructive log-loss regret bounds that often match lower bounds, including optimal constants for specified expert classes.

title: Precise Regret Bounds for Log-loss via a Truncated Bayesian Algorithm

abstract: The paper introduces PaintSeg, a new unsupervised method for segmenting objects without any training. We propose an adversarial masked contrastive painting (AMCP) process, which creates a contrast between the original image and a painted image in which a masked area is painted using off-the-shelf generative models. During the painting process, inpainting and outpainting are alternated, with the former masking the foreground and filling in the background, and the latter masking the background while recovering the missing part of the foreground object. Inpainting and outpainting, also referred to as I-step and O-step, allow our method to gradually advance the target segmentation mask toward the ground truth without supervision or training. PaintSeg can be configured to work with a variety of prompts, e.g. coarse masks, boxes, scribbles, and points. Our experimental results demonstrate that PaintSeg outperforms existing approaches in coarse mask-prompt, box-prompt, and point-prompt segmentation tasks, providing a training-free solution suitable for unsupervised segmentation. Code: https://github.com/lxa9867/PaintSeg.

paragraphs: PaintSeg segments objects by repeatedly modifying an image with existing generative models, without training a segmentation model. Its core process compares the original image with a painted version in which a masked region has been regenerated. Those contrasts guide refinement of the mask that separates the target object from its surroundings.

The procedure alternates two operations. Inpainting masks the foreground and fills the region with background, while outpainting masks the background and recovers missing portions of the foreground object. The authors describe this alternating process as gradually moving the segmentation mask toward the correct object boundary without supervision or additional training.

PaintSeg can accept several kinds of prompts, including coarse masks, boxes, scribbles, and points. The reported experiments show improvements over existing methods for coarse-mask, box, and point prompts. Its training-free claim concerns the segmentation procedure, which uses off-the-shelf generative models as a resource. The contribution demonstrates how repeated image generation and comparison can serve as a mechanism for object segmentation.
summary.tldr: PaintSeg alternates generative inpainting and outpainting to refine prompted object masks without additional training.

title: PaintSeg: Painting Pixels for Training-free Segmentation

abstract: We study the problem of designing mechanisms when agents' valuation functions are drawn from unknown and correlated prior distributions. In particular, we are given a prior distribution $D$, and we are interested in designing a (truthful) mechanism that has good performance for all "true distributions" that are close to $D$ in Total Variation (TV) distance. We show that DSIC and BIC mechanisms in this setting are strongly robust with respect to TV distance, for any bounded objective function $\mathcal{O}$, extending a recent result of Brustle et al. ([BCD20], EC 2020). At the heart of our result is a fundamental duality property of total variation distance. As direct applications of our result, we (i) demonstrate how to find approximately revenue-optimal and approximately BIC mechanisms for weakly dependent prior distributions; (ii) show how to find correlation-robust mechanisms when only ``noisy'' versions of marginals are accessible, extending recent results of Bei et. al. ([BGLT19], SODA 2019); (iii) prove that prophet-inequality type guarantees are preserved for correlated priors, recovering a variant of a result of D{\"u}tting and Kesselheim ([DK19], EC 2019) as a special case; (iv) give a new necessary condition for a correlated distribution to witness an infinite separation in revenue between simple and optimal mechanisms, complementing recent results of Psomas et al. ([PSCW22], NeurIPS 2022); (v) give a new condition for simple mechanisms to approximate revenue-optimal mechanisms for the case of a single agent whose type is drawn from a correlated distribution that can be captured by a Markov Random Field, complementing recent results of Cai and Oikonomou ([CO21], EC 2021).

abstract: While ensuring stability for linear systems is well understood, it remains a major challenge for nonlinear systems. A general approach in such cases is to compute a combination of a Lyapunov function and an associated control policy. However, finding Lyapunov functions for general nonlinear systems is a challenging task. To address this challenge, several methods have been proposed that represent Lyapunov functions using neural networks. However, such approaches either focus on continuous-time systems, or highly restricted classes of nonlinear dynamics. We propose the first approach for learning neural Lyapunov control in a broad class of discrete-time systems. Three key ingredients enable us to effectively learn provably stable control policies. The first is a novel mixed-integer linear programming approach for verifying the discrete-time Lyapunov stability conditions, leveraging the particular structure of these conditions. The second is a novel approach for computing verified sublevel sets. The third is a heuristic gradient-based method for quickly finding counterexamples to significantly speed up Lyapunov function learning. Our experiments on four standard benchmarks demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. For example, on the path tracking benchmark, we outperform recent neural Lyapunov control baselines by an order of magnitude in both running time and the size of the region of attraction, and on two of the four benchmarks (cartpole and PVTOL), ours is the first automated approach to return a provably stable controller. Our code is available at: https://github.com/jlwu002/nlc_discrete.

This paper develops a method for learning neural Lyapunov control across a broad class of discrete-time systems, extending beyond earlier continuous-time or narrowly restricted settings.

Another procedure computes verified sublevel sets, identifying certified portions of the state space. A gradient-based heuristic quickly searches for counterexamples, helping the learning process discover where a candidate certificate fails and speeding up its improvement.

Across four standard benchmarks, the authors report significant gains over leading baselines. On path tracking, both runtime and region-of-attraction size improve by an order of magnitude over recent neural Lyapunov methods. For cartpole and PVTOL, they report the first automated approach to return a provably stable controller. The results connect faster certificate learning with larger verified regions of stable behavior.
summary.tldr: The method combines neural learning and formal verification to produce provably stable controllers for a broad class of discrete-time systems.

title: Neural Lyapunov Control for Discrete-Time Systems

abstract: We present a novel perspective and algorithm for learning directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) from data generated by a linear structural equation model (SEM). First, we show that a linear SEM can be viewed as a linear transform that, in prior work, computes the data from a dense input vector of random valued root causes (as we will call them) associated with the nodes. Instead, we consider the case of (approximately) few root causes and also introduce noise in the measurement of the data. Intuitively, this means that the DAG data is produced by few data generating events whose effect percolates through the DAG. We prove identifiability in this new setting and show that the true DAG is the global minimizer of the $L^0$-norm of the vector of root causes. For data satisfying the few root causes assumption, we show superior performance compared to prior DAG learning methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a directed acyclic graph from data produced by a linear structural equation model. It views that model as a linear transformation of underlying random inputs, which the authors call root causes. The proposed setting assumes that only a few such causes are active, at least approximately, and also allows measurement noise.

The intuition is that a small number of generating events can affect many observed variables as their effects propagate through the graph. The authors develop an algorithm around this perspective and prove identifiability in the new setting. They also show that the true graph globally minimizes the L0 measure of the root-cause vector, which counts its nonzero entries.

This gives sparsity in the generating events a direct role in identifying graph structure. For data that satisfy the few-root-causes assumption, the authors report better performance than prior graph-learning methods. Both the theoretical motivation and the empirical comparison depend on this structured data-generation setting. The contribution is a way to exploit sparse initiating events even when their downstream effects spread broadly through the observed system.
summary.tldr: Assuming few underlying generating events enables identifiable DAG learning and improved performance on data satisfying that assumption.

title: Learning DAGs from Data with Few Root Causes

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is important for deploying reliable machine learning models on real-world applications. Recent advances in outlier exposure have shown promising results on OOD detection via fine-tuning model with informatively sampled auxiliary outliers. However, previous methods assume that the collected outliers can be sufficiently large and representative to cover the boundary between ID and OOD data, which might be impractical and challenging. In this work, we propose a novel framework, namely, Diversified Outlier Exposure (DivOE), for effective OOD detection via informative extrapolation based on the given auxiliary outliers. Specifically, DivOE introduces a new learning objective, which diversifies the auxiliary distribution by explicitly synthesizing more informative outliers for extrapolation during training. It leverages a multi-step optimization method to generate novel outliers beyond the original ones, which is compatible with many variants of outlier exposure. Extensive experiments and analyses have been conducted to characterize and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DivOE. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/DivOE.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks a model to recognize inputs that fall outside its familiar data distribution. Outlier exposure helps by training with auxiliary examples of unfamiliar inputs. This paper addresses a practical difficulty: collecting enough representative outliers to cover the boundary between familiar and unfamiliar data can be challenging.

Diversified Outlier Exposure, or DivOE, expands the usefulness of the outliers already available. It introduces a training objective that explicitly synthesizes informative outliers, diversifying the auxiliary distribution. A multi-step optimization procedure generates examples beyond the original collection, providing extrapolated training material rather than relying entirely on the coverage of collected outliers.

The framework is compatible with many variants of outlier exposure, so its central contribution is a way to enrich their training signal. Extensive experiments and analyses characterize the approach and support its effectiveness for OOD detection. The stated finding is that informative extrapolation improves the use of auxiliary outliers; it does not establish that a finite synthetic collection covers every possible unfamiliar input.
summary.tldr: DivOE synthesizes informative new outliers from available examples to improve out-of-distribution detection.

title: Diversified Outlier Exposure for Out-of-Distribution Detection via Informative Extrapolation

abstract: Conditional independence (CI) testing is a fundamental task in statistics and machine learning, but its effectiveness is hindered by the challenges posed by high-dimensional conditioning variables and limited data samples. This article introduces a novel testing approach to address these challenges and enhance control of the type I error while achieving high power under alternative hypotheses. The proposed approach incorporates a computationally efficient classifier-based conditional mutual information (CMI) estimator, capable of capturing intricate dependence structures among variables. To approximate a distribution encoding the null hypothesis, a $k$-nearest-neighbor local sampling strategy is employed. An important advantage of this approach is its ability to operate without assumptions about distribution forms or feature dependencies. Furthermore, it eliminates the need to derive asymptotic null distributions for the estimated CMI and avoids dataset splitting, making it particularly suitable for small datasets. The method presented in this article demonstrates asymptotic control of the type I error and consistency against all alternative hypotheses. Extensive analyses using both synthetic and real data highlight the computational efficiency of the proposed test. Moreover, it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of type I and II errors, even in scenarios with high-dimensional conditioning sets. Additionally, the proposed approach exhibits robustness in the presence of heavy-tailed data.

paragraphs: Conditional independence testing asks whether two variables remain related after accounting for other variables. It becomes difficult when the conditioning information has many dimensions or the dataset is small. This paper proposes a test combining a classifier-based estimate of conditional mutual information with local sampling based on nearest neighbors.

The classifier estimates potentially complex dependence, while nearest-neighbor sampling approximates a distribution representing the independence hypothesis. The method does not require specified distributional forms or assumptions about feature dependencies. It also avoids splitting the dataset and deriving an asymptotic null distribution for the information estimate, features that make it particularly relevant when samples are scarce.

The authors establish asymptotic control of false positives and consistency against all alternative hypotheses. These are large-sample guarantees rather than an assertion of exact finite-sample error control. Synthetic and real-data evaluations show computational efficiency and lower type I and type II errors than the compared state-of-the-art methods, including with high-dimensional conditioning variables. The reported experiments also show robustness with heavy-tailed data.
summary.tldr: A classifier-based conditional independence test uses nearest-neighbor sampling to support efficient testing with high-dimensional conditioning variables.

title: K-Nearest-Neighbor Local Sampling Based Conditional Independence Testing

abstract: Transformer neural networks can exhibit a surprising capacity for in-context learning (ICL) despite not being explicitly trained for it. Prior work has provided a deeper understanding of how ICL emerges in transformers, e.g. through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, Bayesian inference, or by examining the distributional properties of training data. However, in each of these cases, ICL is treated largely as a persistent phenomenon; namely, once ICL emerges, it is assumed to persist asymptotically. Here, we show that the emergence of ICL during transformer training is, in fact, often transient. We train transformers on synthetic data designed so that both ICL and in-weights learning (IWL) strategies can lead to correct predictions. We find that ICL first emerges, then disappears and gives way to IWL, all while the training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for IWL. The transient nature of ICL is observed in transformers across a range of model sizes and datasets, raising the question of how much to ``overtrain'' transformers when seeking compact, cheaper-to-run models. We find that L2 regularization may offer a path to more persistent ICL that removes the need for early stopping based on ICL-style validation tasks. Finally, we present initial evidence that ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a transformer use information provided in its current context to make predictions. It is often treated as a capability that persists once it appears during training. This paper tests that assumption using synthetic data designed so that either in-context learning or knowledge stored in model weights can produce correct answers.

The authors observe that in-context learning can emerge and later disappear, giving way to in-weights learning even as training loss continues to decrease. They find this pattern across a range of model sizes and datasets. The result shows that improving the training objective can coincide with losing a particular way of solving the task.

This creates a practical question about how long to train compact models when in-context behavior matters. The authors find that L2 regularization may help make that behavior more persistent and avoid reliance on early stopping based on in-context validation tasks. They also present initial evidence that competition between in-context and in-weights circuits may explain the transition, while leaving that causal account tentative.
summary.tldr: In synthetic transformer experiments, in-context learning can disappear with continued training, while L2 regularization may help preserve it.

title: The Transient Nature of Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers

abstract: From clinical development of cancer therapies to investigations into partisan bias, adaptive sequential designs have become increasingly popular method for causal inference, as they offer the possibility of improved precision over their non-adaptive counterparts. However, even in simple settings (e.g. two treatments) the extent to which adaptive designs can improve precision is not sufficiently well understood. In this work, we study the problem of Adaptive Neyman Allocation in a design-based potential outcomes framework, where the experimenter seeks to construct an adaptive design which is nearly as efficient as the optimal (but infeasible) non-adaptive Neyman design, which has access to all potential outcomes. Motivated by connections to online optimization, we propose Neyman Ratio and Neyman Regret as two (equivalent) performance measures of adaptive designs for this problem. We present Clip-OGD, an adaptive design which achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ expected Neyman regret and thereby recovers the optimal Neyman variance in large samples. Finally, we construct a conservative variance estimator which facilitates the development of asymptotically valid confidence intervals. To complement our theoretical results, we conduct simulations using data from a microeconomic experiment.

paragraphs: Sequential experiments can change treatment assignments as observations arrive, potentially improving the precision of causal estimates. This paper asks how closely an adaptive design can approach an ideal Neyman allocation. That benchmark is infeasible in practice because it has access to all potential outcomes, including outcomes that the experimenter cannot observe.

The authors connect this allocation problem to online optimization and introduce two equivalent measures, Neyman Ratio and Neyman Regret, for evaluating adaptive designs. Their Clip-OGD method achieves expected Neyman regret that grows at most on the order of the square root of the experiment length, apart from logarithmic factors. This guarantee implies recovery of the optimal Neyman variance in large samples.

The paper also constructs a conservative variance estimator to support asymptotically valid confidence intervals and supplements the theory with simulations using microeconomic experiment data. The contribution therefore covers both allocation efficiency and uncertainty estimation. Its precision guarantee concerns large-sample behavior, rather than exact equality with the ideal allocation in every finite experiment.
summary.tldr: Clip-OGD adaptively allocates treatments with a regret guarantee that recovers ideal Neyman variance in large samples.

title: CLIP-OGD: An Experimental Design for Adaptive Neyman Allocation in Sequential Experiments

abstract: In an online social network, link recommendations are a way for users to discover relevant links to people they may know, thereby potentially increasing their engagement on the platform. However, the addition of links to a social network can also have an effect on the level of conflict in the network --- expressed in terms of polarization and disagreement. To date, however, we have very little understanding of how these two implications of link formation relate to each other: are the goals of high relevance and conflict reduction aligned, or are the links that users are most likely to accept fundamentally different from the ones with the greatest potential for reducing conflict? Here we provide the first analysis of this question, using the recently popular Friedkin-Johnsen model of opinion dynamics. We first present a surprising result on how link additions shift the level of opinion conflict, followed by explanation work that relates the amount of shift to structural features of the added links. We then characterize the gap in conflict reduction between the set of links achieving the largest reduction and the set of links achieving the highest relevance. The gap is measured on real-world data, based on instantiations of relevance defined by 13 link recommendation algorithms. We find that some, but not all, of the more accurate algorithms actually lead to better reduction of conflict. Our work suggests that social links recommended for increasing user engagement may not be as conflict-provoking as people might have thought.

This paper asks whether relevance and conflict reduction tend to align. It studies that relationship using the Friedkin-Johnsen model of opinion dynamics, which supplies the framework for analyzing how network changes affect opinions.

Real-world data and 13 recommendation algorithms provide different operational definitions of relevance for measuring this gap.

The findings show that some more accurate recommendation algorithms also produce better conflict reduction, although this does not hold for all of them. Relevance therefore need not oppose conflict reduction in the settings studied. The results suggest that engagement-oriented connection recommendations may be less conflict-provoking than commonly assumed, while leaving an important role for the particular recommendation algorithm.
summary.tldr: Under an opinion-dynamics model, some more accurate social-link recommenders also reduce conflict more effectively, but the relationship is not universal.

title: On the Relationship Between Relevance and Conflict in Online Social Link Recommendations

abstract: Generative Language Models (GLMs) have shown impressive performance in tasks such as text generation, understanding, and reasoning. However, the large model size poses challenges for practical deployment. To solve this problem, Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) has become increasingly popular. However, current QAT methods for generative models have resulted in a noticeable loss of accuracy. To counteract this issue, we propose a novel knowledge distillation method specifically designed for GLMs. Our method, called token-scaled logit distillation, prevents overfitting and provides superior learning from the teacher model and ground truth. This research marks the first evaluation of ternary weight quantization-aware training of large-scale GLMs with less than 1.0 degradation in perplexity and achieves enhanced accuracy in tasks like common-sense QA and arithmetic reasoning as well as natural language understanding. Our code is available at https://github.com/aiha-lab/TSLD.

paragraphs: Large generative language models can be difficult to deploy because of their size. Quantization-aware training addresses this by training with restricted numerical representations, but existing approaches can noticeably reduce accuracy. This paper examines ternary-weight models, whose weights use three possible values, and develops a training method intended to preserve their capabilities.

Token-scaled logit distillation transfers information from a teacher model while also using ground-truth training targets. The authors design it specifically for generative language models and report that it prevents overfitting while improving learning from both sources. The contribution focuses on how a highly quantized student is taught during training.

The paper reports an evaluation of large-scale ternary-weight language models with less than 1.0 degradation in perplexity. It also reports enhanced accuracy in common-sense question answering, arithmetic reasoning, and natural-language understanding. These findings support the feasibility of strong generative models under severe weight quantization in the evaluated settings, with distillation helping address the accuracy costs associated with that compression.
summary.tldr: Token-scaled logit distillation supports large ternary-weight language models with less than 1.0 perplexity degradation and reported task-accuracy improvements.

title: Token-Scaled Logit Distillation for Ternary Weight Generative Language Models

abstract: Adversarial attacks have the potential to mislead deep neural network classifiers by introducing slight perturbations. Developing algorithms that can mitigate the effects of these attacks is crucial for ensuring the safe use of artificial intelligence. Recent studies have suggested that score-based diffusion models are effective in adversarial defenses. However, existing diffusion-based defenses rely on the sequential simulation of the reversed stochastic differential equations of diffusion models, which are computationally inefficient and yield suboptimal results. In this paper, we introduce a novel adversarial defense scheme named ScoreOpt, which optimizes adversarial samples at test-time, towards original clean data in the direction guided by score-based priors. We conduct comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and ImageNet. Our experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing adversarial defenses in terms of both robustness performance and inference speed.

Recent studies have suggested that score-based diffusion models are effective in adversarial defenses. Our experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing adversarial defenses in terms of both robustness performance and inference speed.

paragraphs: Small adversarial changes to an image can mislead a neural-network classifier. Diffusion-based defenses use information about clean data to counter these changes, but existing approaches rely on sequentially simulating reverse stochastic differential equations. The paper identifies that simulation process as computationally inefficient and associated with suboptimal defense results.

The proposed method, ScoreOpt, instead optimizes the attacked sample at test time. Score-based priors guide this optimization toward clean data, using the diffusion model's learned information to determine how the input should change. This shifts the defense procedure from sequential reverse-diffusion simulation to direct optimization of the sample being evaluated.

The authors test ScoreOpt on multiple datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet. They report improvements over existing adversarial defenses in both robustness and inference speed. The findings therefore address two practical aspects of a defense together: how well it resists attacks and how much computation it requires at prediction time. The reported advantage is experimental across the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: ScoreOpt uses score-guided test-time optimization to improve both adversarial robustness and inference speed in the reported experiments.

title: Enhancing Adversarial Robustness via Score-Based Optimization

abstract: The binding problem in human cognition, concerning how the brain represents and connects objects within a fixed network of neural connections, remains a subject of intense debate. Most machine learning efforts addressing this issue in an unsupervised setting have focused on slot-based methods, which may be limiting due to their discrete nature and difficulty to express uncertainty. Recently, the Complex AutoEncoder was proposed as an alternative that learns continuous and distributed object-centric representations. However, it is only applicable to simple toy data. In this paper, we present Rotating Features, a generalization of complex-valued features to higher dimensions, and a new evaluation procedure for extracting objects from distributed representations. Additionally, we show the applicability of our approach to pre-trained features. Together, these advancements enable us to scale distributed object-centric representations from simple toy to real-world data. We believe this work advances a new paradigm for addressing the binding problem in machine learning and has the potential to inspire further innovation in the field.

paragraphs: The binding problem asks how a fixed network can represent objects and connect the information belonging to each one. Many unsupervised machine learning approaches use discrete object slots, which the authors argue can restrict representation and make uncertainty difficult to express. Continuous, distributed object representations offer another direction, but an earlier complex-valued autoencoder approach worked only on simple toy data.

Rotating Features extends complex-valued features into higher-dimensional representations. The paper also introduces an evaluation procedure for extracting objects from distributed representations. These contributions address both how object information is represented and how researchers can recover objects from that information to evaluate what the model has learned.

The authors additionally demonstrate that the approach applies to pretrained features. Together, these developments allow distributed object-centric representations to scale from toy examples to real-world data. The result establishes broader applicability for this representation strategy. The authors view it as a promising direction for the binding problem in machine learning, with further innovation remaining a possibility rather than an established outcome.
summary.tldr: Rotating Features generalizes complex-valued object representations to higher dimensions and extends distributed object discovery to real-world data.

title: Rotating Features for Object Discovery

abstract: Since many pre-trained vision transformers emerge and provide strong representation for various downstream tasks, we aim to adapt them to few-shot image classification tasks in this work. The input images typically contain multiple entities. The model may not focus on the class-related entities for the current few-shot task, even with fine-tuning on support samples, and the noise information from the class-independent ones harms performance. To this end, we first propose a method that uses the attention and gradient information to automatically locate the positions of key entities, denoted as position prompts, in the support images. Then we employ the cross-entropy loss between their many-hot presentation and the attention logits to optimize the model to focus its attention on the key entities during fine-tuning. This ability then can generalize to the query samples. Our method is applicable to different vision transformers (e.g., columnar or pyramidal ones), and also to different pre-training ways (e.g., single-modal or vision-language pre-training). Extensive experiments show that our method can improve the performance of full or parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods on few-shot tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/Haoqing-Wang/FORT.

paragraphs: A pretrained vision transformer may represent images well while attending to the wrong entities for a particular classification task. This matters when only a few labeled examples are available: objects unrelated to the target classes can distract the model even after fine-tuning. The paper aims to make adaptation explicitly guide attention toward the entities that distinguish the current classes.

The method first combines attention information with gradients to locate important entities in the labeled support images. These locations become position prompts. It then uses a cross-entropy objective between a many-hot representation of the selected positions and the model’s attention logits. This supplies a direct training signal about where the model should focus.

The learned focus can carry over to query images that were not used as support examples. Experiments show improvements for both full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning on few-shot tasks. The method also applies across different transformer structures and both single-modality and vision-language pretraining, making attention guidance usable in several adaptation settings.
summary.tldr: Automatically locating class-relevant entities and supervising attention improves vision-transformer fine-tuning for few-shot image classification.

title: Focus Your Attention when Few-Shot Classification

abstract: Zero-sum Markov Stackelberg games can be used to model myriad problems, in domains ranging from economics to human robot interaction. In this paper, we develop policy gradient methods that solve these games in continuous state and action settings using noisy gradient estimates computed from observed trajectories of play. When the games are convex-concave, we prove that our algorithms converge to Stackelberg equilibrium in polynomial time. We also show that reach-avoid problems are naturally modeled as convex-concave zero-sum Markov Stackelberg games, and that Stackelberg equilibrium policies are more effective than their Nash counterparts in these problems.

paragraphs: This paper develops learning methods for zero-sum Markov Stackelberg games, which describe sequential interactions with opposing objectives and a leader-follower structure. The target is a Stackelberg equilibrium, so the learning problem accounts for how one player's choices shape the other player's response. The authors address settings with continuous states and actions.

Their algorithms use policy gradients estimated from observed trajectories of play. Those estimates can be noisy, making the approach relevant to learning from interaction rather than requiring exact gradient information. For games with convex-concave structure, the authors prove convergence to a Stackelberg equilibrium in polynomial time. That structural condition is central to the stated efficiency guarantee.

The paper also shows that reach-avoid problems fit naturally into this convex-concave game formulation. In these problems, it finds Stackelberg equilibrium policies more effective than Nash equilibrium policies. This gives the mathematical framework a concrete application and illustrates why the choice of equilibrium concept can matter for the resulting policies.
summary.tldr: Policy gradient methods converge efficiently in convex-concave zero-sum Markov Stackelberg games using noisy trajectory-based gradients.

title: Convex-Concave Zero-Sum Markov Stackelberg Games

abstract: Well-designed prompts can guide text-to-image models to generate amazing images. However, the performant prompts are often model-specific and misaligned with user input. Instead of laborious human engineering, we propose prompt adaptation, a general framework that automatically adapts original user input to model-preferred prompts. Specifically, we first perform supervised fine-tuning with a pretrained language model on a small collection of manually engineered prompts. Then we use reinforcement learning to explore better prompts. We define a reward function that encourages the policy to generate more aesthetically pleasing images while preserving the original user intentions. Experimental results on Stable Diffusion show that our method outperforms manual prompt engineering in terms of both automatic metrics and human preference ratings. Moreover, reinforcement learning further boosts performance, especially on out-of-domain prompts.

paragraphs: A user's description and the wording that works best for an image generator may differ. Effective prompts can depend on the particular model, making manual prompt engineering laborious. This paper introduces prompt adaptation: automatically rewriting an original request into language better suited to the generator while aiming to retain what the user wants.

The method first fine-tunes a pretrained language model on a small collection of manually engineered prompts. It then uses reinforcement learning to search for improved prompts. The reward combines two goals: producing more aesthetically pleasing images and preserving the intention of the original request. This gives the adaptation process an explicit objective beyond imitating example prompts.

Experiments with Stable Diffusion show better results than manual prompt engineering on automatic measures and human preference ratings. Reinforcement learning adds further improvements, especially for out-of-domain prompts. The findings support adapting the language passed to an image model as a useful way to improve generation, with the reported evidence grounded in the evaluated Stable Diffusion setting.
summary.tldr: A language model trained with supervision and reinforcement learning adapts user prompts to improve Stable Diffusion outputs while targeting intent preservation.

title: Optimizing Prompts for Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: Temporal graphs offer more accurate modeling of many real-world scenarios than static graphs. However, neighbor aggregation, a critical building block of graph networks, for temporal graphs, is currently straightforwardly extended from that of static graphs. It can be computationally expensive when involving all historical neighbors during such aggregation. In practice, typically only a subset of the most recent neighbors are involved. However, such subsampling leads to incomplete and biased neighbor information. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework for temporal neighbor aggregation that uses the recurrent neural network with node-wise hidden states to integrate information from all historical neighbors for each node to acquire the complete neighbor information. We demonstrate the superior theoretical expressiveness of the proposed framework as well as its state-of-the-art performance in real-world applications. Notably, it achieves a significant +9.4% improvement on averaged precision in a real-world Ecommerce dataset over existing methods on 2-layer models.

paragraphs: Temporal graphs represent relationships that evolve over time, but gathering information from every past neighbor can be computationally expensive. A common shortcut uses only the most recent neighbors. That shortcut makes the information available to a node incomplete and biased toward recent interactions, potentially overlooking relevant parts of its history.

This paper proposes a different neighbor-aggregation framework based on recurrent neural networks. Each node has its own hidden state, which integrates information from all of its historical neighbors. The framework therefore makes accumulated history part of the node's evolving representation instead of limiting aggregation to a recent subset. This directly addresses the particular information loss introduced by subsampling historical neighbors.

The authors establish superior theoretical expressiveness for the proposed framework and report state-of-the-art performance in real-world applications. A highlighted result is a 9.4% improvement in average precision over existing methods on an e-commerce dataset using two-layer models. The theoretical and empirical findings together support retaining historical neighbor information through recurrent state as a useful design for temporal graph learning.
summary.tldr: Node-specific recurrent states integrate all historical neighbors, improving temporal graph expressiveness and reported real-world prediction performance.

title: Recurrent Temporal Revision Graph Networks

abstract: An agent learning an option in hierarchical reinforcement learning must solve three problems: identify the option's subgoal (termination condition), learn a policy, and learn where that policy will succeed (initiation set). The termination condition is typically identified first, but the option policy and initiation set must be learned simultaneously, which is challenging because the initiation set depends on the option policy, which changes as the agent learns. Consequently, data obtained from option execution becomes invalid over time, leading to an inaccurate initiation set that subsequently harms downstream task performance. We highlight three issues---data non-stationarity, temporal credit assignment, and pessimism---specific to learning initiation sets, and propose to address them using tools from off-policy value estimation and classification. We show that our method learns higher-quality initiation sets faster than existing methods (in MiniGrid and Montezuma's Revenge), can automatically discover promising grasps for robot manipulation (in Robosuite), and improves the performance of a state-of-the-art option discovery method in a challenging maze navigation task in MuJoCo.

paragraphs: A reusable skill in hierarchical reinforcement learning needs a goal, a policy for reaching it, and an initiation set describing where that policy can succeed. The last two must develop together. As the policy improves, earlier execution data can become outdated, making the learned initiation set inaccurate and harming the agent’s subsequent task performance.

The paper identifies three difficulties specific to this learning problem: changing data relevance, assigning credit over time, and pessimism. It addresses them with tools from off-policy value estimation and classification. The central aim is to keep the estimate of where a skill works aligned with the policy currently being learned.

Experiments show faster learning of higher-quality initiation sets in MiniGrid and Montezuma’s Revenge. The method also discovers promising robot grasps in Robosuite and improves a state-of-the-art option-discovery method on a difficult MuJoCo maze task. These results connect better initiation-set learning to practical decisions about when to invoke a skill, as well as to the quality of the skills an agent discovers.
summary.tldr: Combining off-policy value estimation with classification helps agents learn more accurately and quickly where their evolving skills will succeed.

title: Effectively Learning Initiation Sets in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Research in statistical learning has polarized into two general approaches to perform regression analysis: Transductive methods construct estimates directly based on exemplar data using generic relational principles which might suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Conversely, inductive methods can potentially fit highly complex functions at the cost of compute-intensive solution searches. In this work, we leverage the theory of vector-valued Reproducing Kernel Banach Spaces (RKBS) to propose a hybrid approach: We show that transductive regression systems can be meta-learned with gradient descent to form efficient _in-context_ neural approximators of function defined over both finite and infinite-dimensional spaces (operator regression). Once trained, our _Transducer_ can almost instantaneously capture new functional relationships and produce original image estimates, given a few pairs of input and output examples. We demonstrate the benefit of our meta-learned transductive approach to model physical systems influenced by varying external factors with little data at a fraction of the usual deep learning training costs for partial differential equations and climate modeling applications.

paragraphs: Regression can estimate outputs directly from examples using general relationships, or learn a function through an expensive training process. The first approach can struggle in high dimensions; the second can require substantial computation. This paper combines these approaches by learning a transductive system that can infer new functional relationships from a few input-output examples.

The theoretical foundation is vector-valued reproducing kernel Banach spaces. Using this framework, the authors show that transductive regression systems can be meta-learned with gradient descent. Their Transducer performs in-context approximation over both finite-dimensional spaces and infinite-dimensional spaces, extending the approach to operator regression, where the relationships involve functions.

Once trained, the Transducer can capture new relationships and produce image estimates almost immediately from a small example set. The authors demonstrate benefits for modeling physical systems affected by varying external factors, including partial differential equations and climate applications. In those demonstrations, the method uses little data and a fraction of usual deep-learning training costs, emphasizing the benefit of reusing a learned adaptation procedure.
summary.tldr: A meta-learned Transducer rapidly infers new functional relationships from a few examples, including in physical-system and climate-modeling applications.

title: Learning Functional Transduction

abstract: Air pollution poses serious health concerns in developing countries, such as India, necessitating large-scale measurement for correlation analysis, policy recommendations, and informed decision-making. However, fine-grained data collection is costly. Specifically, static sensors for pollution measurement cost several thousand dollars per unit, leading to inadequate deployment and coverage. To complement the existing sparse static sensor network, we propose a mobile sensor network utilizing lower-cost PM2.5 sensors mounted on public buses in the Delhi-NCR region of India. Through this exercise, we introduce a novel dataset AirDelhi comprising PM2.5 and PM10 measurements. This dataset is made publicly available, at https://www.cse.iitd.ac.in/pollutiondata, serving as a valuable resource for machine learning (ML) researchers and environmentalists. We present three key contributions with the release of this dataset. Firstly, through in-depth statistical analysis, we demonstrate that the released dataset significantly differs from existing pollution datasets, highlighting its uniqueness and potential for new insights. Secondly, the dataset quality been validated against existing expensive sensors. Thirdly, we conduct a benchmarking exercise (https://github.com/sachin-iitd/DelhiPMDatasetBenchmark), evaluating state-of-the-art methods for interpolation, feature imputation, and forecasting on this dataset, which is the largest publicly available PM dataset to date. The results of the benchmarking exercise underscore the substantial disparities in accuracy between the proposed dataset and other publicly available datasets. This finding highlights the complexity and richness of our dataset, emphasizing its value for advancing research in the field of air pollution.

paragraphs: AirDelhi addresses a measurement problem behind air pollution modeling: expensive stationary sensors make dense coverage difficult to achieve. The researchers mounted lower-cost particulate matter sensors on public buses in Delhi-NCR to complement the existing static network. This mobile collection effort produced a publicly available dataset containing PM2.5 and PM10 measurements.

The paper evaluates the resulting data in two ways before considering prediction methods. Statistical analysis shows that AirDelhi differs substantially from existing pollution datasets, and comparisons with expensive sensors validate its quality. These steps connect the practical advantage of collecting measurements on buses with evidence about the characteristics and reliability of those measurements.

The authors also benchmark methods for interpolation, filling missing features, and forecasting. They report substantial differences in accuracy between AirDelhi and other public datasets, highlighting that performance does not carry over uniformly across these data sources. Described in the paper as the largest public particulate matter dataset available at the time, AirDelhi offers a resource for studying pollution with finer spatial and temporal detail.
summary.tldr: AirDelhi uses sensors on public buses to provide detailed pollution measurements and benchmark air quality modeling methods.

title: AirDelhi: Fine-Grained Spatio-Temporal Particulate Matter Dataset From Delhi For ML based Modeling

abstract: Plug-and-play (PnP) prior is a well-known class of methods for solving imaging inverse problems by computing fixed-points of operators combining physical measurement models and learned image denoisers. While PnP methods have been extensively used for image recovery with known measurement operators, there is little work on PnP for solving blind inverse problems. We address this gap by presenting a new block-coordinate PnP (BC-PnP) method that efficiently solves this joint estimation problem by introducing learned denoisers as priors on both the unknown image and the unknown measurement operator. We present a new convergence theory for BC-PnP compatible with blind inverse problems by considering nonconvex data-fidelity terms and expansive denoisers. Our theory analyzes the convergence of BC-PnP to a stationary point of an implicit function associated with an approximate minimum mean-squared error (MMSE) denoiser. We numerically validate our method on two blind inverse problems: automatic coil sensitivity estimation in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and blind image deblurring. Our results show that BC-PnP provides an efficient and principled framework for using denoisers as PnP priors for jointly estimating measurement operators and images.

paragraphs: Recovering an image from measurements becomes harder when the measurement process is itself unknown. Such blind inverse problems require estimating both the image and the operator that produced the observations. Existing plug-and-play methods combine physical measurement models with learned denoisers, but their use has largely focused on cases where the measurement operator is known.

The proposed block-coordinate plug-and-play method extends this approach by placing learned denoiser priors on both unknown quantities. This makes denoising part of the joint estimation process for images and measurement operators. The accompanying theory accommodates nonconvex data-fitting objectives and expansive denoisers, broadening the mathematical setting considered for this blind reconstruction problem.

The convergence analysis concerns a stationary point of an implicit function associated with an approximate minimum mean-squared error denoiser; it does not claim recovery of a global optimum. Numerical studies cover automatic MRI coil sensitivity estimation and blind image deblurring. Together, the analysis and experiments support an efficient, principled way to apply learned denoisers when uncertainty extends to the measurement process itself.
summary.tldr: BC-PnP uses learned denoisers to jointly estimate images and unknown measurement operators, with convergence analysis and validation on two blind imaging problems.

title: Block Coordinate Plug-and-Play Methods for Blind Inverse Problems

abstract: The widespread deployment of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) sparks significant interest in their explainability, which plays a vital role in model auditing and ensuring trustworthy graph learning. The objective of GNN explainability is to discern the underlying graph structures that have the most significant impact on model predictions. Ensuring that explanations generated are reliable necessitates consideration of the in-distribution property, particularly due to the vulnerability of GNNs to out-of-distribution data. Unfortunately, prevailing explainability methods tend to constrain the generated explanations to the structure of the original graph, thereby downplaying the significance of the in-distribution property and resulting in explanations that lack reliability.To address these challenges, we propose D4Explainer, a novel approach that provides in-distribution GNN explanations for both counterfactual and model-level explanation scenarios. The proposed D4Explainer incorporates generative graph distribution learning into the optimization objective, which accomplishes two goals: 1) generate a collection of diverse counterfactual graphs that conform to the in-distribution property for a given instance, and 2) identify the most discriminative graph patterns that contribute to a specific class prediction, thus serving as model-level explanations. It is worth mentioning that D4Explainer is the first unified framework that combines both counterfactual and model-level explanations.Empirical evaluations conducted on synthetic and real-world datasets provide compelling evidence of the state-of-the-art performance achieved by D4Explainer in terms of explanation accuracy, faithfulness, diversity, and robustness.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network involves identifying graph structures that strongly influence its predictions. The paper argues that an explanation should also resemble graphs from the relevant data distribution. Otherwise, the network's sensitivity to unfamiliar inputs can undermine the explanation. Methods constrained to structures within the original graph may give insufficient attention to this distributional requirement.

D4Explainer incorporates generative learning of graph distributions into its explanation objective using discrete denoising diffusion. It addresses two explanation tasks within one framework. For an individual example, it generates diverse counterfactual graphs that conform to the data distribution. At the model level, it identifies graph patterns that are especially informative for a particular predicted class.

Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance in explanation accuracy, faithfulness, diversity, and robustness. The central contribution is connecting explanations to a learned distribution of plausible graphs while supporting both individual and class-level analysis. This makes distributional plausibility an explicit part of the explanation process rather than relying solely on structural changes to an input.
summary.tldr: D4Explainer learns graph distributions to generate plausible counterfactual and model-level GNN explanations within a unified diffusion-based framework.

title: D4Explainer: In-distribution Explanations of Graph Neural Network via Discrete Denoising Diffusion

abstract: We investigate bandit convex optimization (BCO) with delayed feedback, where only the loss value of the action is revealed under an arbitrary delay. Let $n,T,\bar{d}$ denote the dimensionality, time horizon, and average delay, respectively. Previous studies have achieved an $O(\sqrt{n}T^{3/4}+(n\bar{d})^{1/3}T^{2/3})$ regret bound for this problem, whose delay-independent part matches the regret of the classical non-delayed bandit gradient descent algorithm. However, there is a large gap between its delay-dependent part, i.e., $O((n\bar{d})^{1/3}T^{2/3})$, and an existing $\Omega(\sqrt{\bar{d}T})$ lower bound. In this paper, we illustrate that this gap can be filled in the worst case, where $\bar{d}$ is very close to the maximum delay $d$. Specifically, we first develop a novel algorithm, and prove that it enjoys a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{n}T^{3/4}+\sqrt{dT})$ in general. Compared with the previous result, our regret bound is better for $d=O((n\bar{d})^{2/3}T^{1/3})$, and the delay-dependent part is tight in the worst case. The primary idea is to decouple the joint effect of the delays and the bandit feedback on the regret by carefully incorporating the delayed bandit feedback with a blocking update mechanism. Furthermore, we show that the proposed algorithm can improve the regret bound to $O((nT)^{2/3}\log^{1/3}T+d\log T)$ for strongly convex functions. Finally, if the action sets are unconstrained, we demonstrate that it can be simply extended to achieve an $O(n\sqrt{T\log T}+d\log T)$ regret bound for strongly convex and smooth functions.
originalAbstract: We investigate bandit convex optimization (BCO) with delayed feedback, where only the loss value of the action is revealed under an arbitrary delay. Let $n,T,\bar{d}$ denote the dimensionality, time horizon, and average delay, respectively. Previous studies have achieved an $O(\sqrt{n}T^{3/4}+(n\bar{d})^{1/3}T^{2/3})$ regret bound for this problem, whose delay-independent part matches the regret of the classical non-delayed bandit gradient descent algorithm. However, there is a large gap between its delay-dependent part, i.e., $O((n\bar{d})^{1/3}T^{2/3})$, and an existing $\Omega(\sqrt{\bar{d}T})$ lower bound. In this paper, we illustrate that this gap can be filled in the worst case, where $\bar{d}$ is very close to the maximum delay $d$. Specifically, we first develop a novel algorithm, and prove that it enjoys a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{n}T^{3/4}+\sqrt{dT})$ in general. Compared with the previous result, our regret bound is better for $d=O((n\bar{d})^{2/3}T^{1/3})$, and the delay-dependent part is tight in the worst case. The primary idea is to decouple the joint effect of the delays and the bandit feedback on the regret by carefully incorporating the delayed bandit feedback with a blocking update mechanism. Furthermore, we show that the proposed algorithm can improve the regret bound to $O((nT)^{2/3}\log^{1/3}T+d\log T)$ for strongly convex functions. Finally, if the action sets are unconstrained, we demonstrate that it can be simply extended to achieve an $O(n\sqrt{T\log T}+d\log T)$ regret bound for strongly convex and smooth functions.

paragraphs: Bandit convex optimization requires choosing actions while observing only the loss of the chosen action. This paper adds arbitrary delays before those losses arrive. It studies regret, the accumulated cost of learning compared with a reference choice, and asks how strongly delayed feedback must affect that cost.

The proposed algorithm uses updates organized into blocks to separate the effects of delay from the effects of limited bandit feedback. Its general regret bound is O(√n T^(3/4) + √(dT)), where n is dimension, T is the number of rounds, and d is maximum delay. The delay term matches the existing lower-bound scale in the worst case where average delay is close to maximum delay.

The improvement over prior work is conditional on the relationship between maximum delay, average delay, dimension, and horizon; it is not claimed for every delay pattern. The authors derive additional improvements for strongly convex losses. With unconstrained action sets and losses that are both strongly convex and smooth, an extension yields O(n√(T log T) + d log T) regret. These stronger results depend on the additional problem structure.
summary.tldr: Block-based updates improve delayed bandit optimization bounds and attain a worst-case-tight delay term under the stated delay regime.

title: Improved Regret for Bandit Convex Optimization with Delayed Feedback

abstract: We build interpretable and lightweight transformer-like neural networks by unrolling iterative optimization algorithms that minimize graph smoothness priors---the quadratic graph Laplacian regularizer (GLR) and the $\ell_1$-norm graph total variation (GTV)---subject to an interpolation constraint. The crucial insight is that a normalized signal-dependent graph learning module amounts to a variant of the basic self-attention mechanism in conventional transformers. Unlike "black-box" transformers that require learning of large key, query and value matrices to compute scaled dot products as affinities and subsequent output embeddings, resulting in huge parameter sets, our unrolled networks employ shallow CNNs to learn low-dimensional features per node to establish pairwise Mahalanobis distances and construct sparse similarity graphs. At each layer, given a learned graph, the target interpolated signal is simply a low-pass filtered output derived from the minimization of an assumed graph smoothness prior, leading to a dramatic reduction in parameter count. Experiments for two image interpolation applications verify the restoration performance, parameter efficiency and robustness to covariate shift of our graph-based unrolled networks compared to conventional transformers.

paragraphs: This paper builds transformer-like networks whose layers correspond to steps of an explicit optimization procedure. The underlying task is interpolation: reconstructing a signal while respecting an interpolation constraint and assumptions about smoothness on a graph. Turning successive optimization steps into network layers gives the architecture a direct interpretation.

The key connection is that a normalized, signal-dependent graph-learning module behaves like a variant of self-attention. Shallow convolutional networks extract compact features for graph nodes, and pairwise Mahalanobis distances define sparse similarity graphs. Given a graph, each layer produces a low-pass filtered signal by minimizing either a quadratic graph Laplacian penalty or a graph total variation penalty.

This construction substantially reduces parameter counts compared with conventional transformers that learn large attention projection matrices. Experiments on two image interpolation applications support the networks’ restoration performance, parameter efficiency, and robustness to covariate shift. The results show how a specified reconstruction objective and learned similarity structure can provide a practical basis for compact, interpretable attention-like processing.
summary.tldr: Unrolling graph-smoothness optimization produces interpretable transformer-like networks with fewer parameters and strong image interpolation results.

title: Interpretable Lightweight Transformer via Unrolling of Learned Graph Smoothness Priors

abstract: We provide the first useful and rigorous analysis of ensemble sampling for the stochastic linear bandit setting. In particular, we show that, under standard assumptions, for a $d$-dimensional stochastic linear bandit with an interaction horizon $T$, ensemble sampling with an ensemble of size of order $\smash{d \log T}$ incurs regret at most of the order $\smash{(d \log T)^{5/2} \sqrt{T}}$. Ours is the first result in any structured setting not to require the size of the ensemble to scale linearly with $T$---which defeats the purpose of ensemble sampling---while obtaining near $\smash{\sqrt{T}}$ order regret. Our result is also the first to allow for infinite action sets.

In particular, we show that, under standard assumptions, for a $d$-dimensional stochastic linear bandit with an interaction horizon $T$, ensemble sampling with an ensemble of size of order $\smash{d \log T}$ incurs regret at most of the order $\smash{(d \log T)^{5/2} \sqrt{T}}$. Ours is the first result in any structured setting not to require the size of the ensemble to scale linearly with $T$---which defeats the purpose of ensemble sampling---while obtaining near $\smash{\sqrt{T}}$ order regret. paragraphs: Ensemble sampling uses a collection of models in a sequential decision problem. This paper provides a rigorous analysis for stochastic linear bandits, where the task has a d-dimensional structure and lasts T interaction rounds. Its central question is whether a relatively small ensemble can still provide a strong regret guarantee over a long horizon.

Under standard assumptions, the authors show that an ensemble of size on the order of d log T incurs regret at most on the order of (d log T)^(5/2)√T. The distinction between these quantities matters: the ensemble grows only logarithmically with the horizon, while the regret bound retains near-√T dependence on the horizon.

The authors identify this as the first structured-setting result achieving that regret behavior without requiring ensemble size to grow linearly with T. Such linear growth would undermine the motivation for ensemble sampling. The analysis also allows infinite action sets, extending its scope beyond problems with a finite list of choices. The contribution is a conditional theoretical guarantee that small ensembles can suffice.
summary.tldr: Under standard assumptions, ensembles of order d log T achieve near-√T horizon dependence in regret for stochastic linear bandits.

title: Ensemble sampling for linear bandits: small ensembles suffice

abstract: Multi-instance partial-label learning (MIPL) is an emerging learning framework where each training sample is represented as a multi-instance bag associated with a candidate label set. Existing MIPL algorithms often overlook the margins for attention scores and predicted probabilities, leading to suboptimal generalization performance. A critical issue with these algorithms is that the highest prediction probability of the classifier may appear on a non-candidate label. In this paper, we propose an algorithm named MIPLMA, i.e., Multi-Instance Partial-Label learning with Margin Adjustment, which adjusts the margins for attention scores and predicted probabilities. We introduce a margin-aware attention mechanism to dynamically adjust the margins for attention scores and propose a margin distributionloss to constrain the margins between the predicted probabilities on candidate and non-candidate label sets. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of MIPLMA over existing MIPL algorithms, as well as other well-established multi-instance learning algorithms and partial-label learning algorithms.
