Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of MIPLMA over existing MIPL algorithms, as well as other well-established multi-instance learning algorithms and partial-label learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Multi-instance partial-label learning gives each training example a bag of instances and a set of candidate labels. A model must work with both the collection of instances and ambiguity about the label. The paper identifies a problem in existing methods: the largest predicted probability can belong to a label outside the candidate set.

The proposed MIPLMA algorithm adjusts margins in two places. A margin-aware attention mechanism dynamically changes margins between attention scores, affecting how the model weighs instances. A margin distribution loss constrains the separation between prediction probabilities assigned to candidate and non-candidate labels. This directly addresses the distinction that the supplied label set establishes.

Experiments show superior performance against existing methods for this combined learning setting, as well as established multi-instance and partial-label algorithms. The findings support treating attention-score margins and label-probability margins as complementary design targets. The contribution is a learning procedure that accounts explicitly for these separations instead of leaving them unaddressed during training.
summary.tldr: MIPLMA improves learning from bags with ambiguous labels by adjusting attention margins and separating candidate from non-candidate label probabilities.

title: Multi-Instance Partial-Label Learning with Margin Adjustment

abstract: We introduce a general detection-based approach to text line recognition, be it printed (OCR) or handwritten text (HTR), with latin, chinese or ciphered characters. Detection-based approaches have until now largely been discarded for HTR because reading characters separately is often challenging, and character-level annotation is difficult and expensive. We overcome these challenges thanks to three main insights: (i) synthetic pre-training with diverse enough data to learn reasonable character localization in any script; (ii) modern transformer-based detectors can jointly detect a large number of instances and, if trained with an adequate masking strategy, leverage consistency between the different detections; (iii) once a pre-trained detection model with approximate character localization is available, it is possible to fine-tune it with line-level annotation on real data, even with a different alphabet. Our approach thus builds on a completely different paradigm than most state-of-the-art methods, which rely on autoregressive decoding, predicting character values one by one, while we treat a complete line in parallel. Remarkably, our method demonstrates good performance on range of scripts, usually tackled with specialized approaches: latin script, chinese script, and ciphers, for which we significantly improve state-of-the-art performances. Our code and models are available at [https://github.com/raphael-baena/DTLR](https://github.com/raphael-baena/DTLR).

paragraphs: This paper treats reading a line of text as a character-detection problem, processing the complete line in parallel. The approach covers printed and handwritten text across Latin, Chinese, and ciphered characters. Detection has been difficult to use for handwriting because individual characters can be ambiguous and character-level annotations are expensive to obtain.

The method combines three ideas. Diverse synthetic pretraining teaches approximate character localization. A transformer detector identifies many characters jointly, while a masking strategy helps it use consistency among detections. Once this initial localization ability exists, the model can be fine-tuned on real data using annotations for whole lines, including data with a different alphabet.

These components make parallel detection practical without requiring character-level annotation for the real-data fine-tuning stage. The authors report good performance across the studied scripts and substantial improvements over prior state-of-the-art results for ciphers. The contribution is a general recognition approach that uses relationships among simultaneous detections, offering a different route from methods that predict characters sequentially.
summary.tldr: Synthetic pretraining and joint character detection enable parallel text-line recognition with line-level fine-tuning annotations.

title: General Detection-based Text Line Recognition

abstract: As text-to-image (T2I) synthesis models increase in size, they demand higher inference costs due to the need for more expensive GPUs with larger memory, which makes it challenging to reproduce these models in addition to the restricted access to training datasets. Our study aims to reduce these inference costs and explores how far the generative capabilities of T2I models can be extended using only publicly available datasets and open-source models. To this end, by using the de facto standard text-to-image model, Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL), we present three key practices in building an efficient T2I model: (1) Knowledge distillation: we explore how to effectively distill the generation capability of SDXL into an efficient U-Net and find that self-attention is the most crucial part. (2) Data: despite fewer samples, high-resolution images with rich captions are more crucial than a larger number of low-resolution images with short captions. (3) Teacher: Step-distilled Teacher allows T2I models to reduce the noising steps. Based on these findings, we build two types of efficient text-to-image models, called KOALA-Turbo & -Lightning, with two compact U-Nets (1B & 700M), reducing the model size up to 54% and 69% of the SDXL U-Net. In particular, the KOALA-Lightning-700M is 4 times faster than SDXL while still maintaining satisfactory generation quality. Moreover, unlike SDXL, our KOALA models can generate 1024px high-resolution images on consumer-grade GPUs with 8GB of VRAMs (3060Ti). We believe that our KOALA models will have a significant practical impact, serving as cost-effective alternatives to SDXL for academic researchers and general users in resource-constrained environments.

paragraphs: Large text-to-image models can require expensive GPUs and substantial memory, limiting access and reproducibility. KOALA investigates how much generation capability can be retained in smaller models using publicly available data and open-source models. Stable Diffusion XL serves as the starting point for studying how to transfer capability into a compact U-Net.

The study identifies three practices. In knowledge distillation, self-attention is the most important component examined. For data, high-resolution images paired with detailed captions matter more than a larger collection of low-resolution images with short captions. Using a teacher already distilled for fewer generation steps also helps the smaller model reduce its step count.

KOALA-Lightning-700M is reported to run four times faster than SDXL while retaining satisfactory generation quality. The models can also generate 1024-pixel images on an 8 GB consumer GPU. Together, the results provide an empirical recipe for making high-resolution generation more accessible under limited hardware resources.
summary.tldr: KOALA uses targeted distillation, richer training data, and efficient teachers to deliver faster, smaller text-to-image models.

title: KOALA: Empirical Lessons Toward Memory-Efficient and Fast Diffusion Models for Text-to-Image Synthesis

abstract: We present the Manuscripts of Handwritten Arabic (Muharaf) dataset, which is a machine learning dataset consisting of more than 1,600 historic handwritten page images transcribed by experts in archival Arabic. Each document image is accompanied by spatial polygonal coordinates of its text lines as well as basic page elements. This dataset was compiled to advance the state of the art in handwritten text recognition (HTR), not only for Arabic manuscripts but also for cursive text in general. The Muharaf dataset includes diverse handwriting styles and a wide range of document types, including personal letters, diaries, notes, poems, church records, and legal correspondences. In this paper, we describe the data acquisition pipeline, notable dataset features, and statistics. We also provide a preliminary baseline result achieved by training convolutional neural networks using this data.

paragraphs: Muharaf is a dataset intended to advance recognition of handwritten Arabic and cursive writing more broadly. It contains more than 1,600 images of historical handwritten pages, with transcriptions produced by experts in archival Arabic. The resource pairs visual examples of writing with expert readings, supplying the supervision needed to study recognition on these documents.

The annotations also describe where text appears. Each page includes polygon coordinates for text lines and basic page elements, connecting the transcribed material to its spatial layout. The collection covers varied handwriting styles and document types, including letters, diaries, notes, poems, church records, and legal correspondence. This variety is a central feature of the dataset.

The paper documents how the material was acquired, describes notable properties, and reports dataset statistics. It also provides a preliminary recognition baseline obtained by training convolutional neural networks on the data. That baseline offers an initial reference for subsequent work, while the main contribution is the expert-transcribed, spatially annotated collection itself.
summary.tldr: Muharaf provides over 1,600 historical Arabic manuscript pages with expert transcriptions, spatial annotations, and a preliminary recognition baseline.

title: Muharaf: Manuscripts of Handwritten Arabic Dataset for Cursive Text Recognition

abstract: Cultural bias is pervasive in many large language models (LLMs), largely due to the deficiency of data representative of different cultures.Typically, cultural datasets and benchmarks are constructed either by extracting subsets of existing datasets or by aggregating from platforms such as Wikipedia and social media.However, these approaches are highly dependent on real-world data and human annotations, making them costly and difficult to scale.Inspired by cognitive theories on social communication, this paper introduces CulturePark, an LLM-powered multi-agent communication framework for cultural data collection.CulturePark simulates cross-cultural human communication with LLM-based agents playing roles in different cultures.It generates high-quality cross-cultural dialogues encapsulating human beliefs, norms, and customs.Using CulturePark, we generated 41,000 cultural samples to fine-tune eight culture-specific LLMs.We evaluated these models across three downstream tasks: content moderation, cultural alignment, and cultural education.Results show that for content moderation, our GPT-3.5-based models either match or outperform GPT-4 on $41$ datasets. Regarding cultural alignment, our models surpass GPT-4 on Hofstede's VSM 13 framework.Furthermore, for cultural education of human participants, our models demonstrate superior outcomes in both learning efficacy and user experience compared to GPT-4. CulturePark proves an important step in addressing cultural bias and advancing the democratization of AI, highlighting the critical role of culturally inclusive data in model training. Code is released at https://github.com/Scarelette/CulturePark.

paragraphs: CulturePark addresses the shortage of culturally representative training data for language models. Building cultural datasets from existing collections, online platforms, and human annotations can be expensive and difficult to scale. The paper proposes generating cultural data through simulated communication between language-model agents assigned roles from different cultures.

These agents produce cross-cultural dialogues about beliefs, norms, and customs. Using this framework, the authors generate 41,000 samples and fine-tune eight culture-specific models. The approach makes simulated social interaction a source of training material, linking the data-generation process directly to the goal of improving models’ handling of cultural differences.

Evaluation covers content moderation, cultural alignment, and cultural education. The GPT-3.5-based models match or exceed GPT-4 on 41 content-moderation datasets and outperform it on the Hofstede VSM 13 cultural-alignment framework. In education involving human participants, they also produce better reported learning outcomes and user experiences than GPT-4. These results support the usefulness of the generated data for the evaluated tasks and measures, demonstrating a concrete way to improve cultural specialization through targeted fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: CulturePark generates cross-cultural dialogues with language-model agents to train models that improve on evaluated cultural tasks.

title: CulturePark: Boosting Cross-cultural Understanding in Large Language Models

abstract: The development of generative language models that can create long and coherent textual outputs via autoregression has lead to a proliferation of uses and a corresponding sweep of analyses as researches work to determine the limitations of this new paradigm. Unlike humans, these '*Large Language Models*' (LLMs) are highly sensitive to small changes in their inputs, leading to unwanted inconsistency in their behavior. One problematic inconsistency when LLMs are used to answer multiple-choice questions or analyze multiple inputs is *order dependency*: the output of an LLM can (and often does) change significantly when sub-sequences are swapped, despite both orderings being semantically identical. In this paper we present , a technique that *guarantees* the output of an LLM will not have order dependence on a specified set of sub-sequences. We show that this method *provably* eliminates order dependency, and that it can be applied to *any* transformer-based LLM to enable text generation that is unaffected by re-orderings. Delving into the implications of our method, we show that, despite our inputs being out of distribution, the impact on expected accuracy is small, where the expectation is over the order of uniformly chosen shuffling of the candidate responses, and usually significantly less in practice. Thus, can be used as a '*dropped-in*' method on fully trained models. Finally, we discuss how our method's success suggests that other strong guarantees can be obtained on LLM performance via modifying the input representations.Code is available at [github.com/reidmcy/set-based-prompting](https://github.com/reidmcy/set-based-prompting.).

paragraphs: A language model can answer differently when the same candidate responses or other input pieces appear in a different order. When those reorderings preserve meaning, this sensitivity creates unwanted inconsistency. This paper presents a method that guarantees independence from the ordering of a specified set of input subsequences.

The method changes input representations and can be applied to any transformer-based language model without fine-tuning. Its guarantee concerns the designated subsequences: rearranging those pieces does not introduce order dependence into the output. This makes the contribution stronger than an empirical reduction in sensitivity, while keeping the scope tied to the inputs selected for order-independent treatment.

The authors also examine accuracy because the modified inputs are outside the model's training distribution. They report a small impact on expected accuracy when averaging over uniformly shuffled candidate responses, with usually smaller effects in practice. The work therefore combines a formal behavioral guarantee with evidence that it can be useful on already trained models, and suggests investigating other guarantees through input-representation changes.
summary.tldr: An input-representation method provably removes dependence on specified subsequence orderings in transformer language models without fine-tuning.

title: Order-Independence Without Fine Tuning

abstract: Many few-shot segmentation (FSS) methods use cross attention to fuse support foreground (FG) into query features, regardless of the quadratic complexity. A recent advance Mamba can also well capture intra-sequence dependencies, yet the complexity is only linear. Hence, we aim to devise a cross (attention-like) Mamba to capture inter-sequence dependencies for FSS. A simple idea is to scan on support features to selectively compress them into the hidden state, which is then used as the initial hidden state to sequentially scan query features. Nevertheless, it suffers from (1) support forgetting issue: query features will also gradually be compressed when scanning on them, so the support features in hidden state keep reducing, and many query pixels cannot fuse sufficient support features; (2) intra-class gap issue: query FG is essentially more similar to itself rather than to support FG, i.e., query may prefer not to fuse support features but their own ones from the hidden state, yet the success of FSS relies on the effective use of support information. To tackle them, we design a hybrid Mamba network (HMNet), including (1) a support recapped Mamba to periodically recap the support features when scanning query, so the hidden state can always contain rich support information; (2) a query intercepted Mamba to forbid the mutual interactions among query pixels, and encourage them to fuse more support features from the hidden state. Consequently, the support information is better utilized, leading to better performance. Extensive experiments have been conducted on two public benchmarks, showing the superiority of HMNet. The code is available at https://github.com/Sam1224/HMNet.

paragraphs: Few-shot segmentation uses labeled support examples to identify the relevant foreground in a query image. Many methods connect support and query features through cross attention, which has quadratic complexity. This paper explores Mamba as a linear-complexity alternative for transferring information between these two feature sequences.

Simply scanning the support first and then the query creates two problems. As query features enter the hidden state, support information gradually fades. Query foreground features can also resemble one another more strongly than they resemble the support foreground, encouraging the model to reuse query information instead of learning from the support examples.

HMNet addresses these problems with two complementary components. Support recapped Mamba periodically reintroduces support features during the query scan. Query intercepted Mamba blocks interactions among query pixels, encouraging greater use of support information held in the state. Experiments on two public benchmarks report superior performance. The contribution is a specific way to preserve and prioritize the reference information that few-shot segmentation depends on when using sequential feature processing.
summary.tldr: HMNet improves few-shot segmentation by refreshing support information and restricting query interactions within a Mamba-based architecture.

title: Hybrid Mamba for Few-Shot Segmentation

abstract: Causal interactions among a group of variables are often modeled by a single causal graph. In some domains, however, these interactions are best described by multiple co-existing causal graphs, e.g., in dynamical systems or genomics. This paper addresses the hitherto unknown role of interventions in learning causal interactions among variables governed by a mixture of causal systems, each modeled by one directed acyclic graph (DAG). Causal discovery from mixtures is fundamentally more challenging than single-DAG causal discovery. Two major difficulties stem from (i) an inherent uncertainty about the skeletons of the component DAGs that constitute the mixture and (ii) possibly cyclic relationships across these component DAGs. This paper addresses these challenges and aims to identify edges that exist in at least one component DAG of the mixture, referred to as the *true* edges. First, it establishes matching necessary and sufficient conditions on the size of interventions required to identify the true edges. Next, guided by the necessity results, an adaptive algorithm is designed that learns all true edges using ${\cal O}(n^2)$ interventions, where $n$ is the number of nodes. Remarkably, the size of the interventions is optimal if the underlying mixture model does not contain cycles across its components. More generally, the gap between the intervention size used by the algorithm and the optimal size is quantified. It is shown to be bounded by the *cyclic complexity number* of the mixture model, defined as the size of the minimal intervention that can break the cycles in the mixture, which is upper bounded by the number of cycles among the ancestors of a node.

paragraphs: Some systems contain several coexisting causal structures, so one directed acyclic graph cannot describe all their interactions. Learning from such mixtures is difficult because the component structures are uncertain, and edges from different individually acyclic graphs can form cycles when considered together. This paper studies how interventions can resolve that uncertainty.

The target is the collection of edges appearing in at least one component graph. The authors establish matching necessary and sufficient conditions on intervention size for identifying these edges. Guided by the necessity results, they design an adaptive algorithm that learns the entire collection using a number of interventions that grows quadratically with the number of variables.

When the mixture contains no cycles across components, the algorithm's intervention size is optimal. More generally, its excess intervention size is bounded using a cyclic complexity number: the smallest intervention needed to break the mixture's cycles. This separates the number of experiments from how many variables each experiment must affect and quantifies the additional difficulty introduced by cross-component cycles.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes intervention requirements and gives an adaptive algorithm for discovering edges across mixtures of causal graphs.

title: Interventional Causal Discovery in a Mixture of DAGs

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has rapidly advanced in recent years, approaching the performance of its supervised counterparts through the extraction of representations from unlabeled data. However, dimensional collapse, where a few large eigenvalues dominate the eigenspace, poses a significant obstacle for SSL. When dimensional collapse occurs on features (e.g. hidden features and representations), it prevents features from representing the full information of the data; when dimensional collapse occurs on weight matrices, their filters are self-related and redundant, limiting their expressive power.Existing studies have predominantly concentrated on the dimensional collapse of representations, neglecting whether this can sufficiently prevent the dimensional collapse of the weight matrices and hidden features. To this end, we first time propose a mitigation approach employing orthogonal regularization (OR) across the encoder, targeting both convolutional and linear layers during pretraining. OR promotes orthogonality within weight matrices, thus safeguarding against the dimensional collapse of weight matrices, hidden features, and representations. Our empirical investigations demonstrate that OR significantly enhances the performance of SSL methods across diverse benchmarks, yielding consistent gains with both CNNs and Transformer-based architectures.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning extracts representations from unlabeled data, but those representations can suffer dimensional collapse: a few directions dominate while others contribute little. In features, this restricts the information represented. In weight matrices, it corresponds to related, redundant filters that limit expressive power. The paper examines collapse throughout the encoder.

Prior work has primarily addressed collapse in the final representations. The authors question whether that is sufficient to protect hidden features and weight matrices as well. Their proposed remedy applies orthogonality regularization to convolutional and linear layers during pretraining, encouraging weight matrices to contain less redundant directions.

The method is intended to safeguard weights, hidden features, and representations together by acting across the encoder. Empirical evaluations show significant improvements for self-supervised methods across diverse benchmarks, with consistent gains in both convolutional and Transformer-based architectures. These findings support treating dimensional collapse as a concern throughout the learned network, with regularization of its weights providing a practical intervention beyond focusing only on output representations.
summary.tldr: Orthogonality regularization throughout the encoder mitigates dimensional collapse and consistently improves evaluated self-supervised CNN and Transformer models.

title: Preventing Dimensional Collapse in Self-Supervised Learning via Orthogonality Regularization

abstract: The conditional quantile treatment effect (CQTE) can provide insight into the effect of a treatment beyond the conditional average treatment effect (CATE). This ability to provide information over multiple quantiles of the response makes the CQTE especially valuable in cases where the effect of a treatment is not well-modelled by a location shift, even conditionally on the covariates. Nevertheless, the estimation of the CQTE is challenging and often depends upon the smoothness of the individual quantiles as a function of the covariates rather than smoothness of the CQTE itself. This is in stark contrast to the CATE where it is possible to obtain high-quality estimates which have less dependency upon the smoothness of the nuisance parameters when the CATE itself is smooth. Moreover, relative smoothness of the CQTE lacks the interpretability of smoothness of the CATE making it less clear whether it is a reasonable assumption to make. We combine the desirable properties of the CATE and CQTE by considering a new estimand, the conditional quantile comparator (CQC). The CQC not only retains information about the whole treatment distribution, similar to the CQTE, but also having more natural examples of smoothness and is able to leverage simplicity in an auxiliary estimand. We provide finite sample bounds on the error of our estimator, demonstrating its ability to exploit simplicity. We validate our theory in numerical simulations which show that our method produces more accurate estimates than baselines. Finally, we apply our methodology to a study on the effect of employment incentives on earnings across different age groups. We see that our method is able to reveal heterogeneity of the effect across different quantiles.

paragraphs: Average treatment effects can conceal differences across an outcome distribution. A treatment might affect lower and higher outcomes differently even among people with similar characteristics. Conditional quantile treatment effects capture such variation, but estimating them can depend strongly on how smoothly the separate quantiles change with those characteristics, rather than on the simplicity of the treatment effect itself.

The paper introduces the conditional quantile comparator, or CQC, to combine distributional information with more favorable estimation properties. Like quantile treatment effects, it retains information beyond the average. The authors argue that it admits more natural examples of smoothness and can benefit from simplicity in an auxiliary quantity, giving the estimator useful structure to exploit.

Finite-sample error bounds establish how the estimator can take advantage of that simplicity. Numerical simulations support the theory and show more accurate estimates than baselines. An application to employment incentives examines earnings across age groups and reveals variation in treatment effects across quantiles. The contribution is a different statistical target for studying treatment heterogeneity throughout a distribution.
summary.tldr: The conditional quantile comparator captures distributional treatment differences while allowing estimation to exploit simpler underlying structure.

title: Conditional Outcome Equivalence: A Quantile Alternative to CATE

abstract: This paper addresses the prevalent issue of label shift in an online setting with missing labels, where data distributions change over time and obtaining timely labels is challenging. While existing methods primarily focus on adjusting or updating the final layer of a pre-trained classifier, we explore the untapped potential of enhancing feature representations using unlabeled data at test-time. Our novel method, Online Label Shift adaptation with Online Feature Updates (OLS-OFU), leverages self-supervised learning to refine the feature extraction process, thereby improving the prediction model. By carefully designing the algorithm, theoretically OLS-OFU maintains the similar online regret convergence to the results in the literature while taking the improved features into account. Empirically, it achieves substantial improvements over existing methods, which is as significant as the gains existing methods have over the baseline (i.e., without distribution shift adaptations).

paragraphs: A deployed classifier may encounter changing data distributions before new labels become available. This paper considers online label-shift adaptation under that constraint. Existing methods largely adjust the final layer of a pretrained classifier, while the authors investigate whether the feature representation itself can also be improved using the unlabeled incoming data.

Their method, OLS-OFU, uses self-supervised learning to update feature extraction at test time. These feature updates become part of the ongoing adaptation process, allowing the prediction model to benefit from a changing representation as well as adjustments to its classification stage. The approach therefore expands which parts of the model participate in responding to distribution changes.

The theoretical analysis preserves online regret convergence similar to existing results while accounting for the improved features. Empirically, the gains over existing adaptation methods are reported to be as substantial as those methods' gains over a baseline with no adaptation. The findings support online representation updates as a meaningful addition to label-shift correction, with both a theoretical treatment and evidence of practical prediction improvements.
summary.tldr: OLS-OFU improves online label-shift adaptation by updating feature representations through self-supervised learning on unlabeled test data.

title: Online Feature Updates Improve Online (Generalized) Label Shift Adaptation

abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is known to improve Large Language Models both empirically and in terms of theoretical approximation power.However, our understanding of the inner workings and conditions of apparition of CoT capabilities remains limited.This paper helps fill this gap by demonstrating how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers in a controlled and interpretable setting.In particular, we observe the appearance of a specialized attention mechanism dedicated to iterative reasoning, which we coined "iteration heads".We track both the emergence and the precise working of these iteration heads down to the attention level, and measure the transferability of the CoT skills to which they give rise between tasks.

paragraphs: Chain-of-thought reasoning can improve language-model performance, but that observation leaves open how the capability develops inside a transformer. This paper studies its emergence in a controlled, interpretable setting. The focus is on connecting iterative reasoning behavior to identifiable attention mechanisms, making the internal computation accessible to closer examination.

The authors observe specialized attention mechanisms that they call iteration heads. These mechanisms are dedicated to iterative reasoning, and the study tracks both their appearance and their detailed operation at the attention level. Following their development connects the emergence of the behavior to changes in the machinery that carries out the computation.

The paper also measures how the resulting chain-of-thought skills transfer between tasks. That adds a behavioral dimension to the mechanistic analysis: it examines how capabilities associated with the observed heads carry across task boundaries. The contribution is a concrete account of chain-of-thought emergence in the studied setting, with attention-level evidence and transfer measurements complementing one another.
summary.tldr: In a controlled transformer setting, the authors identify and trace attention mechanisms associated with emerging iterative chain-of-thought reasoning.

title: Iteration Head: A Mechanistic Study of Chain-of-Thought

abstract: AI model alignment is crucial due to inadvertent biases in training data and the underspecified machine learning pipeline, where models with excellent test metrics may not meet end-user requirements. While post-training alignment via human feedback shows promise, these methods are often limited to generative AI settings where humans can interpret and provide feedback on model outputs. In traditional non-generative settings with numerical or categorical outputs, detecting misalignment through single-sample outputs remains challenging, and enforcing alignment during training requires repeating costly training processes.In this paper we consider an alternative strategy. We propose interpreting model alignment through property testing, defining an aligned model $f$ as one belonging to a subset $\mathcal{P}$ of functions that exhibit specific desired behaviors. We focus on post-processing a pre-trained model $f$ to better align with $\mathcal{P}$ using conformal risk control. Specifically, we develop a general procedure for converting queries for testing a given property $\mathcal{P}$ to a collection of loss functions suitable for use in a conformal risk control algorithm. We prove a probabilistic guarantee that the resulting conformal interval around $f$ contains a function approximately satisfying $\mathcal{P}$. We exhibit applications of our methodology on a collection of supervised learning datasets for (shape-constrained) properties such as monotonicity and concavity. The general procedure is flexible and can be applied to a wide range of desired properties. Finally, we prove that pre-trained models will always require alignment techniques even as model sizes or training data increase, as long as the training data contains even small biases.

paragraphs: A model can score well on a test set while behaving in ways that users do not want. This paper treats alignment as a question about mathematical properties of the model’s behavior, such as whether predictions increase monotonically or follow a concave shape. These requirements concern relationships across outputs, making them difficult to assess from a single prediction.

The authors develop a way to adjust a pretrained model through conformal risk control. They translate queries used to test a desired property into loss functions that the conformal procedure can use. The resulting guarantee is probabilistic: an interval around the original model contains a function that approximately satisfies the property. This does not establish that the original model itself satisfies it.

Applications on supervised learning datasets illustrate the method for shape constraints. The paper also proves that increasing model size or training data does not eliminate the need for alignment when training data retains even small biases. Together, these results motivate checking and addressing desired behavior after training.
summary.tldr: The paper uses conformal risk control to construct intervals around pretrained models that probabilistically contain functions approximately satisfying desired behavioral properties.

title: Aligning Model Properties via Conformal Risk Control

abstract: Image search and retrieval tasks can perpetuate harmful stereotypes, erase cultural identities, and amplify social disparities. Current approaches to mitigate these representational harms balance the number of retrieved items across population groups defined by a small number of (often binary) attributes. However, most existing methods overlook intersectional groups determined by combinations ofgroup attributes, such as gender, race, and ethnicity. We introduce Multi-Group Proportional Representation (MPR), a novel metric that measures representation across intersectional groups. We develop practical methods for estimating MPR, provide theoretical guarantees, and propose optimization algorithms to ensure MPR in retrieval. We demonstrate that existing methods optimizing for equal and proportional representation metrics may fail to promote MPR. Crucially, our work shows that optimizing MPR yields more proportional representation across multiple intersectional groups specified by a rich function class, often with minimal compromise in retrieval accuracy. Code is provided at https://github.com/alex-oesterling/multigroup-proportional-representation.

paragraphs: A retrieval system can appear balanced across individual demographic attributes while still poorly representing groups defined by combinations of those attributes. This paper addresses that intersectional problem in image search and retrieval. It argues that methods centered on a small number of often binary attributes can miss important patterns of representation.

The authors introduce Multi-Group Proportional Representation, or MPR, a metric for measuring representation across intersectional groups. They develop practical estimation methods, provide theoretical guarantees, and propose optimization algorithms that target MPR. The framework handles multiple groups described by a rich function class, broadening which combinations can enter the representation assessment.

The study shows that optimizing existing equal or proportional representation metrics may fail to achieve MPR. Optimizing the new metric produces more proportional representation across multiple intersectional groups, often with only a small reduction in retrieval accuracy. The word often matters: the reported result supports a favorable tradeoff in many evaluated cases rather than eliminating the tradeoff. The contribution makes overlapping group representation an explicit retrieval objective.
summary.tldr: MPR measures and improves proportional representation across intersectional groups, often with little loss of retrieval accuracy.

title: Multi-Group Proportional Representation in Retrieval

abstract: Alignment is a procedure to fine-tune pre-trained large language models (LLMs) to follow natural language instructions and serve as helpful AI assistants. We have observed, however, that the conventional alignment process fails to enhance the factual accuracy of LLMs, and often leads to the generation of more false facts (i.e., *hallucination*). In this paper, we study how to make the LLM alignment process more factual, by first identifying factors that lead to hallucination in both alignment steps: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL).In particular, we find that training the LLM on new or unfamiliar knowledge can encourage hallucination.This makes SFT less factual as it trains on human-labeled data that may be novel to the LLM. Furthermore, reward functions used in standard RL often inadequately capture factuality and favor longer and more detailed responses, which inadvertently promote hallucination.Based on these observations, we propose *FactuaLity-aware AlignMEnt*, comprised of *factuality-aware SFT* and *factuality-aware RL* through direct preference optimization. Experiments show that our proposed *FLAME* guides LLMs to output more factual responses while maintaining their instruction-following capability.

paragraphs: FLAME examines why making a language model more helpful and instruction-following does not necessarily make it more factual. The authors observe that conventional alignment can increase hallucinations. They investigate contributing factors in both supervised fine-tuning and the subsequent preference-oriented training stage, treating factual accuracy as a concern throughout alignment.

One finding is that training on new or unfamiliar knowledge can encourage hallucination. Human-labeled fine-tuning data may contain such knowledge, creating a problem even when the examples are intended to improve the model. The authors also find that standard reward functions inadequately capture factuality and can favor longer, more detailed answers, inadvertently encouraging additional false claims.

The proposed method combines factuality-aware supervised fine-tuning with factuality-aware preference optimization through direct preference optimization. Its design responds to the identified problems in both stages rather than treating factuality solely as an evaluation criterion afterward. Experiments show more factual responses while preserving instruction-following capability, supporting the possibility of improving factuality without sacrificing that central purpose of alignment.
summary.tldr: FLAME adjusts supervised and preference-based alignment to improve factual responses while maintaining instruction following.

title: FLAME : Factuality-Aware Alignment for Large Language Models

abstract: The most advanced diffusion models have recently adopted increasingly deep stacked networks (e.g., U-Net or Transformer) to promote the generative emergence capabilities of vision generation models similar to large language models (LLMs). However, progressively deeper stacked networks will intuitively cause numerical propagation errors and reduce noisy prediction capabilities on generative data, which hinders massively deep scalable training of vision generation models. In this paper, we first uncover the nature that neural networks being able to effectively perform generative denoising lies in the fact that the intrinsic residual unit has consistent dynamic property with the input signal's reverse diffusion process, thus supporting excellent generative abilities.Afterwards, we stand on the shoulders of two common types of deep stacked networks to propose a unified and massively scalable Neural Residual Diffusion Models framework (Neural-RDM for short), which is a simple yet meaningful change to the common architecture of deep generative networks by introducing a series of learnable gated residual parameters that conform to the generative dynamics. Experimental results on various generative tasks show that the proposed neural residual models obtain state-of-the-art scores on image's and video's generative benchmarks. Rigorous theoretical proofs and extensive experiments also demonstrate the advantages of this simple gated residual mechanism consistent with dynamic modeling in improving the fidelity and consistency of generated content and supporting large-scale scalable training.

paragraphs: Increasing the depth of diffusion networks is one route toward stronger image and video generation, but the paper argues that deeper stacks can accumulate numerical propagation errors and impair noise prediction. It investigates how the internal dynamics of residual networks relate to the reverse diffusion process used to generate content.

The authors identify consistency between residual-unit dynamics and reverse diffusion as a basis for effective generative denoising. Building on U-Net and Transformer architectures, they introduce Neural-RDM, a framework that adds learnable gates to residual contributions. These parameters are designed to make the network's residual behavior conform to the dynamics of generation while supporting much deeper architectures.

The paper provides theoretical proofs and experiments supporting the gated mechanism. Across evaluated image and video generation benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art scores, along with improvements in content fidelity, consistency, and support for large-scale training. The contribution ties a relatively simple architectural change to a dynamical explanation of denoising, giving a specific mechanism for pursuing greater depth in generative vision models.
summary.tldr: Neural-RDM adds learnable residual gates aligned with diffusion dynamics to support deeper image and video generators, with strong reported benchmark results.

title: Neural Residual Diffusion Models for Deep Scalable Vision Generation

abstract: Imitation learning (IL) aims to mimic the behavior of an expert in a sequential decision making task by learning from demonstrations, and has been widely applied to robotics, autonomous driving, and autoregressive text generation. The simplest approach to IL, behavior cloning (BC) is thought to incur sample complexity with unfavorable quadratic dependence on the problem horizon, motivating a variety of different online algorithms that attain improved linear horizon dependence under stronger assumptions on the data and the learner’s access to the expert. We revisit the apparent gap between offline and online IL from a learning-theoretic perspective, with a focus on general policy classes up to and including deep neural networks. Through a new analysis of BC with the logarithmic loss, we show that it is possible to achieve horizon-independent sample complexity in offline IL whenever (i) the range of the cumulative payoffs is controlled, and (ii) an appropriate notion of supervised learning complexity for the policy class is controlled. Specializing our results to deterministic, stationary policies, we show that the gap between offline and online IL is not fundamental: (i) it is possible to achieve linear dependence on horizon in offline IL under dense rewards (matching what was previously only known to be achievable in online IL); and (ii) without further assumptions on the policy class, online IL cannot improve over offline IL with the logarithmic loss, even in benign MDPs. We complement our theoretical results with experiments on standard RL tasks and autoregressive language generation to validate the practical relevance of our findings.

paragraphs: Behavior cloning learns to imitate an expert from recorded demonstrations. It is often thought to require a number of samples that grows unfavorably with the length of a decision sequence, motivating online methods with additional expert access. This paper revisits that apparent disadvantage through a learning-theoretic analysis covering policy classes that include deep neural networks.

For behavior cloning trained with logarithmic loss, the authors establish that horizon-independent sample complexity is possible when two quantities are controlled: the range of cumulative payoffs and an appropriate supervised-learning complexity of the policy class. The conclusion is conditional on those controls; the sequence length alone does not determine the learning difficulty.

For deterministic, stationary policies, the analysis further shows that offline imitation can achieve linear horizon dependence with dense rewards. Without additional policy-class assumptions, online imitation cannot improve over offline imitation with logarithmic loss, even in benign decision processes. Experiments on reinforcement-learning tasks and autoregressive language generation support the practical relevance of the analysis. Together, the results challenge the view that an offline-versus-online gap is fundamental.
summary.tldr: A new analysis shows that behavior cloning can avoid unfavorable horizon dependence under explicit payoff and policy-complexity conditions.

title: Is Behavior Cloning All You Need? Understanding Horizon in Imitation Learning

abstract: We study the problem of transfer learning and fine-tuning in linear models for both regression and binary classification. In particular, we consider the use of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a linear model initialized with pretrained weights and using a small training data set from the target distribution. In the asymptotic regime of large models, we provide an exact and rigorous analysis and relate the generalization errors (in regression) and classification errors (in binary classification) for the pretrained and fine-tuned models. In particular, we give conditions under which the fine-tuned model outperforms the pretrained one. An important aspect of our work is that all the results are "universal", in the sense that they depend only on the first and second order statistics of the target distribution. They thus extend well beyond the standard Gaussian assumptions commonly made in the literature. Furthermore, our universality results extend beyond standard SGD training to the test error of a classification task trained using ridge regression.

summary.tldr: The paper derives conditions for beneficial fine-tuning in large linear models using only first- and second-order target-distribution statistics.

title: Universality in Transfer Learning for Linear Models

abstract: Q-learning is widely used algorithm in reinforcement learning (RL) community. Under the lookup table setting, its convergence is well established. However, its behavior is known to be unstable with the linear function approximation case. This paper develops a new Q-learning algorithm, called RegQ, that converges when linear function approximation is used. We prove that simply adding an appropriate regularization term ensures convergence of the algorithm. Its stability is established using a recent analysis tool based on switching system models. Moreover, we experimentally show that RegQ converges in environments where Q-learning with linear function approximation has known to diverge. An error bound on the solution where the algorithm converges is also given.

That bound complements the stability result: convergence concerns whether learning settles, while the error bound describes the quality of the resulting solution. Together, the findings support regularization as a way to stabilize this setting.
summary.tldr: RegQ adds an appropriate regularization term to make Q-learning converge with linear function approximation and bounds the resulting solution error.

title: Regularized Q-Learning

abstract: Much of Bayesian inference centers around the design of estimators for inverse problems which are optimal assuming the data comes from a known prior. But what do these optimality guarantees mean if the prior is unknown? In recent years, algorithm unrolling has emerged as deep learning's answer to this age-old question: design a neural network whose layers can in principle simulate iterations of inference algorithms and train on data generated by the unknown prior. Despite its empirical success, however, it has remained unclear whether this method can provably recover the performance of its optimal, prior-aware counterparts.In this work, we prove the first rigorous learning guarantees for neural networks based on unrolling approximate message passing (AMP). For compressed sensing, we prove that when trained on data drawn from a product prior, the layers of the network approximately converge to the same denoisers used in Bayes AMP. We also provide extensive numerical experiments for compressed sensing and rank-one matrix estimation demonstrating the advantages of our unrolled architecture \--- in addition to being able to obliviously adapt to general priors, it exhibits improvements over Bayes AMP in more general settings of low dimensions, non-Gaussian designs, and non-product priors.

The paper asks whether this process can provably recover the behavior of an optimal, prior-aware method.

The work therefore combines a conditional theoretical result with evidence across more general settings.
summary.tldr: Under a product-prior assumption, unrolled AMP networks provably learn denoisers approximating those of Bayes AMP, with broader benefits demonstrated experimentally.

title: Unrolled denoising networks provably learn to perform optimal Bayesian inference

abstract: This paper studies the properties of solutions to multi-task shallow ReLU neural network learning problems, wherein the network is trained to fit a dataset with minimal sum of squared weights. Remarkably, the solutions learned for each individual task resemble those obtained by solving a kernel regression problem, revealing a novel connection between neural networks and kernel methods. It is known that single-task neural network learning problems are equivalent to a minimum norm interpolation problem in a non-Hilbertian Banach space, and that the solutions of such problems are generally non-unique. In contrast, we prove that the solutions to univariate-input, multi-task neural network interpolation problems are almost always unique, and coincide with the solution to a minimum-norm interpolation problem in a Sobolev (Reproducing Kernel) Hilbert Space. We also demonstrate a similar phenomenon in the multivariate-input case; specifically, we show that neural network learning problems with large numbers of tasks are approximately equivalent to an $\ell^2$ (Hilbert space) minimization problem over a fixed kernel determined by the optimal neurons.

paragraphs: Training several tasks together can change which solutions a neural network prefers. This paper studies shallow ReLU networks that fit their training data while minimizing the sum of squared weights. Its central question concerns the resulting inductive bias: how this preference for small weights shapes the functions learned for individual tasks.

For inputs with a single variable, the authors prove that multi-task interpolation solutions are almost always unique. They also coincide with minimum-norm interpolation solutions in a Sobolev reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This contrasts with the stated single-task setting, whose corresponding minimum-norm problem lies in a different kind of function space and generally has multiple solutions.

For inputs with several variables, the paper establishes a related, approximate connection when the number of tasks is large. Learning then resembles squared-norm minimization using a fixed kernel determined by the optimal neurons. These results explain how sharing a network across tasks can produce kernel-like behavior, with exact and approximate conclusions applying in different settings.
summary.tldr: Multi-task learning in minimum-weight shallow ReLU networks produces kernel-like solutions, with almost-always uniqueness proved for single-variable inputs.

title: A New Neural Kernel Regime: The Inductive Bias of Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Self-supervised word embedding algorithms such as word2vec provide a minimal setting for studying representation learning in language modeling. We examine the quartic Taylor approximation of the word2vec loss around the origin, and we show that both the resulting training dynamics and the final performance on downstream tasks are empirically very similar to those of word2vec. Our main contribution is to analytically solve for both the gradient flow training dynamics and the final word embeddings in terms of only the corpus statistics and training hyperparameters. The solutions reveal that these models learn orthogonal linear subspaces one at a time, each one incrementing the effective rank of the embeddings until model capacity is saturated. Training on Wikipedia, we find that each of the top linear subspaces represents an interpretable topic-level concept. Finally, we apply our theory to describe how linear representations of more abstract semantic concepts emerge during training; these can be used to complete analogies via vector addition.

summary.tldr: An analytically solvable word2vec-like model reveals how topic and semantic subspaces emerge sequentially during training.

title: Closed-Form Training Dynamics Reveal Learned Features and Linear Structure in Word2Vec-like Models

abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) often exhibit limited inferential efficiency in estimating treatment effects due to small sample sizes. In recent years, the combination of external controls has gained increasing attention as a means of improving the efficiency of RCTs. However, external controls are not always comparable to RCTs, and direct borrowing without careful evaluation can introduce substantial bias and reduce the efficiency of treatment effect estimation. In this paper, we propose a novel influence-based adaptive sample borrowing approach that effectively quantifies the "comparability'' of each sample in the external controls using influence function theory. Given a selected set of borrowed external controls, we further derive a semiparametric efficient estimator under an exchangeability assumption. Recognizing that the exchangeability assumption may not hold for all possible borrowing sets, we conduct a detailed analysis of the asymptotic bias and variance of the proposed estimator under violations of exchangeability. Building on this bias-variance trade-off, we further develop a data-driven approach to select the optimal subset of external controls for borrowing. Extensive simulations and real-world applications demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances treatment effect estimation efficiency in RCTs, outperforming existing approaches.

paragraphs: Small randomized trials can struggle to estimate treatment effects precisely. Adding external control participants could help, but those participants may differ from the trial population in consequential ways. This paper develops a method for deciding which external samples to borrow, treating their comparability as something to evaluate individually.

The approach uses influence function theory to quantify each external sample’s comparability. For a chosen borrowing set, the authors derive an estimator that is semiparametrically efficient under an exchangeability assumption. That assumption is central: the efficiency result depends on the selected external controls being appropriately interchangeable with trial controls.

The authors also analyze what happens when exchangeability fails, examining the estimator’s large-sample bias and variance. They use this trade-off to select a borrowing subset from the data. Simulations and real-world applications report improved estimation efficiency over existing approaches. The contribution is therefore both an estimator and a selection procedure: borrowing is guided by its potential to improve precision while accounting for the bias that incompatible controls can introduce.
summary.tldr: An adaptive borrowing method selects external controls to improve trial estimates while accounting for comparability and the bias–variance trade-off.

title: Adaptive Data-Borrowing for Improving Treatment Effect Estimation using External Controls

abstract: Inspired by the remarkable success of foundation models in language and vision, Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) hold significant promise for broad applicability across diverse graph tasks and domains. However, existing GFMs struggle with unstable few-shot fine-tuning, where both performance and adaptation efficiency exhibit significant fluctuations caused by the randomness in the support sample selection and structural discrepancies between the pre-trained and target graphs. How to fine-tune GFMs robustly and efficiently to enable trustworthy knowledge transfer across domains and tasks is the major challenge. In this paper, we propose **GRAVER**, a novel **G**enerative g**RA**ph **V**ocabulari**E**s for **R**obust GFM fine-tuning framework that tackles the aforementioned instability via generative augmentations. Specifically, to identify transferable units, we analyze and extract key class-specific subgraph patterns by ego-graph disentanglement and validate their transferability both theoretically and empirically. To enable effective pre-training across diverse domains, we leverage a universal task template based on ego-graph similarity and construct graph vocabularies via graphon-based generative experts. To facilitate robust and efficient prompt fine-tuning, we grave the support samples with in-context vocabularies, where the lightweight MoE-CoE network attentively routes knowledge from source domains. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of GRAVER over **effectiveness**, **robustness**, and **efficiency** on downstream few-shot node and graph classification tasks compared with **15** state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a graph foundation model with only a few labeled examples can be unstable. Results depend on which examples are selected and how the target graph's structure differs from pretraining graphs. GRAVER addresses both sources of variation through generative augmentation built around reusable graph patterns.

summary.tldr: GRAVER generates reusable graph-pattern vocabularies to improve the effectiveness, stability, and efficiency of few-shot graph foundation model adaptation.

title: GRAVER: Generative Graph Vocabularies for Robust Graph Foundation Models Fine-tuning

abstract: LLM-based agents have shown promising capabilities in a growing range of software engineering (SWE) tasks. However, advancing this field faces two critical challenges. First, high-quality training data is scarce, especially data that reflects real-world SWE scenarios, where agents must interact with development environments, execute code and adapt behavior based on the outcomes of their actions. Existing datasets are either limited to one-shot code generation or comprise small, manually curated collections of interactive tasks, lacking both scale and diversity. Second, the lack of fresh interactive SWE tasks affects evaluation of rapidly improving models, as static benchmarks quickly become outdated due to contamination issues. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel, automated, and scalable pipeline to continuously extract real-world interactive SWE tasks from diverse GitHub repositories. Using this pipeline, we construct SWE-rebench, a public dataset comprising over 21,000 interactive Python-based SWE tasks, suitable for reinforcement learning of SWE agents at scale. Additionally, we use continuous supply of fresh tasks collected using SWE-rebench methodology to build a contamination-free benchmark for agentic software engineering. We compare results of various LLMs on this benchmark to results on SWE-bench Verified and show that performance of some language models might be inflated due to contamination issues.

paragraphs: Software-engineering agents need practice on tasks that require interacting with a development environment, running code, and responding to the results. Collections focused on one-shot code generation do not capture that full process, while manually assembled interactive datasets can be small. SWE-rebench introduces an automated pipeline that continuously collects real-world interactive tasks from diverse GitHub repositories.

summary.tldr: SWE-rebench automatically collects interactive software-engineering tasks for large-scale training and fresh evaluation that probes possible benchmark contamination.

title: SWE-rebench: An Automated Pipeline for Task Collection and Decontaminated Evaluation of Software Engineering Agents

abstract: Modern smartphones often feature asymmetric dual-lens systems, capturing wide-angle and ultra-wide views with complementary perspectives and details. Motion and shake can blur the wide lens, while the ultra-wide lens, despite lower resolution, retains sharper details. This natural complementarity offers valuable cues for video deblurring. However, existing methods focus mainly on single-camera inputs or symmetric stereo pairs, neglecting the cross-lens redundancy in mobile dual-camera systems. In this paper, we propose a practical video deblurring method, AsLeD-Net, which recurrently aligns and propagates temporal reference features from ultra-wide views fused with features extracted from wide-angle blurry frames. AsLeD-Net consists of two key modules: the adaptive local matching (ALM) module, which refines blurry features using $K$-nearest neighbor reference features, and the difference compensation (DC) module, which ensures spatial consistency and reduces misalignment. Additionally, AsLeD-Net uses the reference-guided motion compensation (RMC) module for temporal alignment, further improving frame-to-frame consistency in the deblurring process. We validate the effectiveness of AsLeD-Net through extensive experiments, benchmarking it against potential solutions for asymmetric lens deblurring.

Camera shake may blur the wide-angle video while the lower-resolution ultra-wide view preserves sharper details. This paper builds a video deblurring system around that asymmetry, using the ultra-wide stream as a reference for restoring the wide-angle frames.

The proposed AsLeD-Net repeatedly aligns reference features across time and combines them with features from blurry frames. Its adaptive local matching module refines those blurry features using nearby reference features selected through nearest-neighbor matching. A difference compensation module addresses spatial inconsistency and misalignment, helping the network reconcile information captured through lenses with different views.

A further reference-guided motion compensation module aligns information temporally to improve consistency between restored frames. These components address complementary problems: finding useful sharp detail, aligning it spatially, and carrying it through the video. The authors report extensive experiments against potential solutions for asymmetric-lens deblurring that validate the approach. The contribution is a method designed specifically to exploit the unequal but complementary information already available from mobile dual-camera systems.
summary.tldr: AsLeD-Net uses sharper ultra-wide video to restore blurry wide-angle footage while aligning detail across lenses and time.

title: Asymmetric Dual-Lens Video Deblurring

abstract: Computer use agents are LLM-based agents that can directly interact with a graphical user interface, by processing screenshots or accessibility trees. While these systems are gaining popularity, their safety has been largely overlooked, despite the fact that evaluating and understanding their potential for harmful behavior is essential for widespread adoption. To address this gap, we introduce OS-Harm, a new benchmark for measuring safety of computer use agents. OS-Harm is built on top of the OSWorld environment (Xie et al., 2024) and aims to test models across three categories of harm: deliberate user misuse, prompt injection attacks, and model misbehavior. To cover these cases, we create 150 tasks that span several types of safety violations (harassment, copyright infringement, disinformation, data exfiltration, etc.) and require the agent to interact with a variety of OS applications (email client, code editor, browser, etc.). Moreover, we propose an automated judge to evaluate both accuracy and safety of agents that achieves high agreement with human annotations (0.76 and 0.79 F1 score). We evaluate computer use agents based on a range of frontier models—such as `o4-mini`, `Claude 3.7 Sonnet`, `Gemini 2.5 Pro`—and provide insights into their safety. In particular, all models tend to directly comply with many deliberate misuse queries, are relatively vulnerable to static prompt injections, and occasionally perform unsafe actions. The OS-Harm benchmark is available at https://github.com/tml-epfl/os-harm.

Evaluations include agents based on o4-mini, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.5 Pro. These findings make safety measurable at the level of application interaction, where an agent's behavior includes consequential operations as well as generated text.
summary.tldr: OS-Harm tests computer-use agents on 150 safety tasks and finds substantial misuse compliance, prompt-injection vulnerability, and occasional unsafe actions.

title: OS-Harm: A Benchmark for Measuring Safety of Computer Use Agents

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, ensuring the safety of their outputs during decoding has become a critical challenge. However, existing decoding-time interventions, such as Contrastive Decoding, often force a severe trade-off between safety and response quality. In this work, we propose **CARE**, a novel framework for decoding-time safety alignment that integrates three key components: (1) a guard model for real-time safety monitoring, enabling detection of potentially unsafe content; (2) a rollback mechanism with a token buffer to correct unsafe outputs efficiently at an earlier stage without disrupting the user experience; and (3) a novel introspection-based intervention strategy, where the model generates self-reflective critiques of its previous outputs and incorporates these reflections into the context to guide subsequent decoding steps. The framework achieves a superior safety-quality trade-off by using its guard model for precise interventions, its rollback mechanism for timely corrections, and our novel introspection method for effective self-correction. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework achieves a superior balance of safety, quality, and efficiency, attaining a **low harmful response rate** and **minimal disruption to the user experience** while **maintaining high response quality**.

paragraphs: CARE addresses safety while a language model is generating its response. Existing decoding interventions can reduce unsafe output at a substantial cost to response quality. The paper proposes a coordinated framework that detects potential problems, revises emerging text, and gives the model contextual guidance for correcting its subsequent generation.

Three components work together. A guard model monitors generation for potentially unsafe content. A token buffer supports rolling back problematic output so corrections can happen earlier with little disruption to the user. The model then produces a self-reflective critique of its previous output, and that critique becomes part of the context guiding later decoding.

The authors report that experiments achieve a better balance of safety, quality, and efficiency, with a low harmful-response rate and minimal disruption while retaining high response quality. The significance lies in combining targeted detection with revision and contextual self-correction. The reported outcome is an improved empirical trade-off, with the guard, rollback, and introspection components each serving a distinct part of the correction process.
summary.tldr: CARE combines safety monitoring, buffered rollback, and self-reflective critiques to improve the safety-quality trade-off during language model generation.

title: CARE: Decoding-Time Safety Alignment via Rollback and Introspection Intervention

abstract: A common paradigm to improve the performance of large language models is optimizing for a reward model. Reward models assign a numerical score to an LLM’s output that indicates, for example, how likely it is to align with user preferences or safety goals. However, reward models are never perfect. They inevitably function as proxies for complex desiderata such as correctness, helpfulness, and safety. By overoptimizing for a misspecified reward, we can subvert intended alignment goals and reduce overall performance -- a phenomenon commonly referred to as reward hacking. In this work, we characterize reward hacking in inference-time alignment and demonstrate when and how we can mitigate it by hedging on the proxy reward. We study this phenomenon under Best-of-$n$ (BoN) and Soft Best-of-$n$ (SBoN), and we introduce Best-of-Poisson (BoP) that provides an efficient, near-exact approximation of the optimal reward-KL divergence policy at inference time. We show that the characteristic pattern of hacking as observed in practice (where the true reward first increases before declining) is an inevitable property of a broad class of inference-time mechanisms, including BoN and BoP. To counter this effect, we introduce $\texttt{HedgeTune}$, an efficient algorithm to find the optimal inference-time parameter. We demonstrate that hedging mitigates reward hacking and achieves superior reward-distortion tradeoffs on math, reasoning, and human-preference setups.

paragraphs: A reward model scores language-model responses using an imperfect approximation of qualities such as correctness or helpfulness. Selecting responses ever more aggressively by that score can eventually reduce their actual quality. This paper studies that problem during inference, when outputs are selected or reweighted without necessarily changing the underlying language model.

The analysis covers Best-of-n and Soft Best-of-n selection and introduces Best-of-Poisson. The new mechanism efficiently approximates the optimal policy for a reward objective balanced against KL divergence. The authors show that, for a broad class of inference-time mechanisms including Best-of-n and Best-of-Poisson, true reward inevitably follows the characteristic rise-then-decline pattern of reward hacking.

To manage this effect, HedgeTune efficiently finds the optimal inference-time parameter, moderating how strongly the procedure pursues the proxy reward. Experiments on mathematics, reasoning, and human-preference setups show that this hedging mitigates hacking and improves reward-distortion tradeoffs. The finding is about controlling optimization pressure within these mechanisms, rather than making the reward model a perfect measure of the desired behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes inference-time reward hacking and introduces HedgeTune to moderate proxy optimization and improve reward-distortion tradeoffs.

title: Inference-Time Reward Hacking in Large Language Models

abstract: Understanding how the human brain progresses from processing simple linguistic inputs to performing high-level reasoning is a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. While modern large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to model neural responses to language, their internal representations are highly "entangled," mixing information about lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning. This entanglement biases conventional brain encoding analyses toward linguistically shallow features (e.g., lexicon and syntax), making it difficult to isolate the neural substrates of cognitively deeper processes. Here, we introduce a residual disentanglement method that computationally isolates these components. By first probing an LM to identify feature-specific layers, our method iteratively regresses out lower-level representations to produce four nearly orthogonal embeddings for lexicon, syntax, meaning, and, critically, reasoning. We used these disentangled embeddings to model intracranial (ECoG) brain recordings from neurosurgical patients listening to natural speech. We show that: 1) This isolated reasoning embedding exhibits unique predictive power, accounting for variance in neural activity not explained by other linguistic features and even extending to the recruitment of visual regions beyond classical language areas. 2) The neural signature for reasoning is temporally distinct, peaking later (~350-400ms) than signals related to lexicon, syntax, and meaning, consistent with its position atop a processing hierarchy. 3) Standard, non-disentangled LLM embeddings can be misleading, as their predictive success is primarily attributable to linguistically shallow features, masking the more subtle contributions of deeper cognitive processing. Our work provides compelling neural evidence for an abstract reasoning computation during language comprehension and offers a robust framework for mapping distinct cognitive functions from artificial models to the human brain.

paragraphs: Language-model representations mix vocabulary, syntax, meaning, and reasoning. That mixture complicates efforts to connect model features with brain activity, because strong predictions may mainly reflect simpler linguistic information. This paper develops a residual-disentanglement procedure to separate these contributions before using them to predict neural recordings.

The method first probes a language model to identify layers associated with particular features. It then successively regresses out lower-level representations, producing four nearly orthogonal embeddings corresponding to lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning. The authors use these embeddings to model intracranial recordings from neurosurgical patients listening to natural speech.

The isolated reasoning embedding explains neural variation beyond the other linguistic features, including activity in visual regions outside classical language areas. Its neural signature peaks later, around 350–400 milliseconds, consistent with a processing hierarchy. The study also finds that ordinary entangled embeddings can hide these deeper contributions behind stronger shallow-feature predictions. These results support distinct reasoning-related computation during language comprehension and a more differentiated approach to comparing models with brain responses.
summary.tldr: Separating linguistic features from model embeddings reveals reasoning-related brain activity with distinct predictive and temporal properties.

title: Far from the Shallow: Brain-Predictive Reasoning Embedding through Residual Disentanglement

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often concentrate their attention on a few specific tokens referred to as *attention sinks*. Common examples include the first token, a prompt-independent sink, and punctuation tokens, which are prompt-dependent. While the tokens causing the sinks often lack direct semantic meaning, the presence of the sinks is critical for model performance, particularly under model compression and KV-caching. Despite their ubiquity, the function, semantic role, and origin of attention sinks—especially those beyond the first token—remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation demonstrating that attention sinks: *catch* a sequence of tokens, *tag* them using a common direction in embedding space, and *release* them back into the residual stream, where tokens are later retrieved based on the tags they have acquired. Probing experiments reveal these tags carry semantically meaningful information, such as the truth of a statement. These findings extend to reasoning models, where the mechanism spans more heads and explains greater variance in embeddings, or recent models with query-key normalization, where sinks remain just as prevalent. To encourage future theoretical analysis, we introduce a minimal problem which can be solved through the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism, and where it emerges through training.
