paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples from a model after training. This matters when data must be withdrawn for privacy or regulatory reasons. The paper addresses a central difficulty: existing approaches either depend on restrictive assumptions or do not provide formal assurances that the requested influence has been removed.

The proposed method fine-tunes the model on retained data while introducing noise. Its theoretical basis connects unlearning to privacy amplification through stochastic post-processing: randomized processing provides a route to controlling the remaining influence of removed data. The retain set supplies the information used for continued training, while the noisy procedure supports the unlearning guarantee.

The method requires no assumptions about the loss function, giving it broad applicability across learning settings. The authors analyze the trade-offs between computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, then evaluate the approach empirically. They report that it combines formal guarantees with effective practical performance and improves over existing baselines, making certified removal compatible with continued model usefulness in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Noisy fine-tuning on retained data provides certified neural-network unlearning without assumptions about the loss function.

title: Certified Unlearning for Neural Networks

abstract: Language Models (LMs) often encounter knowledge conflicts when parametric memory contradicts contextual knowledge. Previous works attribute this conflict to the interplay between "memory heads" and "context heads", attention heads assumed to promote either memory or context exclusively. In this study, we go beyond this fundamental assumption by uncovering a critical phenomenon we term the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory, where highly influential attention heads simultaneously contribute to both memory and context. Building upon this insight, we propose Just Run Twice (JuICE), a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric beliefs or contextual knowledge without requiring fine-tuning. JuICE identifies a set of reliable attention heads and leverages a dual-run approach to mitigate the superposition effects. Extensive experiments across 11 datasets and 6 model architectures demonstrate that JuICE sets the new state-of-the-art performance and robust generalization, achieving significant and consistent improvement across different domains under various conflict types. Finally, we theoretically analyze knowledge conflict and the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads, which further elucidates the effectiveness of JuICE in these settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/GaotangLi/JUICE.
originalAbstract: Language Models (LMs) often encounter knowledge conflicts when parametric memory contradicts contextual knowledge. Previous works attribute this conflict to the interplay between "memory heads" and "context heads", attention heads assumed to promote either memory or context exclusively. In this study, we go beyond this fundamental assumption by uncovering a critical phenomenon we term the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory, where highly influential attention heads simultaneously contribute to both memory and context. Building upon this insight, we propose Just Run Twice (JuICE), a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric beliefs or contextual knowledge without requiring fine-tuning. JuICE identifies a set of reliable attention heads and leverages a dual-run approach to mitigate the superposition effects. Extensive experiments across 11 datasets and 6 model architectures demonstrate that JuICE sets the new state-of-the-art performance and robust generalization, achieving significant and consistent improvement across different domains under various conflict types. Finally, we theoretically analyze knowledge conflict and the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads, which further elucidates the effectiveness of JuICE in these settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/GaotangLi/JUICE.

paragraphs: A language model can face a conflict between information stored in its parameters and information supplied in the current context. Earlier explanations assign separate attention heads to memory and context. This paper finds that influential heads can contribute to both simultaneously, a phenomenon the authors call superposition of contextual information and parametric memory.

Just Run Twice, or JuICE, uses this observation to intervene in attention at inference time. It identifies reliable attention heads and uses a dual-run procedure to reduce the effects of their mixed contributions. The intervention can steer the model toward either its parametric beliefs or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning. That flexibility addresses which information source the model follows when the sources disagree.

Experiments across eleven datasets and six model architectures report state-of-the-art performance and consistent improvements across domains and conflict types. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis of knowledge conflicts and superposition in attention heads. Together, the findings connect a revised account of attention-head behavior with a practical way to control knowledge preference during inference.
summary.tldr: JuICE uses two inference runs and attention interventions to steer language models toward stored or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning.

title: Taming Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is widely used to align models with human preferences, particularly to enhance the safety of responses generated by LLMs. This method traditionally relies on choosing preferred responses from response pairs. However, due to variations in human opinions and the difficulty of making an overall comparison of two responses, there is a growing shift towards a fine-grained annotation approach, assessing responses based on multiple specific metrics or rules. Selecting and applying these rules efficiently while accommodating the diversity of preference data remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce a dynamic approach that adaptively selects the most critical rules for each pair of responses. We develop a mathematical framework that leverages the maximum discrepancy between each paired responses and theoretically show that this strategy optimizes the mutual information between the rule-based labeling and the hidden ground-truth preferences. We then train an 8B reward model using the adaptively labeled preference dataset and evaluate its performance on RewardBench. As of May 25, 2025, our model achieved the highest safety performance on the leaderboard, outperforming various larger models.

paragraphs: Reward models used in reinforcement learning from human feedback often learn from comparisons between pairs of responses. Overall comparisons can be difficult because people disagree and responses differ along several dimensions. RuleAdapter instead considers specific evaluation rules and chooses which rules matter most for each response pair.

Its selection strategy uses the largest discrepancy between the paired responses. The authors develop a mathematical framework showing that this strategy optimizes mutual information between rule-based labels and hidden ground-truth preferences. In plain terms, the selection aims to make the resulting labels as informative as possible about the underlying preference within that framework.

The adaptively labeled dataset is then used to train an eight-billion-parameter reward model. On RewardBench, the model achieved the highest safety performance on the leaderboard as of May 25, 2025, surpassing various larger models. This dated result supports the value of selecting relevant rules for individual comparisons. It suggests that improving the information in preference labels can produce a strong safety reward model without relying solely on greater model size.
summary.tldr: RuleAdapter selects informative rules for each response pair, producing preference labels that train a highly competitive safety reward model.

title: RuleAdapter: Dynamic Rules for training Safety Reward Models in RLHF

abstract: Neural networks (NNs) have emerged as promising tools for solving constrained optimization problems in real-time. However, ensuring constraint satisfaction for NN-generated solutions remains challenging due to prediction errors. Existing methods to ensure NN feasibility either suffer from high computational complexity or are limited to specific constraint types. We present Bisection Projection, an efficient approach to ensure NN solution feasibility for optimization over general compact sets with non-empty interiors. Our method comprises two key components: (i) a dedicated NN (called IPNN) that predicts interior points (IPs) with low eccentricity, which naturally accounts for approximation errors; (ii) a bisection algorithm that leverages these IPs to recover solution feasibility when initial NN solutions violate constraints. We establish theoretical guarantees by providing sufficient conditions for IPNN feasibility and proving bounded optimality loss of the bisection operation under IP predictions. Extensive evaluations on real-world non-convex problems demonstrate that Bisection Projection achieves superior feasibility and computational efficiency compared to existing methods, while maintaining comparable optimality gaps.

paragraphs: Neural networks can quickly propose solutions to constrained optimization problems, but prediction errors can make those solutions violate constraints. Bisection Projection adds a feasibility-recovery mechanism for optimization over compact sets with non-empty interiors. This stated setting includes a broader range of constraints than methods restricted to particular constraint types.

The approach first uses a dedicated network, IPNN, to predict interior points with low eccentricity. These points support a bisection procedure that restores feasibility when an initial neural prediction lies outside the allowed set. The interior-point design accounts for approximation errors, making the quality and placement of these predictions central to the correction process.

The authors provide sufficient conditions for IPNN feasibility and prove a bound on the optimality loss caused by bisection under interior-point predictions. These are conditional theoretical guarantees, rather than an unrestricted statement about arbitrary predictions. Evaluations on real-world non-convex problems report better feasibility and computational efficiency than existing methods, with comparable optimality gaps. The method thus connects fast correction with explicit control over solution quality.
summary.tldr: Bisection Projection uses learned interior points to repair infeasible neural optimization outputs efficiently, with conditional feasibility and optimality guarantees.

title: Efficient Bisection Projection to Ensure Neural-Network Solution Feasibility for Optimization over General Set

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a fundamental tool for modeling complex graph structures across diverse applications. However, directly applying pretrained GNNs to varied downstream tasks without fine-tuning-based continual learning remains challenging, as this approach incurs high computational costs and hinders the development of Large Graph Models (LGMs). In this paper, we investigate an efficient and generalizable dataset distillation framework for Graph Continual Learning (GCL) across multiple downstream tasks, implemented through a novel Lightweight Graph Neural Tangent Kernel (LIGHTGNTK). Specifically, LIGHTGNTK employs a low-rank approximation of the Laplacian matrix via Bernoulli sampling and linear association within the GNTK. This design enables efficient capture of both structural and feature relationships while supporting gradient-based dataset distillation. Additionally, LIGHTGNTK incorporates a unified subgraph anchoring strategy, allowing it to handle graph-level, node-level, and edge-level tasks under diverse input structures. Comprehensive experiments on several datasets show that LIGHTGNTK achieves state-of-the-art performance in GCL scenarios, promoting the development of adaptive and scalable LGMs.

paragraphs: Adapting pretrained graph neural networks to a succession of downstream tasks can require expensive fine-tuning. This paper investigates dataset distillation as a way to make graph continual learning more efficient and generalizable. The aim is to condense useful task information into distilled data while supporting several kinds of graph prediction.

The central tool is LIGHTGNTK, a lightweight graph neural tangent kernel. It combines a low-rank approximation of the graph Laplacian, constructed through Bernoulli sampling, with linear association inside the kernel. This design captures relationships involving both graph structure and features while allowing gradient-based dataset distillation. A unified subgraph anchoring strategy lets the framework accommodate predictions about whole graphs, individual nodes, and edges despite differences in their input structures.

Experiments on several datasets report state-of-the-art performance in graph continual learning scenarios. The contribution therefore combines an efficient kernel construction with a common treatment of multiple task types. The findings support this framework as a route toward more adaptive and scalable large graph models, rather than requiring a separate distillation formulation for each prediction level.
summary.tldr: LIGHTGNTK uses a lightweight graph kernel and unified subgraph anchoring to support efficient dataset distillation across graph continual learning tasks.

title: Efficient Graph Continual Learning via Lightweight Graph Neural Tangent Kernels-based Dataset Distillation

abstract: Attention mechanism is a fundamental component of the transformer model and plays a significant role in its success. However, the theoretical understanding of how attention learns to select tokens is still an emerging area of research. In this work, we study the training dynamics and generalization ability of the attention mechanism, under classification problems with label noise. We show that, with the characterization of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the token selection of attention mechanism achieves “benign overfitting”, i.e., maintaining high generalization performance despite fitting label noise. Our work also demonstrates an interesting delayed acquisition of generalization after an initial phase of overfitting. Finally, we provide experiments to support our theoretical analysis using both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Attention helps a Transformer choose which tokens to use, but its learning behavior is not yet fully understood. This paper examines that selection process in classification problems containing incorrect training labels. The question is how fitting those noisy labels relates to the model’s ability to perform well on examples beyond the training set.

The authors analyze both training dynamics and generalization through the signal-to-noise ratio. Within that characterization, they show that attention’s token selection can exhibit benign overfitting: it can fit label noise while retaining strong generalization. The result connects the balance between useful signal and noise to whether fitting the training data remains compatible with successful prediction.

The analysis also reveals delayed generalization following an initial period of overfitting. This makes the timing of learning part of the explanation: an early overfitting phase does not necessarily describe the eventual behavior. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical account. The contribution concerns attention’s token-selection mechanism under the studied noisy-label classification setting.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how attention can fit noisy labels yet generalize well, including cases where generalization emerges after initial overfitting.

title: Benign Overfitting in Token Selection of Attention Mechanism

abstract: Performativity, the phenomenon where outcomes are influenced by predictions, is particularly prevalent in social contexts where individuals strategically respond to a deployed model. In order to preserve the high accuracy of machine learning models under distribution shifts caused by performativity, Perdomo et al. (2020) introduced the concept of performative risk minimization (PRM). While this framework ensures model accuracy, it overlooks the impact of the PRM on the underlying distributions and the predictions of the model. In this paper, we initiate the analysis of the impact of PRM, by studying performativity for a sequential performative risk minimization problem with binary random variables and linear performative shifts. We formulate two natural measures of impact. In the case of full information, where the distribution dynamics are known, we derive explicit formulas for the PRM solution and our impact measures. In the case of partial information, we provide performative-aware statistical estimators, as well as simulations. Our analysis contrasts PRM to alternatives that do not model data shift and indicates that PRM can have amplified side effects compared to such methods.

paragraphs: Predictions can change the outcomes they are intended to predict, especially when people respond strategically to a deployed model. Performative risk minimization accounts for the resulting distribution shifts when optimizing accuracy. This paper asks a further question: how does that optimization affect the underlying distribution and the model’s predictions over time?

The authors study a sequential problem with binary random variables and linear performative shifts. They introduce two measures of impact. When the distribution dynamics are fully known, they derive explicit expressions for both the risk-minimizing solution and these measures. When information is partial, they develop statistical estimators that account for performativity and provide simulations.

The analysis compares performative risk minimization with alternatives that do not model the induced data shift. It indicates that accounting for the shift can produce amplified side effects relative to those alternatives. Thus, preserving predictive accuracy and controlling a model’s effects on its environment are distinct concerns. The conclusion is established in the paper’s binary-variable, linear-shift setting.
summary.tldr: In a binary-variable setting with linear performative shifts, optimizing for prediction-induced changes can amplify side effects compared with methods that ignore them.

title: On the Impact of Performative Risk Minimization for Binary Random Variables

abstract: Aligning Large Language Model (LLM) responses with human preferences is vital for building safe and controllable AI systems. While preference optimization methods based on Plackett-Luce (PL) and Bradley-Terry (BT) models have shown promise, they face challenges such as poor handling of harmful content, inefficient use of dispreferred responses, and, specifically for PL, high computational costs. To address these issues, we propose Hard Preference Sampling (HPS), a novel framework for robust and efficient human preference alignment. HPS introduces a training loss that prioritizes the most preferred response while rejecting all dispreferred and harmful ones. It emphasizes “hard” dispreferred responses — those closely resembling preferred ones — to enhance the model’s rejection capabilities. By leveraging a single-sample Monte Carlo sampling strategy, HPS reduces computational overhead while maintaining alignment quality. Theoretically, HPS improves sample efficiency over existing PL methods and maximizes the reward margin between preferred and dispreferred responses, ensuring clearer distinctions. Experiments on HH-RLHF and PKU-Safety datasets validate HPS’s effectiveness, achieving comparable BLEU and reward scores while greatly improving reward margins and thus reducing harmful content generation.

paragraphs: Hard Preference Sampling addresses how language models learn to favor human-preferred answers and reject undesirable ones. The authors identify weaknesses in existing preference methods, including inefficient use of rejected responses, difficulty handling harmful content, and high computation for methods based on the Plackett-Luce model. HPS changes both the training objective and how training examples are sampled.

Its loss prioritizes the most preferred response while pushing against all dispreferred and harmful responses. Particular emphasis goes to hard dispreferred answers: responses that closely resemble preferred ones and therefore require a sharper distinction. A single-sample Monte Carlo strategy reduces computational overhead while maintaining alignment quality.

The theoretical analysis establishes improved sample efficiency over existing Plackett-Luce methods and maximization of the reward margin between preferred and dispreferred answers. Experiments on HH-RLHF and PKU-Safety report comparable BLEU and reward scores alongside substantially better reward margins and reduced harmful generation. The findings suggest that learning clearer preference boundaries can improve rejection behavior without sacrificing the reported measures of response quality.
summary.tldr: HPS emphasizes difficult rejected responses to improve preference separation and reduce harmful generation with lower sampling overhead.

title: HPS: Hard Preference Sampling for Human Preference Alignment

abstract: Predictive code completion greatly accelerates how quickly developers work. In spreadsheets, despite being much more common, such auto-completion features are virtually non-existent. To address this gap, we introduce a benchmark for systems that observe a sequence of user actions in a spreadsheet and predict future actions. Two challenges are (1) the absence of edit histories in public spreadsheet corpora and (2) the complex space of spreadsheet actions (spatial, temporal, composite). To address (1), we manually curate 52 sequences of 12K actions that recreate spreadsheets from public corpora, seeded by parametrized heuristics and LLM refinement. To address (2), we propose an online evaluation that expects a prediction after each user action, accepts or rejects that prediction, updates the future actions upon acceptance, and repeats this until the target spreadsheet is obtained. We use multiple baseline predictors (including zero-shot LLMs, fine-tuned SLMs, and classical models) and analyze different properties that our benchmark teaches us, including but not limited to: properties of saved actions and false positives, efficiency, effect of user profiles, effect of triggers, and effect of context.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a benchmark for systems that watch spreadsheet editing and predict what the user will do next. Building such a benchmark is difficult because public spreadsheet collections generally lack editing histories. Spreadsheet actions also combine location, timing, and operations that may contain multiple steps.

The authors manually curate 52 sequences comprising 12,000 actions that recreate spreadsheets from public collections. Parametrized heuristics and language-model refinement help seed this process. They also introduce an online evaluation procedure: after each user action, the predictor proposes an action, the evaluation accepts or rejects it, and accepted predictions change the remaining action sequence.

This design evaluates suggestions within an evolving workflow, continuing until the target spreadsheet is completed. The authors compare zero-shot language models, fine-tuned small language models, and classical predictors. Their analysis covers saved actions, false positives, efficiency, user profiles, prediction triggers, and available context. The contribution is a dataset and evaluation framework for studying how next-action assistance interacts with spreadsheet work.
summary.tldr: A spreadsheet benchmark evaluates next-action predictions through editing workflows that change when suggestions are accepted.

title: A Benchmark and Framework for Evaluating Next Action Predictions in Spreadsheets

abstract: High-quality data is essential for modern machine learning, yet many valuable corpora are sensitive and cannot be freely shared. Synthetic data offers a practical substitute for downstream development, and large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful engines for generating it. However, existing private text generation methods are severely inefficient: they are data-intensive, computationally slow, and often require large private corpora or batch sizes to achieve usable quality. We introduce EPSVec, a differentially-private lightweight alternative that steers LLM generation using dataset vectors-directions in activation space that capture the distributional gap between private data and public priors. EPSVec extracts and sanitizes steering vectors just once and then performs standard decoding. This decouples the privacy budget from generation, enabling arbitrarily many synthetic samples without additional privacy cost and yielding strong fidelity even in low-data regimes. Furthermore, we enhance our method by utilizing pretrained (base) models and introducing fixed-shot prompting to boost generation diversity and fidelity. Our experiments demonstrate that EPSVec outperforms existing baselines in distributional alignment and downstream utility, particularly in low-data regimes, while significantly reducing computational overhead.

paragraphs: Sensitive text collections can be valuable for developing models even when the original records cannot be shared. Private synthetic-data generation aims to provide useful substitutes, but existing approaches can demand large private datasets and substantial computation. EPSVec addresses this by concentrating the privacy-sensitive work into a single extraction and sanitization stage.

The method builds dataset vectors: directions in a language model’s activation space that summarize how the private data distribution differs from public priors. Once sanitized with differential privacy, these vectors steer ordinary decoding. Generation therefore does not consume additional privacy budget for each new synthetic sample. The authors also use pretrained base models and fixed-shot prompting to improve the diversity and fidelity of generated text.

Experiments report better distributional alignment and downstream utility than existing baselines, particularly when little private data is available, alongside substantially lower computational overhead. The key practical result is that a reusable private steering representation can support repeated generation. The no-additional-privacy-cost claim applies to generation from the vectors after the initial private extraction and sanitization.
summary.tldr: EPSVec privately extracts reusable activation-space steering vectors, enabling efficient synthetic text generation without additional privacy cost per sample.

title: EPSVec: Efficient and Private Synthetic Data Generation via Dataset Vectors

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection requires accurately classifying in-distribution (ID) samples while effectively distinguishing anomalous OOD data. However, existing methodologies predominantly rely on real-valued magnitude features, neglecting the semantic richness embedded in phase information, and often lack a systematic theoretical framework for quantitatively modeling uncertainty. To address this dual limitation of incomplete feature representation and insufficient uncertainty modeling, the trustworthy quantum evidence neural network (TrustworthyQENN) is proposed, a novel quantum-inspired framework bridging complex-valued representation learning under the framework of generalized quantum evidence theory (GQET). Specifically, supervised complex-valued contrastive learning (SCVCL) is proposed to synchronize amplitude distributions with phase correlations, thereby enforcing high intra-class compactness and inter-class separability for ID data. A quantum evidence generation mechanism based on GQET is subsequently devised, where the OOD state is formally grounded in the generalized quantum basic probability amplitudes (GQBPAs) within a Hilbert space. Furthermore, the generalized quantum evidential combination rule (GQECR) is leveraged to fuse multi-view quantum evidence, thereby achieving trustworthy inference. Extensive experiments on the MSTAR, EuroSAT, and FUSAR-Ship benchmarks substantiate the superiority of TrustworthyQENN, which achieves a peak AUROC of 95.94% on the MSTAR dataset while consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods across all evaluated scenarios.

paragraphs: TrustworthyQENN addresses the joint task of classifying familiar samples and detecting data outside the training distribution. The paper identifies two weaknesses in existing approaches: reliance on magnitude features that omit phase information, and insufficient theoretical structure for representing uncertainty. It proposes a quantum-inspired framework combining complex-valued representations with generalized quantum evidence theory.

Supervised complex-valued contrastive learning coordinates amplitude distributions and phase correlations to make familiar classes compact and distinct. An evidence-generation mechanism then represents the out-of-distribution state using generalized quantum probability amplitudes in a Hilbert space. A further combination rule fuses evidence from multiple views, connecting representation learning with the framework’s treatment of uncertainty.

These results support the proposed combination of phase-aware features and evidential modeling for the tested classification and anomaly-detection settings. The framework is described as quantum-inspired.
summary.tldr: TrustworthyQENN combines complex-valued contrastive features with quantum-inspired uncertainty modeling to improve out-of-distribution detection.

title: TrustworthyQENN: A Quantum Evidential Neural Network Based on Complex-Valued Contrastive Learning for Uncertainty Pattern Classification

abstract: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences is often formulated via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). However, the standard Bradley-Terry instantiation of DPO is limited in modeling common departures from transitivity in human preferences. To address this, recent work has introduced Self-Play Preference Optimization (SPPO), which iteratively refines the policy by training on self-generated win-lose pairs. Our investigation, however, reveals a critical instability in SPPO: the optimization is prone to policy degeneration when the preference oracle assigns overly confident wins to semantically indistinguishable responses. To mitigate this, we propose $\textit{S}$-SPPO, a dual-space semantic calibration framework comprising: i) $\textit{Supervision Calibration}$ via semantic gating, which anneals win rate targets toward the maximum-entropy baseline as semantic overlap increases; and ii) $\textit{Representation Calibration}$ via latent repulsion to enforce geometric diversity to prevent manifold collapse and maintain latent diversity between chosen and rejected samples. Theoretically, we show that the calibration preserves the constant-sum game structure, facilitating convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Empirically, $\textit{S}$-SPPO avoids the performance degradation seen in prior methods, achieving 52.19% win rate and 47.46% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 with Llama-3-8B, without using additional human-annotated preferences during training.

This paper identifies a failure mode when the preference oracle confidently favors one response over another with essentially the same meaning. Those overconfident distinctions can destabilize optimization and cause the policy’s performance to deteriorate.

S-SPPO calibrates both supervision and internal representations. Semantic gating moves win-rate targets toward the maximum-entropy baseline as response meanings overlap, weakening unjustified preference certainty. A latent repulsion mechanism maintains geometric diversity between chosen and rejected samples, addressing collapse in the representation space. Together, the components adjust both the learning signal and the representations affected by it.

The theoretical analysis shows that calibration preserves the constant-sum game structure, facilitating convergence to a Nash equilibrium. Empirically, S-SPPO avoids the degradation observed in prior methods. With Llama-3-8B, it reaches a 52.19% win rate and 47.46% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 without additional human-annotated training preferences. The findings support accounting for semantic equivalence when generating preference supervision through self-play.
summary.tldr: S-SPPO stabilizes self-play preference learning by reducing overconfident judgments between similar responses and preserving representation diversity.

title: $\textitS$-SPPO: Semantic-Calibrated Self-Play Preference Optimization

abstract: Recent research has established empirical scaling laws to predict model performance on multi-domain data mixtures. However, a theoretical understanding of these model loss behaviors remains absent. In this work, we propose a unified framework to explain the underlying mechanics of data mixing. Our approach extends theoretical perspectives originally developed for standard neural scaling laws (e.g., Kaplan and Chinchilla) to the multi-domain setting. Based on the distributional assumption that domains overlap on fundamental skills while diverging on specialized skills, we identify two key factors that govern the domain losses of models trained on different data mixtures: Capacity Competition, where the allocation of finite model capacity couples domain losses globally, and Noise Reduction, where optimal weights shift toward harder-to-learn domains to minimize overall noise. Empirical evaluations show that our framework outperforms existing baselines by fitting the loss landscape with a lower Mean Relative Error and identifying higher-performing training mixtures. Most importantly, our model successfully extrapolates across scales, predicting highly effective mixtures for large, unseen scales using parameters fitted on smaller ones. In addition, our model achieves these results using significantly fewer free parameters than previous empirical laws. Our code is available https://github.com/meiqwq/Explaining-Data-Mixing-Scaling-Laws.

paragraphs: Choosing how much training data to draw from each domain changes a model’s performance across those domains. Existing empirical scaling laws describe these effects, but the paper seeks an explanation for their shape. It extends theoretical ideas from standard neural scaling laws to training mixtures containing several domains.

Parameters fitted at smaller scales also predict effective mixtures at larger, unseen scales. These results suggest that the proposed mechanisms can support practical mixture selection as well as explanation, with extrapolation across scale being a central reported finding.
summary.tldr: A framework based on shared skills, finite capacity, and noise reduction explains data-mixture losses and predicts effective mixtures at unseen scales.

title: Explaining Data Mixing Scaling Laws

abstract: We propose SALSA-V, a multimodal video-to-audio generation model capable of synthesizing highly synchronized, high-fidelity long-form audio from silent video content. Our approach introduces a masked diffusion objective, enabling audio-conditioned generation and the seamless synthesis of audio sequences of unconstrained length. Additionally, by integrating a shortcut loss into our training process, we achieve rapid generation of high-quality audio samples in as few as eight sampling steps, paving the way for near-real-time applications without requiring dedicated fine-tuning or retraining. We demonstrate that SALSA-V significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both audiovisual alignment and synchronization with video content in quantiative evaluation and a human listening study. Furthermore, our use of random masking during training enables our model to match spectral characteristics of reference audio samples, broadening its applicability to professional audio synthesis tasks such as Foley generation and sound design.

Its masked diffusion objective also permits audio-conditioned generation, so reference sound can participate in the synthesis process. The authors describe this design as supporting seamless audio sequences without a fixed length constraint.

The model produces high-quality samples in as few as eight steps, without requiring separate fine-tuning or retraining for that capability. summary.tldr: SALSA-V generates long, synchronized video-conditioned audio with reference-audio control and high-quality sampling in as few as eight steps.

title: SALSA-V: Shortcut-Augmented Long-form Synchronized Audio from Videos

abstract: Machine learning methods that predict protein fitness from sequence remain sensitive to changes in data distributions, limiting generalization across common conditions encountered in protein engineering. Practically, protein engineers are thus left wondering about the effective utility of ML tools. The FLIP benchmark established protocols for testing generalization under some domain shifts, but it was limited to measurements of stability, binding, and viral capsid viability. We introduce FLIP2, a protein fitness benchmark spanning seven new datasets, including enzymes, protein-protein interactions, and light-sensitive proteins, as well as splits that measure generalization relevant to real-world protein engineering campaigns. Evaluating a suite of benchmark models across these datasets and suites reveals that simpler models often matched or outperformed fine-tuned protein language models on FLIP2, challenging the utility of existing transfer learning techniques. Provenance for all datasets has been recorded and we redistribute all data CC-BY 4.0 to facilitate continued progress.

paragraphs: Predicting protein fitness from sequence is useful only if models remain effective under the data changes encountered in protein engineering. The paper argues that this generalization remains uncertain in practice. The earlier FLIP benchmark tested some distribution shifts, but its measurements covered stability, binding, and viral capsid viability.

FLIP2 expands that evaluation with seven new datasets, including enzymes, protein-protein interactions, and light-sensitive proteins. It also introduces data splits intended to test generalization relevant to real engineering campaigns. These splits make the benchmark about performance under meaningful shifts in available data, alongside the broader range of protein settings.

Across the evaluated datasets and test suites, simpler models often match or outperform fine-tuned protein language models. This result questions how reliably existing transfer-learning methods deliver practical advantages in these settings; it does not establish that simpler models always win. The authors record dataset provenance and redistribute the data under CC-BY 4.0, supporting continued comparisons using a shared, documented resource.
summary.tldr: FLIP2 broadens realistic protein-fitness evaluation and finds that simpler models often rival or outperform fine-tuned protein language models.

title: FLIP2: Expanding Protein Fitness Landscape Benchmarks for Real-World Machine Learning Applications

abstract: Tokenization is a key component of autoregressive (AR) generative models, converting raw data into more manageable units for modeling. Commonly, tokens describe local information, such as regions of pixels in images or word pieces in text, and AR generation predicts these tokens in a fixed order. A worthwhile question is whether token structures affect the ability to steer the generation through test-time search, where multiple candidate generations are explored and evaluated by a verifier. Using image generation as our testbed, we hypothesize that recent 1D ordered tokenizers with coarse-to-fine structure can be more amenable to search than classical 2D grid structures. This is rooted in the fact that the intermediate states in coarse-to-fine sequences carry semantic meaning that verifiers can reliably evaluate, enabling effective steering during generation. Through controlled experiments, we find that AR models trained on coarse-to-fine ordered tokens exhibit improved test-time scaling behavior compared to grid-based counterparts. Moreover, we demonstrate that, thanks to the ordered structure, pure test-time search over token sequences (i.e., without training an AR model) can perform training-free text-to-image generation when guided by an image-text verifier. Beyond this, we systematically study how classical search algorithms (best-of-$N$, beam search, lookahead search) interact with different token structures, as well as the role of different verifiers and AR priors.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether the way images are converted into tokens changes how effectively generation can be improved through search. In test-time search, a system explores candidate outputs and uses a verifier to judge them. Conventional image tokens describe locations on a grid, whereas ordered tokens can describe an image progressively, moving from broad structure toward finer details.

The proposed explanation is that coarse-to-fine sequences produce meaningful intermediate images. A verifier can assess these partial results and guide subsequent choices before generation finishes. Controlled experiments support this hypothesis: autoregressive models using ordered tokens benefit more from additional search than their grid-based counterparts.

The authors also demonstrate text-to-image generation by searching ordered token sequences without training an autoregressive model, using an image-text verifier for guidance. This training-free result concerns the autoregressive generation component. The study further examines best-of-N, beam search, and lookahead search alongside different verifiers and autoregressive priors. Together, the findings show that token structure influences both what a model learns and how effectively search can steer its outputs.
summary.tldr: Coarse-to-fine image tokens make intermediate generations easier to evaluate, improving search-guided generation in the reported experiments.

title: (1D) Ordered Tokens Enable Efficient Test-Time Search

abstract: Large-scale, multi-subject widefield calcium imaging provides unprecedented access to brain-wide cortical dynamics. However, the high dimensionality, complex spatiotemporal structure, and substantial task-irrelevant activity in widefield recordings have largely restricted modeling efforts to single-session analyses, limiting scalability and generalization. While multi-subject pretrained models have been explored for some neural modalities, multi-subject models for widefield calcium imaging have not yet been demonstrated; further, subject-invariant zero-shot behavior decoding remains elusive for multi-subject models across neural modalities more broadly. As a first step toward foundation modeling of widefield data, we introduce WiCAT, a multi-subject model that leverages self-supervised pretraining to both outperform single-session models and enable zero-shot behavior decoding on unseen subjects. WiCAT introduces an atlas-grounded tokenization scheme without session-specific components and learns globally shared spatiotemporal representations. Across multiple widefield datasets, the pretrained model supports lightweight downstream decoding, transfers across subjects, tasks, and datasets, and outperforms baseline models. Notably, the model also achieves robust zero-shot continuous behavior decoding and left-out brain region reconstruction on unseen subjects.

paragraphs: WiCAT studies how to learn shared representations from widefield calcium imaging collected across multiple subjects. These recordings capture cortical dynamics but contain high-dimensional spatial and temporal structure alongside substantial activity unrelated to the task. Such complexity has largely confined modeling to individual sessions, limiting the ability to reuse what a model learns elsewhere.

The model uses self-supervised pretraining and an atlas-grounded scheme for turning recordings into tokens. The tokenization has no session-specific components, allowing the model to learn globally shared spatiotemporal representations. This design supports a common representation across recordings, rather than requiring a separate session-specific component to organize each one.

Across multiple widefield datasets, WiCAT outperforms baseline models and supports lightweight downstream decoding. The reported transfers span subjects, tasks, and datasets. Particularly significant are continuous behavior decoding without adaptation to unseen subjects and reconstruction of left-out brain regions on those subjects. These results establish a step toward foundation modeling for widefield data, showing that a shared anatomical organization can support representations useful beyond the recordings used for pretraining.
summary.tldr: WiCAT uses atlas-grounded self-supervised representations to transfer widefield calcium-imaging models across subjects and decode behavior on unseen subjects.

title: Cross-Subject Modeling for Widefield Calcium Imaging via Atlas-Aligned Spatiotemporal Tokenization

abstract: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) avoid pixel reconstruction by predicting latent representations, but standard formulations remain deterministic and provide limited uncertainty estimates for planning and control. We introduce Variational JEPA (VJEPA), a probabilistic extension that learns predictive distributions over future latent states using a latent-space variational objective, without autoregressive observation likelihoods. We show that VJEPA links JEPA-style self-supervised learning to predictive state representations and Bayesian filtering, and that its latent variables can serve as sufficient information states for control when they preserve task-relevant predictive information. We also propose Bayesian JEPA (BJEPA), which combines a learned dynamics expert with modular prior experts through a Product of Experts, enabling constraint-aware prediction and zero-shot prior swapping. Experiments on Noisy-TV systems, nonlinear and image-based benchmarks, STL-10 with a ViT encoder, and DMC Cheetah-run show that predictive JEPA-family objectives are more robust to high-variance nuisance distractors than reconstruction-based world-model baselines. These results position probabilistic latent prediction as a principled framework for robust, uncertainty-aware, reconstruction-free world models.

paragraphs: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures predict latent representations rather than reconstructing observations such as pixels. Standard versions are deterministic, limiting their ability to express uncertainty for planning and control. VJEPA extends this approach to learn distributions over future latent states through a variational objective operating in latent space.

The authors connect this formulation with predictive state representations and Bayesian filtering. They show that its latent variables can provide sufficient information for control when those variables preserve task-relevant predictive information. A second variant, BJEPA, combines a learned dynamics expert with modular prior experts through a Product of Experts, supporting constraint-aware predictions and swapping priors without additional training.

Experiments cover Noisy-TV systems, nonlinear and image-based benchmarks, STL-10 with a vision transformer encoder, and DMC Cheetah-run. The results show greater robustness to high-variance nuisance distractions than reconstruction-based world-model baselines. Together, these findings support probabilistic latent prediction as a route to uncertainty-aware world models, while the control interpretation remains conditional on retaining the predictive information relevant to the task.
summary.tldr: VJEPA adds probabilistic latent prediction to JEPA, while BJEPA incorporates modular priors; experiments show improved robustness to nuisance distractions.

title: VJEPA: Variational Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures as Probabilistic World Models

abstract: Diffusion models can unintentionally memorize training samples, raising concerns about privacy and copyright. While recent methods can detect memorization, they often rely on global or model-specific signals and provide limited insight into where memorization appears within a generated image. We provide a geometric characterization of local memorization as a coordinate-wise variance collapse. However, such collapse can also arise from intrinsic data constraints rather than overfitting. To isolate overfitting-driven memorization, we propose curvature-difference methods that subtract the curvature of an underfitted baseline, either the unconditional model or a less-trained version of itself. We further derive a score-difference proxy that provides a geometric explanation for the widely used score-difference-based detection metric. Experiments on Stable Diffusion, evaluated against ground-truth memorization masks, show that our method outperforms the prior attention-based localization method. Code is available at https://github.com/Gwangho99/mem-curv-diff.

paragraphs: Detecting that a generated image contains memorized training content does not reveal which parts of the image are affected. This paper studies localization, seeking a spatially detailed account of memorization in diffusion models. Its geometric characterization links local memorization to a collapse in variation along individual coordinates.

Reduced variation alone is ambiguous because genuine constraints in the data can produce a similar pattern. To distinguish overfitting from those constraints, the authors subtract the curvature of an underfitted baseline from the curvature being examined. The baseline can be an unconditional model or a less-trained version of the same model. This comparison is intended to isolate the component associated with overfitting.

The paper also derives a score-difference proxy that gives a geometric interpretation to an existing memorization-detection metric. Experiments with Stable Diffusion compare localization against ground-truth memorization masks and outperform a prior attention-based method. The results support using differences in local geometry to identify where memorization occurs, while explicitly accounting for the ambiguity between learned data constraints and overfitting.
summary.tldr: Curvature differences against an underfitted baseline help localize memorized image regions while accounting for intrinsic data constraints.

title: Localizing Memorized Regions in Diffusion Models via Coordinate-Wise Curvature Differences

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated strong generative performance; however, generated samples often fail to fully align with human intent. This paper studies an efficient test-time scaling method for sampling from regions with higher human-aligned reward values. Existing methods for computing the expected future reward (EFR) face important limitations: backward rollout incurs prohibitively high sampling costs, while Tweedie-based approaches, including Sequential Monte Carlo and gradient guidance, suffer from bias and inherent sampling issues. We show that the EFR at any $\mathbf{x}_t$ can be computed using only marginal samples from a pre-trained diffusion model, enabling closed-form reward guidance without neural backpropagation. To further improve efficiency, we introduce a few-step lookahead sampling and an accurate solver that guides particles toward high-reward lookahead samples. We refer to this sampling scheme as LiDAR sampling. LiDAR achieves the same GenEval performance as the latest gradient guidance method for SDXL with a 9.5$\times$ speedup. We release the code at https://github.com/aailab-kaist/Diffusion-LiDAR-Sampling.

We refer to this sampling scheme as LiDAR sampling. LiDAR achieves the same GenEval performance as the latest gradient guidance method for SDXL with a 9.5$\times$ speedup. paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate strong samples while still missing aspects of human intent. Reward-guided sampling spends extra computation during generation to favor better-aligned outputs. A central challenge is estimating the future reward of a partially denoised sample: full rollouts are expensive, while the alternative approximations discussed in this paper introduce bias and sampling difficulties.

The authors show that expected future reward at a diffusion state can be computed using marginal samples from a pretrained diffusion model. This yields closed-form reward guidance without neural backpropagation. They then introduce a few-step lookahead procedure and a solver that steers sampling particles toward promising lookahead samples, forming the method they call LiDAR sampling.

For SDXL, LiDAR matches the GenEval performance of the latest gradient-guidance method used in the comparison while delivering a 9.5-fold speedup. That result concerns a specific model, evaluation, and comparator. Its broader significance is methodological: the paper connects an alternative expression for future reward to a sampling procedure that reduces the cost of steering generation toward high-reward outcomes.
summary.tldr: LiDAR uses sample-based future-reward guidance and short lookahead to steer diffusion generation efficiently without neural backpropagation.

title: Lookahead Sample Reward Guidance for Test-Time Scaling of Diffusion Models

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have markedly expanded the competence of graphical user-interface (GUI) systems, propelling them beyond controlled simulations into complex, real-world environments across diverse platforms. However, practical usefulness is still bounded by the reliability of visual grounding, i.e., mapping textual references to exact on-screen elements. This limitation prevents the system from accurately performing pointer-level actions such as clicking or dragging. To address it, we introduce GUI-Spotlight – a model trained for image-grounded reasoning that dynamically invokes multiple specialized tools to iteratively narrow its focus to the relevant region of the screen, thereby substantially improving visual grounding accuracy. On the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark, GUI-Spotlight trained with only 18.5K training samples achieves 52.8% accuracy, surpassing V2P-7B (50.6% with 9.6M training samples) and GTA-1-7B (50.1% with 1.56M training samples).

paragraphs: A graphical interface agent must connect an instruction to the exact element visible on a screen before it can click or drag reliably. This task, called visual grounding, remains a practical bottleneck even as multimodal models become more capable. GUI-Spotlight addresses that bottleneck with a model trained to reason from the interface image.

The method dynamically invokes multiple specialized tools and repeatedly narrows its attention to the relevant screen region. Its central idea is to make locating an element an adaptive sequence of focus refinements. The model can use successive stages to concentrate on the part of the image that matters for resolving the textual reference into a precise on-screen target.

On ScreenSpot-Pro, GUI-Spotlight achieves 52.8% accuracy after training with 18,500 samples. The abstract compares this with V2P-7B at 50.6% using 9.6 million samples and GTA-1-7B at 50.1% using 1.56 million. These results show higher grounding accuracy with substantially fewer training samples in the reported comparison, supporting iterative focus refinement as a useful approach to interface localization.
summary.tldr: GUI-Spotlight uses tool-assisted focus refinement to improve screen-element localization with substantially fewer training samples in the reported comparison.

title: GUI-Spotlight: Adaptive Iterative Focus Refinement for Enhanced GUI Visual Grounding

abstract: The de facto approach in video object-centric learning maintains temporal consistency through learned dynamics modules that predict future object representations, called slots. We demonstrate that these predictors function as expensive approximations of discrete correspondence problems. Modern self-supervised vision backbones already encode instance-discriminative features that distinguish objects reliably. Exploiting these features eliminates the need for learned temporal prediction. We introduce Grounded Correspondence, a framework that replaces learned transition functions with deterministic bipartite matching. Slots initialize from salient regions in frozen backbone features. Frame-to-frame identity is maintained through Hungarian matching on slot representations. The approach requires zero learnable parameters for temporal modeling yet achieves competitive performance on MOVi-D, MOVi-E, and YouTube-VIS. Project page: https://magenta-sherbet-85b101.netlify.app/

paragraphs: Video object-centric learning represents objects as slots and must keep those representations associated with the same objects across frames. Common approaches learn a dynamics model to predict future slots. This paper argues that these predictors act as costly approximations to a correspondence problem: determining which current object matches which earlier object.

Grounded Correspondence uses instance-discriminative features already present in modern self-supervised vision backbones. Slots begin from salient regions in the frozen backbone's features. Hungarian matching then establishes frame-to-frame associations between slot representations, replacing a learned temporal transition with deterministic bipartite matching.

The framework requires no learnable parameters for temporal modeling and achieves competitive results on MOVi-D, MOVi-E, and YouTube-VIS. The zero-parameter claim applies specifically to the temporal component; the approach still relies on the backbone's learned visual features. Its significance is that sufficiently informative object features can support temporal identity through direct matching, making a separate learned predictor unnecessary in the demonstrated framework. This reframes temporal consistency around correspondence rather than forecasting future representations.
summary.tldr: Grounded Correspondence maintains video object identities through deterministic matching, achieving competitive results without learned temporal parameters.

title: Rethinking Temporal Consistency in Video Object-Centric Learning: From Prediction to Correspondence

abstract: Verifying whether a language model is genuinely reasoning or pattern-matching remains an open problem: learned verifiers are expensive, and output-based heuristics are brittle. We show that valid mathematical reasoning induces a measurable, training-free spectral signature in transformer attention. By treating each attention matrix as a weighted token graph, we extract four diagnostics: Fiedler value, High-Frequency Energy Ratio (HFER), spectral entropy, and smoothness, that require no learned parameters. Experiments across seven models from four architectural families yield effect sizes up to Cohen’s $d = 3.30$ ($p < 10^{-116}$), enabling $85$-$96$% single-threshold classification accuracy. Two findings sharpen the interpretation. First, Platonic validity: the spectral signal tracks logical coherence rather than compiler acceptance, proofs rejected for timeouts or missing imports are correctly classified as valid, a distinction confirmed by a manual audit ($\kappa = 0.82$, $n = 51$). Second, architectural determinism: Sliding Window Attention shifts the discriminative feature from HFER to smoothness ($d = 2.09$, $p < 10^{-48}$), showing that attention design governs which spectral channel encodes reasoning quality. Causal ablation confirms the signature traces induction-head circuits. The method generalises to informal chain-of-thought ($d = 0.78$, $p < 10^{-3}$), and in proof search, HFER reranking improves Best-of-16 Pass@1 by $+4.4$-$6.6$%, matching $98$% of the AUC of fully supervised probes with zero labels. Spectral graph analysis is a principled, architecture-aware primitive for reasoning verification.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether mathematical reasoning can be assessed through a transformer's internal attention patterns. It treats each attention matrix as a weighted graph connecting tokens and extracts four spectral diagnostics: Fiedler value, high-frequency energy ratio, spectral entropy, and smoothness. These measurements require no learned parameters, offering a training-free signal for distinguishing valid reasoning.

Across seven models from four architectural families, single-threshold classification reaches 85–96% accuracy. The signal follows logical coherence closely enough to recognize valid proofs rejected because of timeouts or missing imports, with support from a manual audit. Attention architecture also matters: sliding-window attention shifts the useful diagnostic from high-frequency energy toward smoothness.

Causal ablations trace the signature to induction-head circuits. The authors also report generalization to informal chains of thought and improved proof search when candidates are reranked using high-frequency energy. Best-of-16 Pass@1 improves by 4.4–6.6%. Together, the findings support an architecture-aware verification approach whose useful internal measurement depends on the attention design.
summary.tldr: Training-free spectral measurements of attention distinguish valid mathematical reasoning and improve proof selection, with the most useful measurement depending on architecture.

title: Geometry of Reason: Spectral Signatures of Valid Mathematical Reasoning

abstract: Post-training endows pretrained LLMs with a variety of desirable skills, including instruction-following, reasoning, and others. However, these post-trained LLMs only encode knowledge up to a cut-off date, necessitating continual adaptation. Unfortunately, existing solutions cannot simultaneously learn new knowledge from an adaptation document corpora and mitigate the forgetting of earlier learned capabilities. To address this, we introduce Distillation via Split Contexts (DiSC), a simple context-distillation based approach for continual knowledge adaptation. DiSC derives student and teacher distributions by conditioning on distinct segments of the training example and minimizes the KL divergence between the shared tokens. This allows us to efficiently apply context-distillation without requiring explicit generation steps during training. We run experiments on four post-trained models and two adaptation domains. Compared to prior finetuning and distillation methods for continual adaptation, DiSC consistently reports the best trade-off between learning new knowledge and mitigating forgetting of previously learned skills like instruction-following, reasoning, and factual knowledge.

paragraphs: Post-trained language models acquire useful abilities such as instruction following and reasoning, but their stored knowledge still needs updating. Adapting them to new documents can interfere with those earlier abilities. This paper introduces Distillation via Split Contexts, or DiSC, to improve the trade-off between absorbing new knowledge and retaining previously learned skills.

DiSC creates teacher and student distributions by conditioning on different segments of the same training example. It then minimizes their KL divergence on shared tokens, encouraging agreement between the distributions. This arrangement applies context distillation without an explicit text-generation stage during training, providing an efficient way to transfer information from context into model behavior.

The authors evaluate four post-trained models across two adaptation domains. Compared with prior fine-tuning and distillation approaches, DiSC consistently achieves the best reported balance between new knowledge acquisition and reduced forgetting of instruction following, reasoning, and factual knowledge. The finding concerns an improved trade-off, rather than a claim that all forgetting disappears. It supports split-context distillation as a practical approach to continued knowledge adaptation after post-training.
summary.tldr: DiSC uses split-context distillation to update language-model knowledge while improving retention of previously learned post-training abilities.

title: Updating Parametric Knowledge with Context Distillation Retains Post-Training Capabilities

abstract: AI developers face a dual-use dilemma. An AI capability that helps one user cure a disease can help another synthesize one. This dilemma could be resolved with access control, limiting dual-use AI capabilities to trusted deployments with a legitimate need. A gold standard for access control would be to serve separate models with different capabilities to different users. However, training and deploying multiple models is prohibitively expensive. To address this challenge, we propose gradient-routed auxiliary modules (GRAM), a pre-training method that adds modules to a neural network and selectively updates them to induce specialization. Ablating a module at inference time removes its capability from the network, approximating a model trained on filtered data. We evaluate GRAM on synthetic stories and realistic dual-use data spanning virology, cybersecurity, nuclear physics, and specialized code. These experiments show that GRAM disables targeted capabilities while preserving the rest, and resists their recovery under finetuning better than post-hoc unlearning. Most importantly, a Chinchilla-optimal scaling analysis from 50M to 5B parameters shows that the gap between data-filtered and full-data models widens with scale on removed capabilities but stays small on retained ones, and that GRAM closely tracks data filtering. GRAM’s training cost is independent of the number of supported capability profiles, yielding a 5$\times$ reduction over data filtering in our 5-profile setting.

paragraphs: The paper explores capability access control through modular pretraining. Serving separate models with different knowledge could restrict sensitive capabilities, but training many models is expensive. Gradient-routed auxiliary modules, or GRAM, adds specialized modules during pretraining and selectively directs their updates. Removing a module at inference approximates a model trained with the corresponding data filtered out.

Experiments cover synthetic stories and dual-use material in virology, cybersecurity, nuclear physics, and specialized code. The authors report that module removal disables targeted capabilities while preserving others. In their evaluations, those capabilities also resist recovery through fine-tuning better than capabilities removed by post-hoc unlearning.

A compute-optimal scaling analysis from 50 million to 5 billion parameters finds that data filtering increasingly separates models on removed capabilities while leaving a small gap on retained ones. GRAM closely follows this behavior. Its training cost does not depend on the number of supported capability profiles, producing a fivefold reduction relative to data filtering in the evaluated five-profile setting. These findings support pretraining-time specialization as a practical access-control approach.
summary.tldr: GRAM specializes removable modules during pretraining to restrict selected capabilities while preserving others and reducing multi-profile training costs.

title: Modular Pretraining Enables Access Control

abstract: High-dimensionality of data is often regarded as a fundamental statistical impediment in Machine Learning and AI. The purpose of this paper is to clarify, on the contrary, when and how high-dimensionality may be beneficial. In the setting of a general random function model of data we delineate between three notions of dimensionality: effective dimension $p_{\mathrm{eff}}$, measuring total variability across feature directions; correlation rank $r$, measuring functional complexity across samples; and latent intrinsic dimension $d$ of manifold structure hidden in data. Via a generalized Hanson-Wright inequality, we show that increasing $p_{\mathrm{eff}}$ drives a blessing of dimensionality phenomenon, whereby data dot-products concentrate about their expectations. In turn, we show that, under mild continuity assumptions (ensuring that features bring additional information as dimension grows), persistence diagrams recover latent homology when $p_{\mathrm{eff}} \in \omega (\log n)$ as $n\to\infty$. Informed by our theory, we revisit the ground-breaking neuroscience discovery of toroidal structure in grid-cell activity made by Gardner et al. (2022): our findings provide the first empirical evidence that this structure is isometric to a flat torus model of physical space, suggesting that grid cell activity conveys a geometrically faithful representation of the real world.

paragraphs: This paper asks when having many dimensions helps reveal structure in data. It distinguishes effective dimension, which measures variability across feature directions; correlation rank, which measures functional complexity across samples; and latent intrinsic dimension, which describes the hidden manifold. Separating these quantities clarifies why a large feature space need not imply equally complex underlying structure.

Within a general random function model, the authors show that increasing effective dimension makes data dot products concentrate around their expected values. Under continuity assumptions ensuring that added features provide additional information, persistence diagrams recover latent homology when effective dimension grows faster than the logarithm of the sample count. Thus, the beneficial result depends on informative dimension growth and the stated assumptions.

The authors also revisit evidence of toroidal structure in grid-cell activity. Their analysis provides the first reported empirical evidence that this structure is isometric to a flat torus model of physical space. This suggests a geometrically faithful representation, extending the interpretation beyond identifying a toroidal topological shape.
summary.tldr: The paper distinguishes three dimensions of data and shows conditions under which increasing effective dimension helps recover hidden geometric structure.

title: How High is ‘High’? Rethinking the Roles of Dimensionality in Topological Data Analysis and Manifold Learning

abstract: Open-weight coding agents should hold a fundamental advantage over closed-source systems because they can specialize to private codebases, encoding repository-specific information directly in their weights. Yet the cost and complexity of training has kept this advantage theoretical until now. We present Soft-Verified Efficient Repository Agents (SERA), an efficient method for training coding agents that enables the rapid and cheap creation of agents specialized to private codebases. Using Soft Verified Generation (SVG), we generate thousands of trajectories from any code repository, without requiring unit tests. Beyond repository specialization, we apply SVG to a larger corpus of codebases, generating 200,000+ synthetic trajectories. Using only supervised finetuning (SFT), SERA achieves leading results among fully open-source (open data, method, code) models while matching the performance of open-weight models like Devstral-Small-2. Creating SERA models is 26x cheaper than reinforcement learning and 57x cheaper than previous synthetic data methods to reach equivalent performance. We use our dataset to provide detailed analysis of scaling laws, ablations, and confounding factors for training coding agents. Overall, we believe our work will greatly accelerate research on open coding agents and showcase the advantage of open-source models that can adapt to private codebases.

Training cost and complexity have made that advantage difficult to realize. SERA introduces an efficient training approach intended to make specialized coding agents faster and cheaper to create.

The dataset also supports analyses of scaling, ablations, and confounding factors, helping connect training choices to observed coding-agent performance rather than presenting specialization only as a theoretical benefit.
summary.tldr: SERA trains competitive, repository-specialized coding agents using synthetic trajectories and supervised fine-tuning at substantially reduced reported cost.

title: SERA: Soft-Verified Efficient Repository Agents

abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal reward models (RMs) have substantially improved post-training for visual generative models. However, current RMs face inherent limitations: (1) visual inputs consume large context budgets, forcing fewer frames and causing a loss of details; and (2) all visual information is packed into the initial prompt, exacerbating forgetting during chain-of-thought reasoning. To overcome these issues, we introduce VR-Thinker, a thinking-with-image RM equipped with visual reasoning operation and a configurable visual memory window. This allows the RM to actively acquire visual evidence, improving reasoning fidelity and reliability. We activate visual reasoning via a reinforcement fine-tuning pipeline: (i) Cold Start with curated visual chain-of-thought data to distill basic operation formatting; (ii) select samples with correct judgments, then conduct Rejection sampling Fine-Tuning on these high-quality traces to further enhance reasoning; and (iii) apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to strengthen reasoning. Our approach delivers state-of-the-art accuracy among open-source models on video preference benchmarks: a 7B VR-Thinker achieves 80.5% on VideoGen Reward, 82.3% on GenAI-Bench, and 75.6% on MJ-Bench-Video.

paragraphs: Video reward models judge generated videos, but visual inputs consume substantial context and can become harder to use as reasoning continues. Packing all visual evidence into the initial prompt also limits how many frames can be included. VR-Thinker addresses these issues by allowing the model to actively acquire visual evidence during reasoning.

The model combines a visual reasoning operation with a configurable visual memory window. Training proceeds through three stages: curated visual reasoning traces teach the operation format; rejection sampling retains traces with correct judgments for further fine-tuning; and Group Relative Policy Optimization strengthens reasoning. This sequence develops both the ability to use visual operations and the reasoning needed to make preference judgments.

The seven-billion-parameter model achieves 80.5% accuracy on VideoGen Reward, 82.3% on GenAI-Bench, and 75.6% on MJ-Bench-Video. The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy among open-source models on these video preference benchmarks. The results support accessing visual evidence throughout reasoning as a useful way to improve the reliability of video reward judgments.
summary.tldr: VR-Thinker actively gathers visual evidence during reasoning and achieves leading reported open-source accuracy on video preference benchmarks.

title: VR-Thinker: Boosting Video Reward Models through Think-with-Image Reasoning

abstract: Mean Field Games (MFGs) provide a principled framework for modelling interactions in large population systems. However, algorithmic progress has been limited since model-free methods are high variance and exact methods scale poorly. Recent Hybrid Structural Methods (HSMs) reduce variance while maintaining tractability by leveraging low-dimensional individual state and action spaces and known transition dynamics to compute the exact expected return conditioned on Monte Carlo rollouts of common noise. However, HSMs have not been extended to partially observable settings. We propose Recurrent Structural Policy Gradient (RSPG), the first history-aware HSM for MFGs with public partial information. RSPG achieves an order-of-magnitude faster convergence than model-free RL methods while learning history-aware behaviour, unlike current HSMs. To facilitate research into MFGs, we also introduce MFAX, our JAX-based framework for MFGs that supports both analytic and sample-based mean-field updates.
