paragraphs: Mean field games describe interactions within large populations. Learning methods face a trade-off: model-free approaches can have high variance, while exact methods can be difficult to scale. Hybrid structural methods exploit small individual state and action spaces and known transition dynamics to retain some exact computation while sampling shared randomness.

Existing hybrid methods had not handled partial observability. Recurrent Structural Policy Gradient, or RSPG, extends this approach to mean field games with public partial information. Its history-aware formulation allows behavior to depend on information accumulated over time, addressing a setting where current observations do not reveal everything relevant to a decision.

The paper reports convergence an order of magnitude faster than model-free reinforcement learning methods, while learning history-dependent behavior unavailable to the existing hybrid methods considered. It also introduces MFAX, a JAX framework supporting both analytic and sample-based mean-field updates. Together, the algorithm and framework extend structured learning to the studied partial-information setting and provide tools for investigating large-population decision problems.
summary.tldr: RSPG adds history-aware learning to hybrid structural methods for partially observable mean field games, with substantially faster reported convergence.

title: Recurrent Structural Policy Gradient for Partially Observable Mean Field Games

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a promising approach to improve correctness in LLMs, however, in many scientific problems, the objective is not necessarily to produce the correct answer, but instead to produce a diverse array of candidates which satisfy a set of constraints. We study this challenge in the context of materials generation. To this end, we introduce PLaID++, an LLM post-trained for stable and property-guided crystal generation. We find that applying naive preference optimization to a coordinate-based crystal representation leads to mode collapse. Hence, we introduce a compact, symmetry-informed Wyckoff text representation which improves computational efficiency and encourages generalization from physical priors. By encoding symmetry constraints directly into text and guiding model outputs towards desirable chemical space, PLaID++ generates structures that are thermodynamically stable, unique, and novel at a $>$50% greater rate than prior methods. We further demonstrate that unified training across conditional and unconditional tasks are mutually beneficial in data-sparse regimes. Our work demonstrates the potential of adapting post-training techniques from natural language processing to materials design, paving the way for targeted and efficient discovery of novel materials.

paragraphs: Materials generation seeks many useful candidates that satisfy constraints, rather than a single correct response. PLaID++ adapts language-model post-training to this goal for crystal structures. The authors find that straightforward preference optimization with a coordinate-based representation causes mode collapse, undermining the desired diversity of generated candidates.

They introduce a compact text representation informed by crystal symmetry through Wyckoff information. Encoding symmetry directly provides physical structure for learning, improves computational efficiency, and encourages generalization. Post-training then guides generation toward desirable chemical regions while supporting both stability-focused and property-guided design.

PLaID++ generates structures that are thermodynamically stable, unique, and novel at a rate more than 50% higher than prior methods. The authors also find that training conditional and unconditional generation together benefits both tasks when data are scarce. These findings show why representation matters in scientific post-training: the format of a candidate can help align optimization with physical constraints while preserving the diversity that discovery requires.
summary.tldr: PLaID++ combines preference-aligned post-training with symmetry-informed crystal text to improve the rate of stable, unique, and novel material generation.

title: PLaID++: A Preference Aligned Language Model for Targeted Inorganic Materials Design

abstract: Scaling test-time compute via long Chain-of-Thought unlocks remarkable gains in reasoning capabilities, yet it faces practical limits due to the linear growth of KV cache and quadratic attention complexity. In this paper, we introduce AccordionThinking, an end-to-end framework where LLMs learn to self-regulate the granularity of the reasoning steps through dynamic summarization. This mechanism enables a Fold inference mode, where the model periodically summarizes its thought process and discards former thoughts to reduce dependency on historical tokens. We apply reinforcement learning to incentivize this capability further, uncovering a critical insight: the accuracy gap between the highly efficient Fold mode and the exhaustive Unfold mode progressively narrows and eventually vanishes over the course of training. This phenomenon demonstrates that the model learns to encode essential reasoning information into compact summaries, achieving effective compression of the reasoning context. Our AccordionThinker demonstrates that with learned self-compression, LLMs can tackle complex reasoning tasks with minimal dependency token overhead without compromising solution quality, and it achieves a 3$\times$ throughput while maintaining accuracy on a 48GB GPU memory configuration, while the structured step summaries provide a human-readable account of the reasoning process.

paragraphs: Long reasoning traces give language models more room to solve difficult problems, but retaining those traces increases memory use and attention costs. AccordionThinking trains a model to control how much detail it carries forward. It periodically turns earlier reasoning into compact step summaries, allowing subsequent reasoning to depend on a shorter history.

The framework offers a Fold mode that discards previous thoughts after summarizing them, alongside an exhaustive Unfold mode. Reinforcement learning encourages summaries that preserve the information needed to continue solving the problem. During training, the reported accuracy difference between these modes gradually disappears, indicating that the model learns useful compression rather than simply shortening its output.

The resulting AccordionThinker achieves three times the throughput while maintaining accuracy in the reported 48GB GPU memory configuration. That result ties the efficiency gain to a specific deployment setting. The structured summaries also provide a readable account of the reasoning process. Together, the findings show how learned summarization can reduce the context required for reasoning while preserving solution quality in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: AccordionThinking learns to replace long reasoning histories with compact summaries, achieving threefold throughput while maintaining accuracy in the reported configuration.

title: Accordion-Thinking: Self-Regulated Step Summaries for Efficient and Readable LLM Reasoning

abstract: Recent advances in autoregressive video diffusion have enabled real-time frame streaming, however, existing methods still suffer from visual error accumulation including visual fidelity and motion degradation over long-horizon. To address these challenges, we introduce Deep Forcing, a training-free extension of autoregressive video diffusion models that stabilizes long video generation through two complementary mechanisms. Deep Sink preserves approximately half of the sliding context window as persistent sink tokens and realigns their temporal RoPE phases to the current timeline, thereby maintaining global context during extended rollouts. Participative Compression performs importance-aware KV cache pruning, retaining only tokens that actively participate in recent attention while removing redundant or degraded history, effectively mitigating error accumulation under out-of-distribution lengths. Together, these components enable over 12$\times$ length extrapolation (e.g., 5s-trained $\rightarrow$ 60s+) without sacrificing inference speed, while improving visual fidelity and motion dynamics compared to prior methods. Our results demonstrate that Deep Forcing can achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art training-based methods trained specifically for long video generation.

paragraphs: Autoregressive video diffusion can generate frames as a stream, but visual mistakes can accumulate as generation continues. Image quality and motion may deteriorate when the model produces videos much longer than those used in training. Deep Forcing addresses this problem by changing how the model retains and uses context, without additional training.

It adjusts their temporal positional phases to the current timeline so that this older context remains usable during extended generation. Participative Compression manages the stored attention information by retaining tokens that contribute to recent attention and pruning redundant or degraded history.

Together, these mechanisms support more than twelvefold length extrapolation, including extending a model trained on five-second videos to over sixty seconds. The authors report improved visual fidelity and motion without sacrificing inference speed. They also report performance comparable to leading methods trained specifically for long videos, suggesting that context preservation and selective removal can substantially improve long-duration generation.
summary.tldr: Deep Forcing extends video generation without retraining by preserving useful global context and pruning attention history that no longer helps.

title: Deep Forcing: Training-Free Long Video Generation with Deep Sink and Participative Compression

abstract: In single-cell research, tracing and analyzing high-throughput single-cell differentiation trajectories is crucial for understanding biological processes. Key to this is the robust modeling of hierarchical structures that govern cellular development. Traditional methods face limitations in computational cost, performance, and stability. VAE-based approaches have made strides but still require branch-specific network modules, limiting their scalability and stability, while often suffering from posterior collapse.To overcome these challenges, we introduce HDTree, a generative modeling framework designed for robust lineage inference. HDTree captures tree relationships within a hierarchical latent space using a unified hierarchical codebook and employs a quantized diffusion process to model continuous cell state transitions. By aligning the generative process with the Waddington landscape, this method not only improves stability and scalability but also enhances the biological plausibility of inferred lineages. HDTree’s effectiveness is demonstrated through comparisons on both general-purpose and single-cell datasets, where it outperforms existing methods in lineage inference accuracy, reconstruction quality, and hierarchical consistency. These contributions enable accurate and efficient modeling of cellular differentiation paths, offering reliable insights for biological discovery.

paragraphs: Inferring cellular lineages means reconstructing how cell states develop along branching differentiation paths. Modeling this hierarchy reliably is difficult when methods become expensive or unstable as branches multiply. HDTree addresses these issues with a generative framework that represents developmental relationships within a shared hierarchical latent space.

Its unified hierarchical codebook captures tree relationships without relying on a separate network module for each branch. A quantized diffusion process models continuous transitions between cell states. The generative process is aligned with the Waddington landscape, connecting the model's organization to the developmental picture used to describe cellular differentiation. The authors report improved stability, scalability, and biological plausibility.

These outcomes cover complementary requirements: identifying developmental paths, representing the observed data, and maintaining coherent branching relationships. The contribution is a shared generative structure that supports those requirements together, offering a more accurate and efficient way to model differentiation trajectories.
summary.tldr: HDTree combines a shared hierarchical codebook with quantized diffusion to improve the accuracy and consistency of inferred cellular lineages.

title: HDTree: Generative Modeling of Cellular Hierarchies for Robust Lineage Inference

abstract: The rapid evolution of audio deepfakes requires robust detection capable of generalizing to unseen attacks. One-class learning offers inherent robustness for this task by characterizing real speech distributions to detect anomalies. However, establishing a compact decision boundary without spoof supervision remains a fundamental challenge. Existing relaxed approaches often compromise this strictness by introducing auxiliary negative samples, which biases the boundary toward seen artifacts and degrades generalization to unseen attacks. To address this, we propose CA-SOADD, a framework that refines the acceptance region by constructing off-manifold boundary probes. Our proposed centroid-anchored tri-objective learning paradigm simultaneously enforces centroid compactness and a centroid-referenced margin against these probes, thereby explicitly tightening the acceptance region without treating them as an explicit negative class. We further extend the framework to heterogeneous settings through domain-conditioned centroids. Experiments on ASVSpoof and MLAAD benchmarks demonstrate that our strict real-only method consistently outperforms strong baselines under unseen attack types and domain shifts, with its effectiveness further validated through extensive ablation studies.

paragraphs: One-class audio deepfake detection learns the characteristics of genuine speech and rejects recordings that fall outside them. Its central difficulty is defining a sufficiently tight acceptance region without training on spoof examples. The paper argues that introducing auxiliary negatives can orient the boundary toward familiar artifacts and weaken generalization to unseen attacks.

CA-SOADD constructs off-manifold boundary probes to refine that region while retaining real-only training. Its centroid-anchored learning objective encourages genuine examples to remain compact and imposes a centroid-referenced margin against the probes. The probes help shape the boundary without being treated as an explicit negative class. Domain-conditioned centroids extend the approach to heterogeneous data settings.

Experiments on ASVSpoof and MLAAD show consistent improvements over strong baselines under unseen attack types and domain shifts, with ablations supporting the framework's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to tighten acceptance around genuine speech without relying on labeled spoof examples. This directly addresses the tension between learning a useful rejection boundary and avoiding dependence on already encountered attack artifacts.
summary.tldr: CA-SOADD uses centroid-based constraints and boundary probes to improve audio deepfake detection while training strictly on real speech.

title: Learning Tight Rejection Boundaries without Negatives for Strict One-Class Audio Deepfake Detection

abstract: The unordered nature of point cloud data poses significant challenges to conventional architectures primarily designed for structured data. Spiking neural networks (SNN), by virtue of their inherent sparsity and dynamics, are particularly well-suited for processing point clouds to effectively extract meaningful features. We propose SpikeNet, a novel spiking neural network architecture for energy-efficient and robust point cloud analysis. We introduce spiking-driven sparse attention mechanism coined the Spiking Vector Mask Transformer (SVMT). By dynamically aligning the sparsity of point cloud data through binary spiking masks, SVMT eliminates the need for softmax and multiplication operations, significantly improving computational efficiency. We also propose a Dynamic Sparse Spiking Residual (DSSR) structure and integrate it with SVMT to form the Spiking Neural Network (SpikeNet) for point cloud classification and segmentation. SpikeNet overcomes the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency in previous SNN methods, achieving collaborative optimization of performance and energy-efficiency. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that SpikeNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in shape classification and segmentation tasks, comparable to artificial neural network (ANN) based methods. Our source code is in supplementary material and will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Point clouds represent shapes through unordered collections of points, making them difficult for architectures designed around structured inputs. SpikeNet uses spiking neural networks to process this data, drawing on their sparse activity and dynamics. The goal is to support shape classification and segmentation while improving both predictive performance and energy efficiency.

Its main attention component, the Spiking Vector Mask Transformer, uses binary spiking masks to adapt attention to point-cloud sparsity. The mechanism removes the need for softmax and multiplication operations in that attention computation. A Dynamic Sparse Spiking Residual structure complements the attention module, and the two components form the complete SpikeNet architecture.

Benchmark experiments report state-of-the-art classification and segmentation performance, with results comparable to conventional artificial neural network methods. The authors describe this as joint progress on accuracy and efficiency relative to earlier spiking approaches. The architectural contribution is to make sparse spike-driven computation central to attention and residual processing, aligning the processing mechanism with the sparse character of point-cloud data.
summary.tldr: SpikeNet combines binary-mask attention and sparse spiking residual processing for accurate, energy-efficient point-cloud analysis.

abstract: Discovering additive structure is an important step towards understanding a complex multi-dimensional function because it allows the function to be expressed as the sum of lower-dimensional components. When variables interact, however, their effects are not additive and must be modeled and interpreted simultaneously. We present a new approach for the problem of interaction detection. Our method is based on comparing the performance of unrestricted and restricted prediction models, where restricted models are prevented from modeling an interaction in question. We show that an additive model-based regression ensemble, Additive Groves, can be restricted appropriately for use with this framework, and thus has the right properties for accurately detecting variable interactions.

When variables interact, however, their effects are not additive and must be modeled and interpreted simultaneously. We present a new approach for the problem of interaction detection. Our method is based on comparing the performance of unrestricted and restricted prediction models, where restricted models are prevented from modeling an interaction in question. paragraphs: A complicated function becomes easier to understand when it can be written as a sum of simpler components, each involving fewer variables. Interactions complicate that picture: some variables have joint effects that cannot be represented additively and must be modeled together. The paper focuses on detecting these statistical interactions.

Its strategy compares two prediction models. One can represent the interaction being investigated; the other is explicitly prevented from representing it. Comparing their predictive performance provides a way to assess the importance of allowing that joint effect. The key design requirement is a model family whose restrictions can target the interaction in question.

The authors show that Additive Groves, a regression ensemble based on an additive model, can be restricted in the required way. This gives the ensemble the properties needed for accurate interaction detection within their framework. The contribution connects prediction and interpretation: model comparisons are used to investigate which variables need to be understood jointly when describing a complex function.
summary.tldr: Comparing unrestricted Additive Groves with versions that forbid a particular interaction provides a framework for detecting joint variable effects.

title: Detecting statistical interactions with additive groves of trees

abstract: We address the task of actively learning a segmentation system: given a large number of unsegmented images, and access to an oracle that can segment a given image, decide which images to provide, to quickly produce a segmenter (here, a discriminative random field) that is accurate over this distribution of images. We extend the standard models for active learner to define a system for this task that first selects the image whose expected label will most reduce the uncertainty of the other unlabeled images, and thenafter greedily selects, from the pool of unsegmented images, the most informative image. The results of our experiments, over two real-world datasets (segmenting brain tumors within magnetic resonance images; and segmenting the sky in real images) show that training on very few informative images (here, as few as 2) can produce a segmenter that is as good as training on the entire dataset.

We extend the standard models for active learner to define a system for this task that first selects the image whose expected label will most reduce the uncertainty of the other unlabeled images, and thenafter greedily selects, from the pool of unsegmented images, the most informative image. The results of our experiments, over two real-world datasets (segmenting brain tumors within magnetic resonance images; and segmenting the sky in real images) show that training on very few informative images (here, as few as 2) can produce a segmenter that is as good as training on the entire dataset.

paragraphs: Training an image segmenter requires images with regions labeled, and choosing which images to annotate can affect how much supervision is needed. This paper studies active selection from a large pool of unsegmented images, assuming access to an oracle that can supply a segmentation for any selected image.

The learner trains a discriminative random field and chooses images according to their expected information value. It first selects the image whose anticipated labeling would most reduce uncertainty about the remaining unlabeled images. It then continues with greedy selection of the most informative image from the pool. The selection process is aimed at accuracy over the image distribution.

Experiments cover brain tumor segmentation in magnetic resonance images and sky segmentation in ordinary images. In these evaluations, training on very few informative images, in some cases as few as two, can match training on the entire dataset. This is an empirical finding for the studied settings. It illustrates how carefully chosen annotations can supply much of the useful supervision contained in a larger labeled collection.
summary.tldr: Active image selection sometimes matched full-dataset segmentation training with as few as two annotated images in the reported experiments.

title: Learning to segment from a few well-selected training images

abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are very powerful sequence models that do not enjoy widespread use because it is extremely difficult to train them properly. Fortunately, recent advances in Hessian-free optimization have been able to overcome the difficulties associated with training RNNs, making it possible to apply them successfully to challenging sequence problems. In this paper we demonstrate the power of RNNs trained with the new Hessian-Free optimizer (HF) by applying them to character-level language modeling tasks. The standard RNN architecture, while effective, is not ideally suited for such tasks, so we introduce a new RNN variant that uses multiplicative (or ``gated'') connections which allow the current input character to determine the transition matrix from one hidden state vector to the next. After training the multiplicative RNN with the HF optimizer for five days on 8 high-end Graphics Processing Units, we were able to surpass the performance of the best previous single method for character-level language modeling -- a hierarchical non-parametric sequence model. To our knowledge this represents the largest recurrent neural network application to date.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can model sequences, but training them effectively is difficult. This paper uses advances in Hessian-free optimization to apply them to character-level language modeling. The task provides a concrete test of whether improved optimization can make these powerful sequence models useful on challenging data.

The authors also modify the network architecture. Their multiplicative recurrent network uses gated connections so that the current input character determines the transition matrix between successive hidden states. This gives the incoming character a direct role in selecting how the network's internal state changes, addressing the authors' concern that a standard recurrent architecture is not ideally suited to the task.

After five days of training on eight high-end GPUs, the model outperforms the best previous single method identified in the abstract, a hierarchical non-parametric sequence model. The authors also describe it, to their knowledge, as the largest recurrent-network application at that time. The reported result combines an architectural change with an optimizer capable of training it effectively at substantial scale.
summary.tldr: A multiplicative recurrent network trained with Hessian-free optimization surpasses the previous best single method for character-level language modeling.

title: Generating Text with Recurrent Neural Networks
